Mara Venn, 38, Media Preservation Archivist at the Allegheny Regional Archive, distrusts nostalgia as sanitized distortion. Her father Elias died after dementia and alcohol dependence, obsessed with a nonexistent daughter, Ruth: chipped tooth, fear of storms, attic sleeping place, and being taken by “the wrong family.” He bought duplicate yellow raincoats, searched for Ruth, wrote her name compulsively, and once said Mara had promised to watch her. Records confirm Mara was an only child. Mara viewed Ruth as grief without an object, though the fixation remains troubling.

At a failing thrift shop, Mara bought a swollen, mold-clouded VHS for three dollars. Its crooked label reads **HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97**, with the final “7” retraced. The shell is bowed, marked by a rust-colored line near a screw and an apparently fresh greasy thumbprint. Its provenance is unstable: the shopkeeper variously mentioned a cardboard box, the Voss house, a church, or a Miller Road cleanout, then claimed to remember only “three dollars.” He became unsettled under questioning, later could not recall whether he had left the shop door unlocked, and the tape’s former space beneath a crate was inexplicably empty. The label and origin resist reliable recollection.

Mara logged it as unverified-origin media with suspected exterior contamination and sealed it in a gasketed isolation cabinet with a dehumidifier, intending to inspect it without playback. The archive rule is **DO NOT PLAY UNCATALOGED MEDIA.** While thinking about Elias’s Ruth memories, Mara briefly imagined the tape showing a chipped-tooth child, recognized this as an intrusive thought rather than memory, and felt chest pressure. She also rediscovered an unsent, returned letter to Elias—“I know you missed her”—whose paper felt inexplicably warm. The sealed tape has made at least one faint mechanical click.

Daniel Reyes, 26, born in 1994 and a temporary employee of three weeks, is curious about obsolete technology and eager to prove equipment works. He brought a repaired Panasonic television/VCR to the workbench, despite Mara’s instruction not to handle the cassette. At 8:21 the next morning, with Mara away at the loading dock, he removed the tape from isolation and played it. The VCR was temperamental, and he viewed roughly ten minutes, rewinding once; playback then failed with an error code.

The footage showed a yellow-sided house with white porch rails, green door, browned lawn, blue plastic pool, sprinkler, and a woman in a red bathing suit. Two children ran through the water. Daniel immediately identified the older boy as himself and the girl as his sister Lily, though his personnel file and known history identify him as an only child. The girl had a chipped front tooth. The tape triggered vivid, emotionally certain memories not previously present or verifiable: Lily’s tooth being damaged while eating an apple; a blue envelope beneath the sugar jar; a basement window with a lightning-bolt crack; a concrete basement, rusted furnace, canned peaches, and fuse box; a dog named Pickle with one white paw and a scar over its eye; a yellow-linoleum kitchen, burn mark, pantry floorboard, refrigerator drawing beneath a lemon magnet, upstairs bedrooms, and family routines.

Daniel also recalled Lily fearing the basement window, sleeping with the closet light on, hating peas, and being present in his childhood. He remembered Pickle’s death after a summer storm and burying the dog with a spoon. He heard or supplied a lullaby from “Elena,” his mother: “Go to sleep, little river stone / the moon has a house of its own—.” His established memories of Elena and growing up in Newark/New Jersey (apartment, radiator, rice, St. Vincent’s night work, Lincoln Elementary, broken wrist) conflicted with the yellow-house memories. He could not provide dates, hospital names, photographs, or other verifiable evidence for Lily. The tape’s memories felt “returned,” physically sensory, and as authoritative as real pain.

The footage often showed only partial or static images while inducing details not visible on-screen. It showed a basement window, a blurred dog-like shape, an open house door, and finally a small dirty hand waving. Daniel heard water, dog tags, and laughter; at one point he thought he saw Lily behind the window. The cassette became warm after ejection. Daniel laughed and nearly sobbed when he recognized “Pickle.” The tape appears capable of implanting alternate-childhood memories in people born after 1990, potentially with individualized family members and histories.

Mara returned to find Daniel holding the cassette and the television displaying static. He initially said he had “got it working,” then described the yellow house, woman, two children, and identified himself and Lily. Mara asked whether he had ever had a sister named Lily, whether he had photographs, and about his mother Elena. Daniel insisted the records were wrong or incomplete and became angry when Mara distinguished “actual” memories from tape-induced ones. He said Lily was still at the house and demanded to watch the rest. Mara recognized the danger, sealed the cassette in a clear evidence bag with gloves, marked the time, forbade further playback, and planned to contact the director. She did not yet establish full containment or medical procedures.

Daniel briefly grabbed Mara’s wrist when she tried to secure the cassette, warning that she would “erase” Lily. After sealing, the room felt emptier. He continued repeating that Lily was his sister. Beneath the television’s static, a child laughed; both noticed it. Daniel then saw—or believed he saw—a small wet handprint slide down the corridor door’s glass, leaving no mark. Mara’s expression became distant and guarded, suggesting the imagery or Daniel’s account may be affecting her despite no confirmed playback.

Current unresolved threads: the tape’s origin, anomalous label/provenance and apparent displacement; the relationship between Elias’s Ruth delusions and the tape’s chipped-tooth sibling imagery; whether the anomaly creates alternate biographies, retrieves suppressed memories, or targets existing grief; Daniel’s implanted Lily/Pickle/yellow-house memories and possible ongoing contamination from handling or playback; whether Mara has been exposed cognitively through proximity or observation; the tape’s unseen remainder and possible effects of repeated playback; Daniel’s condition and containment; and the archive’s forthcoming response, including formal procedures, breach documentation, subject testimony, and the moral question of whether to suppress, destroy, study, or preserve the recording.

chapters.name: Lily
chapters.content:
## Lily

Daniel had not slept.

At eleven the next morning he was still wearing the clothes from the day before: gray archive polo, black jeans, one shoelace untied. He sat at the workbench beside the evidence bag, watching the cassette as if it might speak.

The television had been unplugged and moved across the room. Mara had coiled the power cord twice around it. None of that mattered. Daniel had handled the tape. He had watched it. Whatever had happened was already inside him, if inside was the right word.

“I need to call your mother,” Mara said.

Daniel looked up. His eyes were bloodshot, but his face held an exhausted happiness. It was private and oddly tender, as if someone stood just beyond Mara’s shoulder.

“She’ll know,” he said.

“About Lily?”

“About everything.”

Mara opened his personnel file, though she knew the details by heart. Daniel Reyes, born March 14, 1994, Newark, New Jersey. Emergency contact: Elena Reyes, mother. No siblings listed.

“Your mother lives in New Jersey?”

“Piscataway now. She moved after the house.”

“What house?”

He gave her an impatient look. “The yellow one.”

A wet handprint marked the corridor glass behind him. Mara had wiped it away earlier and checked both sides. The glass was dry. Daniel had watched without comment.

Now he reached toward the evidence bag. Mara put her hand over it.

“No.”

“I’m not going to play it.”

“You’re not going to touch it.”

“It’s sealed.”

“That doesn’t make it safe.”

He looked at the cassette. “It’s not dangerous.”

“What did you see after the footage ended?”

“It didn’t end. The VCR stopped.”

“There may not be anything else.”

“There’s more on it.”

Mara kept her hand on the bag. “Tell me about Lily.”

Daniel’s face softened.

“She was eleven months younger than me. People thought we were twins because she was tall. She stood on the bottom stair and refused to come down until someone promised not to look at her. She said the stairs made her legs feel backward.”

“When did that happen?”

“Which time?”

He laughed. The sound carried unmistakable affection, the warmth of an old private joke.

“She was afraid of the basement window,” he continued. “There was a crack shaped like lightning. She thought something had struck the glass from the other side.”

“What was outside?”

“Trees. A fence. Mr. Voss’s shed. He had white hair in his ears and kept his riding mower in the garage when it rained.”

The details came without effort. He did not construct them. They surfaced complete.

“Did you have swimming lessons?”

“At the community pool. Lily hated the water at first. She said chlorine made her teeth taste like pennies. Mom sat on the bleachers in her red suit. She had a striped cover-up, but she wouldn’t wear it because she said it made her look like a wrapped sandwich.”

Mara glanced at the clock. The fluorescent tubes hummed overhead.

“What did your mother sing during storms?”

Daniel’s expression changed.

“The river song.”

“Can you sing it?”

He hesitated, embarrassed, then sang softly:

“Go to sleep, little river stone,  
the moon has a house of its own.  
Lie in the dark where the cool reeds grow,  
dream of the places the tide won’t know.”

He stopped.

“What comes next?”

“I don’t know.”

“Try.”

“I said I don’t know.”

His anger was sudden. Mara lifted her hands.

“Okay.”

He rubbed his palms against his jeans. “Lily hated thunderstorms.”

“You said she was afraid of the basement window.”

“And storms.”

“Were you afraid?”

“No. I pretended not to be.”

“Why?”

“She’d come into my room with her blanket around her shoulders. If I said I was scared too, she’d cry. So I told her storms were just the sky moving furniture.”

“Who told you that?”

“Dad. Then Lily said the sky was rearranging furniture because it was bored with the old layout.”

Daniel laughed again, but his hands had begun to tremble.

Mara pushed a cup of water toward him. “Tell me about the dog.”

“Pickle?”

“Yes.”

“Brown mutt. White paw, scar over the left eye. He belonged to Lily, though he liked me better.” His smile faltered. “He got out during a storm. We found him near the drainage ditch.”

“When?”

“Summer. The same summer.”

“What year?”

He hesitated. “Ninety-seven.”

“You were three.”

“I know how old I was.”

“Swimming lessons, a dog’s death—”

“I remember.”

“Do you remember being three?”

His jaw tightened. “I remember being me.”

He stood and paced between the workbench and the shelves.

“There was a birthday party,” he said. “Lily got a ceramic plate with blue flowers. It was cracked through the middle, but Mom said we could use it if we didn’t put anything hot on it. We ate cake from it because she wanted the biggest piece.”

“Whose birthday?”

“Mine.”

“How old were you?”

“Seven.”

The answer seemed to catch him. Mara waited.

“The tape is labeled Summer ’97,” she said.

“That doesn’t mean the party was in ’97.”

“Then when?”

“I know what year it was.”

“You were born in 1994.”

“I know.”

“The memories can’t all belong to the same summer.”

Daniel turned on her. “Why are you doing this?”

“I’m trying to establish what you remember.”

“You’re trying to prove it didn’t happen.”

“I’m trying to distinguish what happened from what feels as though it happened.”

“To whom?”

“To you.”

“It happened to me.”

The silence that followed was broken by a truck passing outside, tires hissing on wet pavement.

“She had a chipped tooth,” Daniel said.

“I know.”

“From an apple. She bit down on a seed. Mom said it was nothing, but Lily kept touching it with her tongue. She said the apple wanted the tooth back.”

Mara had not told him about the tooth. He had seen it in the footage, though only for an instant. The girl’s face had been blurred by tracking distortion, but the white chip had shown clearly.

“Where is she now?” Daniel asked.

Mara said nothing.

“Lily.”

“I don’t know.”

“She’s at the house.”

“There is no house.”

His face emptied. The hurt that crossed it was disproportionate, immediate, and utterly sincere.

“You’ve never seen it,” he said.

“No.”

“You don’t know.”

“I know where you were raised. I know where your mother lives. I know where you went to school.”

“That’s paperwork.”

“Paperwork is evidence.”

“It’s not evidence against her.”

Mara pulled the public records database up on the terminal. Daniel stood across from her, watching.

His birth certificate listed Elena Reyes as his mother and no second child. Newark records showed one Reyes birth in 1994. St. Vincent’s had no infant death under the family name. She searched property records for Elena and Roberto Reyes. There was no yellow house, no address matching the description.

Daniel’s breathing became shallow.

“Maybe the name changed,” he said.

“Whose?”

“The house. The family.”

“Why?”

He looked at the screen. “Because she was taken.”

“By whom?”

“The wrong family.”

The phrase struck Mara with the force of recognition. Her father had used it for years.

She opened the emergency contact record. Elena Reyes, fifty-eight, respiratory therapist at St. Vincent’s Medical Center. The same hospital Daniel had identified as part of his real childhood.

Mara called.

The phone rang six times.

“Hello?”

The voice was older, tired, and wary.

“Mrs. Reyes? My name is Mara Venn. I work with Daniel at the Allegheny Regional Archive.”

“What happened?”

“He’s safe. There was an incident involving a piece of media he handled.”

“Is he hurt?”

“No.”

Daniel had moved beside her. “Put me on.”

Mara covered the receiver. “Stay calm.”

“I am calm.”

He took the phone.

“Mom?”

He listened. His face brightened, then tightened.

“No, I’m okay. I found something.”

Another pause.

“Do you remember the yellow house?”

His eyes fixed on Mara.

“Do you remember Lily?”

He listened again, then mouthed, *She knows.*

“You do remember her.”

Mara heard Elena’s voice faintly through the receiver. The words were indistinct, but the tone was unmistakably panicked.

“Mom, you sang it. The river song. You sang it when the storms came.”

He turned away.

“Don’t say that.”

His voice had become young.

“Don’t say she was never there.”

A longer silence.

“She was my sister,” he said. “You can’t just decide she wasn’t.”

The phone slipped from his hand and struck the floor. Elena had disconnected.

For several seconds he stood motionless.

Mara retrieved the phone. “I’m sorry.”

“She’s scared.”

“Of what?”

“Of losing her.”

“Lily?”

He nodded.

“Did she say Lily’s name?”

“No.” His voice was low. “She said there was no one by that name.”

Mara checked Daniel’s school and medical records. They confirmed his upbringing in Newark: Lincoln Elementary, a broken wrist at age nine, an apartment near a radiator, Elena’s night work. There was no yellow house, no sister, no dog named Pickle.

Daniel watched the records appear.

“Maybe they’re wrong.”

“Every record?”

“Maybe Mom had a reason.”

“Your mother has a documented history. You grew up in an apartment.”

“I know where I grew up.”

“Then say it.”

He looked at her.

“Say what you know.”

“The apartment. The radiator. Mom coming home smelling like bleach and coffee. Lincoln Elementary. Breaking my wrist.” He touched his left wrist. “Rice for dinner when money was tight.”

“Good.”

“But it was flat.”

“What was flat?”

“My real childhood. It was like reading about someone else.”

“And now?”

“Now it has weather.”

The phrase stayed with Mara.

Daniel sank into the chair. His eyes moved to the evidence bag.

“I know the apartment was real,” he said. “I know Mom worked nights. I know she took care of me. But I can feel Lily’s hand on my shoulder when the thunder started.”

Mara sat opposite him.

“Tell me.”

“She’d stand behind me in the hallway. She was always taller than me, even though she was younger. She’d say, ‘Don’t look at the window.’ I’d say, ‘I’m not.’ And she’d say, ‘You are.’”

“What did she look like?”

“Brown hair, lighter in summer. A cowlick here.” He touched the left side of his forehead. “Gray eyes, except they looked green when she was sick. The chipped tooth.”

“What did she look like when she was sick?”

“Pale. Sweaty. Knees pulled up. Mom put a washcloth on her neck, and Lily hated it because it smelled like the basement.”

“What did the basement smell like?”

“Damp concrete. Rust. Canned peaches.”

Mara entered the words into the incident field, then deleted them.

Daniel saw.

“Why?”

“I don’t know whether writing these things down is safe.”

“Safe for who?”

“Everyone.”

“She isn’t dangerous.”

“I’m not talking about Lily.”

He covered his face. When he spoke, his voice was muffled.

“She was there.”

Mara had watched families grieve over objects recovered from ruined houses: a fused photograph, a child’s shoe, a wedding dress browned by floodwater. She had always believed grief required an object, even if the object was only a body or a grave.

Her father had grieved Ruth without either.

Now Daniel was grieving a girl he had never met.

That was the horror—not simply that he believed in Lily, but that the belief had given him a history complete enough to lose.

Mara reached across the table, stopping before she touched him.

“I’m here,” she said.

Daniel lifted his face.

“Can you help me find her?”

Mara looked at the sealed cassette, its warped label and retraced final digit.

“I don’t know,” she said.

It was not the answer he wanted. It was the only one she could give.

Daniel nodded as though she had promised something.

Behind them, from the unplugged television, came a faint sound like water moving through pipes.

Then, very softly, a child laughed.
chapters.summary:
Mara Venn, 38, Media Preservation Archivist at the Allegheny Regional Archive, distrusts nostalgia as sanitized distortion. Her father Elias died after dementia and alcohol dependence, obsessed with a nonexistent daughter, Ruth: chipped tooth, storm phobia, attic sleeping place, and being taken by “the wrong family.” He bought duplicate yellow raincoats, searched for Ruth, wrote her name compulsively, and once said Mara had promised to watch her. Records confirm Mara was an only child. Mara regarded Ruth as grief without an object, but the fixation remains troubling.

At a failing thrift shop, Mara bought a swollen, mold-clouded VHS for three dollars. Its crooked label reads **HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97**, with the final “7” retraced. The bowed shell bears a rust-colored line near a screw and an apparently fresh greasy thumbprint. Its provenance is unstable: the shopkeeper variously cited a cardboard box, the Voss house, a church, or a Miller Road cleanout, then remembered only “three dollars.” He became unsettled, forgot whether he had left the shop door unlocked, and the tape’s former space beneath a crate was inexplicably empty. The label and origin resist reliable recollection.

Mara logged it as unverified-origin media with suspected exterior contamination and sealed it in a gasketed isolation cabinet with a dehumidifier, intending inspection without playback. Archive rule: **DO NOT PLAY UNCATALOGED MEDIA.** While thinking of Elias’s Ruth memories, Mara briefly imagined the tape showing a chipped-tooth child, recognized this as an intrusive thought rather than memory, and felt chest pressure. She also rediscovered an unsent, returned letter to Elias—“I know you missed her”—whose paper felt inexplicably warm. The sealed tape has made at least one faint mechanical click.

Daniel Reyes, 26, born in 1994 and a temporary employee of three weeks, is curious about obsolete technology and eager to prove equipment works. He brought a repaired Panasonic television/VCR to the workbench despite Mara’s instructions. At 8:21 the next morning, while Mara was at the loading dock, he removed the tape and played roughly ten minutes, rewinding once before playback failed with an error code.

The footage showed a yellow-sided house with white porch rails, green door, browned lawn, blue plastic pool, sprinkler, and a woman in a red bathing suit. Two children ran through the water. Daniel immediately identified the older boy as himself and the girl as his sister Lily, though his personnel file and known history identify him as an only child. The girl had a chipped front tooth. The tape implanted vivid, emotionally certain memories that conflict with Daniel’s documented childhood: Lily’s tooth damaged by an apple seed; a blue envelope beneath the sugar jar; a basement window with a lightning-shaped crack; concrete basement, rusted furnace, canned peaches, fuse box; yellow-linoleum kitchen, burn mark, pantry floorboard, refrigerator drawing beneath a lemon magnet; upstairs bedrooms and family routines; and a dog named Pickle, brown with one white paw and a scar over its left eye.

Daniel remembers Lily as eleven months younger, tall enough to be mistaken for his twin, with brown hair, a summer cowlick, gray/green eyes, and a chipped tooth. She feared the basement window and thunderstorms, slept with the closet light on, hated peas and chlorine, and sometimes stood behind Daniel in the hallway during storms, warning him not to look at the window. Their mother wore a red bathing suit at the community pool and a striped cover-up she disliked. Lily once refused to descend the stairs because they made her legs feel backward. Daniel remembers Lily’s ceramic blue-flowered birthday plate cracked through the middle, her wanting the largest piece of cake, and her saying an apple wanted her tooth back.

He remembers Pickle’s death after escaping during a storm and being found near a drainage ditch; Daniel buried the dog with a spoon. He associates these events with “the same summer,” sometimes saying 1997, despite being born in 1994, and also recalls being seven at a birthday party. He cannot reconcile the tape’s date with the implanted chronology. The footage showed only partial/static images while inducing details not visible on-screen: a basement window, blurred dog-like shape, open house door, and a small dirty hand waving. Daniel heard water, dog tags, and laughter, and thought he saw Lily behind the window. The cassette became warm after ejection.

Daniel also recalls a lullaby sung by his mother Elena during storms:

“Go to sleep, little river stone,  
the moon has a house of its own.  
Lie in the dark where the cool reeds grow,  
dream of the places the tide won’t know.”

He cannot supply the rest. His established memories remain intact but feel emotionally flat beside the implanted history: growing up as Elena’s only child in a Newark apartment near a radiator; Elena working night shifts; rice dinners when money was tight; Lincoln Elementary; and breaking his wrist at age nine. Daniel describes the documented childhood as “like reading about someone else,” while the false one “has weather.” He can nonetheless affirm both sets of memories and physically feels Lily’s hand on his shoulder during thunder.

After playback, Mara found Daniel holding the cassette and the television displaying static. He initially claimed he had “got it working,” then demanded to watch the rest because Lily was still at the house. Mara sealed the cassette in a clear evidence bag with gloves, marked the time, forbade further playback, and planned to contact the director. Daniel briefly grabbed Mara’s wrist, warning that she would “erase” Lily. Beneath the television’s static, a child laughed; both heard it. Daniel then saw—or believed he saw—a small wet handprint slide down the corridor door’s glass, leaving no mark. Mara’s expression became distant and guarded, suggesting possible influence through proximity, observation, or Daniel’s testimony, though she has not confirmed playback exposure.

The following day Daniel had not slept. He remained at the workbench in his archive clothes, watching the evidence bag with exhausted, private happiness, as if Lily stood just beyond Mara. Mara had unplugged and moved the television and coiled its cord, but Daniel insisted the tape was not dangerous and that it contained more. A wet handprint again appeared on the corridor glass despite Mara having wiped and checked it; it left no residue.

Mara questioned Daniel extensively and documented his testimony. He insisted Lily was real and became angry when Mara distinguished factual evidence from memories that merely felt factual. He said Lily might have been “taken,” using the phrase “the wrong family,” which directly echoes Elias’s language about Ruth. He claimed the yellow house or family may have changed names. Public records and property searches found no yellow house, no matching address, no second Reyes birth, no infant death under the family name, and no evidence of Lily or Pickle. Daniel’s records consistently support his Newark apartment childhood and only-child status.

Mara called Daniel’s mother, Elena Reyes, 58, now living in Piscataway and working as a respiratory therapist at St. Vincent’s Medical Center—the same hospital associated with Daniel’s documented childhood. Elena answered anxiously, asking whether Daniel was hurt. Daniel took the phone and asked whether she remembered the yellow house, Lily, and the river song. Her tone became panicked. Daniel said, “She knows,” and insisted that Elena had sung the song during storms. Elena denied Lily’s existence and disconnected. Daniel interpreted her fear as fear of losing Lily, then said she was scared. He remained convinced Lily had been his sister, despite Elena’s denial.

Mara recognizes the central horror as Daniel’s grief for a person he has never verifiably encountered: the anomaly has supplied not merely belief but a history complete enough to lose. Daniel asks Mara to help find Lily. Mara cannot promise this, but says she does not know; Daniel accepts the answer as if it were a promise. From the unplugged television comes a faint sound like water moving through pipes, followed by a child’s soft laughter.

Current anomaly assessment: the tape appears capable of implanting alternate-childhood memories in people born after 1990, potentially generating individualized relatives, houses, pets, family routines, and emotional histories rather than replaying objective footage. It may create alternate biographies, retrieve suppressed memories, or target existing grief. It can induce sensory details beyond visible footage and may have effects through handling, proximity, observation, or discussion. The significance of the repeated chipped-tooth girl, “wrong family” language, and overlap with Elias’s Ruth obsession is unresolved.

Current unresolved threads: the tape’s origin and provenance instability; the anomalous label, retraced “7,” greasy print, warmth, clicks, and possible displacement; the unseen remainder of the recording and consequences of repeated playback; Daniel’s ongoing contamination, sleep deprivation, fixation, and physical/emotional safety; whether Elena has been affected or is concealing something; whether Mara is becoming exposed through proximity or testimony; the meaning and reality-status of Lily, Pickle, the yellow house, the wet handprint, water sounds, and child laughter; and the archive’s forthcoming response, including formal containment procedures, medical/psychological monitoring, breach documentation, subject testimonies, and the moral question of whether to suppress, destroy, study, or preserve the recording.

chapters.name: The Photograph
chapters.content:
Elena answered on the fourth ring.

Her face appeared in the archive’s borrowed monitor, flattened by the poor connection. Behind her was a kitchen Mara did not recognize at first: pale cabinets, a refrigerator crowded with magnets, a framed lighthouse.

She glanced at Mara, then at Daniel.

“Is he hurt?”

“No,” Mara said. “Not physically.”

Daniel sat beside her at the worktable, still wearing yesterday’s clothes. He had slept for less than an hour and refused to leave the evidence bag unattended. The cassette lay inside it beneath an opaque sheet of plastic.

“Mom,” he said.

His voice softened when he said it. For a moment he sounded like a boy calling from the bottom of a staircase.

Elena’s mouth tightened. “What happened?”

“I need to ask you something.”

“Daniel, if this is about the police—”

“It’s not.” He looked at Mara. “Tell her.”

Mara kept her hands folded. “Daniel viewed an unverified recording at the archive. Since then he’s reported memories that conflict with his documented history. He remembers a house, a dog, and a sister named Lily.”

Elena did not move.

“No,” she said.

Daniel swallowed. “You know what I’m talking about.”

“No.”

“The yellow house.”

“No.”

“Lily.”

Elena’s gaze dropped below the camera. Her fingers tightened around the device.

“You were an only child,” she said.

“I know what my records say.”

“You were an only child.”

“Was she younger than me?”

“Daniel—”

“Eleven months. Her tooth was chipped because she bit an apple seed. You told her it was foolish to blame the apple, but you let her put it under her pillow anyway.”

Elena’s face went slack.

Mara had heard the details before, but they seemed different spoken into Elena’s kitchen. The memories had crossed a distance and entered the family.

“Mom,” Daniel said more quietly. “Did we have a dog?”

“No.”

“Pickle.”

“No.”

“He died during a storm. I buried him near a drainage ditch.”

Elena stood so quickly the image lurched toward the ceiling.

“Stop,” she said.

“Why are you scared?”

“I’m not scared.”

“You are.”

“Daniel, you need to come home.”

Mara reached for the keyboard. Daniel caught her wrist.

“Don’t,” he whispered. “She has to tell me.”

Mara unmuted the microphone. “Mrs. Reyes, did Daniel ever mention Lily before yesterday?”

“No.”

“Did anyone in your family have a child named Lily?”

Elena looked directly into the camera. Her eyes were wet.

“Is she still there?” she asked.

The room seemed to contract around the words.

Daniel released Mara’s wrist. “What?”

Elena appeared to hear herself only then. Terror replaced confusion.

“Is Lily still there?” she repeated.

“Where?” Daniel asked.

“In the house.”

“What house?”

The connection gave a thin electronic chirp.

“Elena,” Mara said. “What house?”

Elena shook her head. “I don’t know you.”

“You called me by name.”

“I don’t know you.”

“Mom—”

“Don’t bring her home.”

The call ended.

The monitor went black, reflecting Mara, Daniel, and the evidence bag on the table. Condensation had formed inside the plastic around the cassette. A bead of water slid toward one corner.

Daniel stared at the dead screen.

“She remembers,” he said.

“I heard her.”

“She remembers the house.”

“She asked if Lily was still there.”

“That means she knows where she is.”

“Or it means she was frightened and confused.”

Daniel turned toward her. “You heard her.”

Mara wanted to tell him there was no Lily, no house, no dog. The words had once seemed sufficient. Now Elena had denied Lily with the conviction of someone defending herself from a known danger, then asked whether Lily was still there.

Mara thought of her father watching the road for Ruth. She had called his grief an illness because the alternative was admitting she did not know what had happened to him.

“Your apartment is ten minutes away,” she said. “I’m coming with you.”

Daniel’s relief was immediate and painful.

They left through the side entrance. Mara locked the archive, checked the lock twice, and checked the cabinet where the tape had been stored. It was empty; she had moved the cassette to a gasketed evidence container before the call. As she reached the car, she heard a child laughing somewhere inside the building.

The sound stopped when she turned the key.

Daniel lived above a shuttered barber shop in Bloomfield. The building’s brick façade had been painted brown-red, blistering around the windows. He fumbled with his keys.

“I don’t remember it looking like this,” he said.

“Your apartment?”

“The whole building.”

“You’ve lived here for two years.”

“I know.”

Inside, the apartment smelled of dust, coffee grounds, and citrus detergent. Dishes filled the sink. A jacket hung over a chair. On the refrigerator, a lemon-shaped magnet held a takeout menu.

Daniel stopped.

“The lemon.”

“What about it?”

“It was on our refrigerator.”

“Lots of people have lemon magnets.”

“Ours had a drawing underneath it.”

“What kind of drawing?”

“A house. Lily drew the windows too large.”

He crossed the kitchen and opened the refrigerator. The magnet remained in place. Beneath it was a pale rectangle where paper had once been attached, the paint cleaner than the surrounding surface.

Daniel inhaled sharply.

Mara took down the magnet. A faint pencil line showed on the door. It might have been a scratch, or the beginning of a square.

“Did you put something here?” she asked.

“No.”

“Did Lily?”

“She drew the chimney crooked.”

“The line doesn’t show a chimney.”

“It used to.”

Mara replaced the magnet.

Daniel went into the living room. Above his desk hung a framed photograph Mara recognized from his personnel file: Daniel at eighteen outside a brick building in winter, one hand lifted against the glare.

He removed it from the wall.

“This.”

He turned the frame over. “I took this in college.”

“Yes.”

“Why is it here?”

“Because it’s your photograph.”

“No.”

He held it toward her.

The photograph had changed.

The brick building was gone. In its place stood the yellow-sided house, white porch rails bright beneath a summer sky. Two children stood in the browned grass beside the blue plastic pool. The older boy was thin, dark-haired, and squinting at the camera. The girl wore a green swimsuit and held a red cup. Her front tooth was chipped.

The boy was Daniel.

For several seconds neither spoke.

“I told you,” he said.

Mara leaned close without touching the glass. Along the bottom edge, in faded blue ink, someone had written:

DANNY & LILY — JULY 1997

“Did you alter this?” she asked.

His face hardened. “You think I printed it and put it in the frame?”

“I think something altered it.”

“The photograph knows her name?”

Mara put on gloves and removed the frame’s backing. The photograph was held by four bent metal tabs. Beneath it lay a second image.

She slid it out.

The original showed Daniel outside the brick building.

Both images were the same size. The newer-looking one had no adhesive residue, torn edges, or sign of replacement. Nothing explained how one had become the other.

Daniel came close enough for his shoulder to touch hers.

“That’s Lily.”

“I know what you call her.”

“She’s not a name.”

“Daniel.”

“She’s right there.”

Mara placed the altered photograph on archival paper. “When did you last see the original?”

“This morning.”

“Before you came to the archive?”

“No. I left it here.”

“Did anyone else have access?”

“My landlord has a key.”

“Could he have—”

“No.”

“Could you have seen the image differently because of exposure?”

He stared at her.

Mara heard how the question sounded. Not whether the photograph had changed, but whether Daniel’s mind had changed around it.

“Sorry,” she said.

“Don’t be.”

He took the picture from the table and held it against his chest.

“I remember this day,” he said. “We were waiting for Mom to come out of the house. Lily had cut her foot in the grass. She wouldn’t cry because she thought I’d tell.”

“There’s no blood in the image.”

“It was before the picture.”

“Who took it?”

“Dad.”

“You told me your father died when you were six.”

“Not ours.”

“Daniel.”

He looked down. “I don’t know.”

That answer sounded real.

He set the photograph on the desk and opened drawers. Receipts, pens, batteries, a dead charger. In the bottom drawer he found a shoebox marked TAXES and emptied it onto the floor.

“What are you looking for?” Mara asked.

“I don’t know.”

A birthday card slid from beneath the papers.

It was white with a blue border. On the front, a cartoon cake bore seven candles. Across it, in purple letters:

HAPPY BIRTHDAY, TWINS!

Daniel picked it up.

The envelope was addressed in block letters:

DANNY AND LILY REYES  
YELLOW HOUSE  
MILLER ROAD

There was no stamp. The flap had been opened and resealed with clear tape.

Mara crouched beside him. “Where did this come from?”

“I’ve never seen it.”

“Is that your handwriting?”

“No.”

Inside, in blue ink, was one sentence:

TO THE TWO OF YOU—DON’T FIGHT OVER THE CORNER PIECE THIS YEAR.

Daniel’s breathing grew shallow.

“The cake,” he said. “Lily always wanted the corner because it had more icing. She said the middle pieces were lonely.”

He touched the writing with one gloved finger.

“Who sent it?”

“I don’t know.”

The paper smelled faintly of wet cardboard.

Mara took an evidence camera from her bag, photographed the card, and stopped. The camera was offline, the file secured, the procedure adequate. Yet adequacy had begun to feel like superstition. The photograph on the wall had changed without assistance, and the card had appeared among Daniel’s tax documents in a locked apartment.

She opened her notebook and wrote the date. The final digit looked retraced.

Daniel read the card again.

“Put it down,” Mara said.

He did, but reluctantly.

Mara examined the envelope. The address had no number, town, or state. Miller Road existed in several Pennsylvania counties. None of the properties she had searched contained a yellow house matching Daniel’s description.

The altered photograph remained on the desk between them.

“What happens if we show this to your mother?” she asked.

“She’ll say it isn’t real.”

“She might.”

“She asked if Lily was still there.”

“Yes.”

“Then she knows.”

“Or the anomaly made her ask.”

“That’s the same thing.”

“No. It isn’t.”

He looked at her as if she had failed him.

Mara removed the photograph from its frame and sealed it in a transparent sleeve. The two children seemed to shift when she looked away and back. The girl’s eyes were gray-green; her hair had a summer cowlick. The chipped tooth was small enough to miss unless one knew to search for it.

Mara knew that face.

Not from Daniel’s descriptions. From somewhere older: a hallway, a child’s hand in hers, a chipped tooth, her father calling from another room.

The impression vanished, leaving the clean, hollow pain of a tooth pulled from the wrong mouth.

She pressed her fingers to the table.

Daniel noticed. “What?”

“Nothing.”

“You remember her.”

“No.”

“You do.”

“I remember being frightened.”

“Of what?”

Mara looked at the girl in the photograph. “I don’t know.”

The house behind the children had a green door. Its porch sagged slightly on the left. Beneath the steps was a dark rectangle, possibly a basement window.

Mara closed the sleeve.

“We’re taking these back to the archive.”

Daniel reached for the photograph.

“No.”

“It’s mine.”

“It was taken from your apartment by something we don’t understand.”

“You mean from my life.”

“I mean it may be evidence.”

His face twisted. “Everything is evidence to you.”

“That’s my job.”

“And what am I?”

The question hung between them.

Mara thought of the cassette, the handprint that left no residue, and Elena asking if Lily was still there. She thought of her father’s duplicate yellow raincoats, bought for a child who had never needed one.

“You’re a person,” she said.

Daniel laughed once. “Then help me find my sister.”

Mara looked at the photograph.

The girl’s hand had moved.

It no longer held the red cup. It rested against the boy’s shoulder, fingers curled into his shirt.

Mara blinked. The cup was back in the girl’s hand.

She did not tell Daniel.

Instead she sealed the photograph and birthday card in separate sleeves, recorded where each had been found, and put them in her bag. Her notes were precise, but precision no longer felt like protection. It was only a record of the moment before the next version replaced it.

At the door, Daniel stopped.

“Do you hear that?”

Mara listened.

Water moved through pipes behind the wall. Then came a soft scrape, like a child dragging a fingertip down glass.

Daniel opened the door.

The hallway was empty. At the far end, beneath the broken light, a small wet handprint gleamed on the painted wall.

By the time Mara looked directly at it, there was nothing there.

She closed the door and locked it.

In her bag, the altered photograph pressed against the birthday card. Through the fabric she imagined two children standing together in the grass, waiting for someone to come home.

Daniel remembers a yellow house with a concrete basement, lightning-cracked basement window, rusted furnace, canned peaches, fuse box, yellow-linoleum kitchen, burn mark, pantry floorboard, refrigerator drawing beneath a lemon magnet, upstairs routines, and a community pool where their mother wore a red bathing suit and disliked striped cover-ups. Lily had a blue-flowered ceramic birthday plate cracked through the middle, wanted the largest cake piece, and said an apple wanted her tooth back.

The alternate history includes a brown dog named Pickle with one white paw and a scar over its left eye. Pickle escaped during a storm, died near a drainage ditch, and was buried by Daniel with a spoon. Daniel associates these events with “the same summer,” sometimes calling it 1997 despite being born in 1994, and also recalls being seven at a birthday party. The tape’s partial/static footage induced details not visibly present—basement, dog-like shape, open door, dirty waving hand—and sounds of water, dog tags, and laughter. Daniel thought he saw Lily behind the basement window. The cassette became warm after ejection.

Daniel also recalls a storm lullaby sung by his mother Elena:

“Go to sleep, little river stone,  
the moon has a house of its own.  
Lie in the dark where the cool reeds grow,  
dream of the places the tide won’t know.”

He cannot provide the rest. His documented childhood memories remain accessible but emotionally flat beside the implanted history: only-child life with Elena near a Newark radiator, rice dinners during financial hardship, Lincoln Elementary, and a broken wrist at nine. He briefly grabbed Mara’s wrist, accusing her of trying to “erase” Lily. A child laughed beneath the television static, and both heard it. Daniel then reported or perceived a small wet handprint sliding down the corridor door’s glass; it left no residue. Similar handprints later appeared and vanished despite cleaning and checking. The unplugged television has emitted water-like sounds and child laughter. Possible transmission through handling, proximity, observation, or discussion remains unresolved.

Daniel was sleep-deprived and fixated but continued insisting Lily was real. Mara documented his testimony and searched public records: no yellow house, matching address, second Reyes birth, infant death, Lily, or Pickle can be verified. Daniel uses “the wrong family,” echoing Elias’s language about Ruth. The overlap suggests the anomaly may target existing grief, generate recurring figures, access suppressed memories, or link victims through an unknown narrative.

Mara contacted Elena Reyes, 58, Daniel’s mother, now a respiratory therapist at St. Vincent’s Medical Center. During a video call, Elena initially denied Lily, the yellow house, and Pickle. When Daniel supplied specific details, Elena became visibly terrified, ordered him to stop, told him to come home, and unexpectedly asked, **“Is she still there?”** and then **“Is Lily still there?”** She warned, “Don’t bring her home,” claimed not to know Mara despite addressing her by name, and ended the call. Daniel interpreted this as proof Elena remembered Lily; Mara considers possible anomaly-induced confusion or concealed knowledge. The call indicates the anomaly may affect or reach witnesses who did not knowingly view the tape.

Mara accompanied Daniel to his Bloomfield apartment. He reported the building and kitchen felt wrong despite having lived there two years. A lemon-shaped refrigerator magnet covered a pale rectangle and faint pencil lines resembling the start of a house drawing; Daniel said Lily had drawn a house with oversized windows and a crooked chimney.

In the apartment, the image instead showed the alternate yellow house in summer, Daniel as a child beside Lily near the blue pool, and blue-ink text: **DANNY & LILY — JULY 1997**. The image had no replacement marks, adhesive residue, or physical explanation. Behind it remained the original photograph, proving the altered version was a separate anomalous manifestation or transformation. Daniel supplied another implanted memory of the scene: Lily had cut her foot in the grass and refused to cry because she feared Daniel would tell. He inconsistently introduced a possible father who did not fit his documented memory, saying “Not ours,” then admitted he did not know.

Daniel found a birthday card in a tax-document shoebox he had never seen before. It was addressed:

**DANNY AND LILY REYES  
YELLOW HOUSE  
MILLER ROAD**

The unstamped, resealed envelope contained: **TO THE TWO OF YOU—DON’T FIGHT OVER THE CORNER PIECE THIS YEAR.** Daniel connected it to Lily’s remembered preference for the cake’s icing-heavy corner piece and her belief that middle pieces were lonely. The card smelled faintly of wet cardboard. Miller Road exists in multiple Pennsylvania counties, but no matching yellow house has been identified. Mara photographed and separately bagged the altered photograph and card, recording their locations and condition.

While examining the photograph, Mara experienced an intrusive, possibly implanted impression of a hallway, a child’s hand, a chipped tooth, and Elias calling from another room, accompanied by an old fear she could not identify. She denied remembering Lily when Daniel accused her of doing so. The image showed a green door, sagging porch, and possible basement window. Mara briefly saw Lily’s hand move from holding a red cup to resting on Daniel’s shoulder, then revert; she did not tell Daniel. This is the strongest indication that Mara may be developing exposure effects through proximity, testimony, or handling anomalous derivative objects, though she has not played the tape.

At Daniel’s apartment door, both heard water moving through pipes and a fingertip-like scrape on glass. A wet handprint appeared beneath a broken hallway light, then vanished when directly observed. Mara returned with the altered photograph and birthday card sealed separately, while Daniel demanded help finding Lily. She told him he was a person, not merely evidence, but could not promise Lily’s existence or recovery.

Current anomaly assessment: the VHS can implant alternate childhoods in people born after 1990, including relatives, homes, pets, routines, chronology, sensory memories, grief, and bodily/emotional certainty. It may alter or generate physical media and potentially environmental traces. Effects may spread beyond direct viewing. The tape’s unseen remainder, label, retraced date, warmth, clicks, greasy print, unstable origin, and possible displacement remain unexplained. Lily, Pickle, the yellow house, Miller Road, the wet handprints, water sounds, child laughter, and the recurring “wrong family” motif remain unresolved.

Immediate concerns: Daniel’s fixation, insomnia, grief, and safety; Elena’s apparent fear and possible exposure; Mara’s emerging intrusive imagery; the altered photograph and birthday card as derivative anomalies; whether Lily is an implanted construct, a displaced person, an alternate-biography artifact, or something capable of crossing into the subjects’ world; and whether the archive should suppress, destroy, preserve, or study the tape. Formal containment procedures, medical/psychological monitoring, subject testimonies, and a breach incident log remain forthcoming.

chapters.name: A Memory of Ruth
chapters.content:
### A Memory of Ruth

Mara waited until Daniel had gone home before she tried to destroy the tape.

She told herself this was procedural. The altered photograph and birthday card were sealed in separate evidence bags on her desk, and the original cassette sat inside the isolation cabinet, where the dehumidifier breathed steadily through its vents. She had written three pages of observations, none of them adequate. She had called Elena Reyes twice and received no answer. She had checked the archive’s exterior doors, the corridor windows, the television’s power cord, and the door beneath which Daniel had seen the wet handprint descend.

Nothing in the building had been wet.

Nothing in the building had laughed.

At 11:43 p.m., with the winter rain ticking against the high windows, Mara unlocked the cabinet.

The cassette was warm.

She touched it through nitrile gloves and felt heat gathered inside the swollen plastic shell, as if it had been left on a dashboard beneath summer sun. The crooked label had darkened at the edges. HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97. The final seven was still retraced, the second stroke pressing through the paper and into the adhesive beneath. A greasy thumbprint curved across the lower corner.

Mara stared at it.

She had cleaned fingerprints from hundreds of objects. Prints were maps of contact, not messages. This one looked fresh enough to belong to someone standing just outside the cabinet, waiting for her to notice.

“Stop behaving like a haunted-house prop,” she said.

The archive answered with the dehumidifier’s low mechanical hum.

She carried the cassette to the loading bay, where the industrial shredder stood beneath a yellow sign: AUTHORIZED MATERIALS ONLY. It was designed for damaged boxes, packing foam, obsolete plastic housings, and other refuse that would jam an ordinary office machine. Its twin toothed rollers could chew through a telephone directory in seconds.

Mara had used it once to destroy a batch of mold-contaminated microfilm reels. The reels had emerged as black curls and transparent teeth.

She removed the cassette from its bag and placed it in the hopper.

For a moment it rested there, unremarkable except for the slight bulge of the casing.

Mara pressed the green button.

The rollers engaged with a rising metallic whine. The tape shifted forward. One corner caught between the teeth. The label tore.

Then the machine stopped.

Not jammed. Stopped.

The warning light remained green. The motor continued to hum without turning, exerting some enormous, useless pressure beneath the housing.

Mara hit the emergency stop, then the reverse switch. The rollers groaned backward. A length of brown-black magnetic tape emerged, slick and shining, and hung between the teeth.

She reached for the service lever.

The cassette clicked.

It was a small sound, almost delicate: the internal mechanism of a VHS accepting a command.

Mara froze.

From somewhere inside the shredder came the faint rush of water.

Not the sound of a pipe. Not rain. Water moving in a confined space, with a hollow slap against a wall. Beneath it came a child’s laughter, muffled by distance or by the thickness of the machine.

She pulled the lever anyway.

The rollers lurched. The cassette shot downward.

Mara flinched as the teeth closed. Plastic cracked. The sound of water vanished. A strip of tape whipped upward and slapped against the metal guard. She grabbed the emergency stop again.

The hopper was empty.

On the floor beneath the rollers lay a dozen fragments of black plastic, several torn label fibers, and one intact white spindle.

The cassette itself was gone.

Mara crouched, searching the catch tray. There was no shell, no magnetic ribbon, no recognizable piece of housing. The machine’s lower compartment was sealed by a bolted plate. She fetched a wrench from the maintenance cabinet, loosened the bolts, and opened it.

Inside, beneath the rollers, the cassette sat whole.

It had not passed through. It had not been crushed. It was lying on the angled steel plate as if someone had placed it there after the machine stopped.

The label was unmarked.

Mara shut the compartment.

She did not call anyone. Calling someone would make the thing official, and she was not yet prepared to decide what official meant. She was an archivist. She had a chain-of-custody form for every object that entered the building. She knew how to quarantine mold, isolate nitrate film, test for chemical off-gassing, and document the accidental exposure of a technician to a century-old preservation solvent.

She did not have a form for a cassette that refused to be shredded.

The film furnace was in the old processing room, past the freight elevator and the records vault. It had been installed when the archive still accepted industrial quantities of obsolete film. The furnace was not truly a furnace in the dramatic sense; it was a ceramic-lined destruction chamber, temperature-controlled and vented through a scrubber system. It could reduce cellulose acetate and polyester film to ash, though the process took time.

Mara carried the cassette there in a steel tray.

She read the operating instructions twice. She checked the temperature gauge. She opened the chamber and placed the tape on the ceramic grate.

The plastic shell seemed smaller in the furnace’s white interior.

She thought of Daniel’s face when he had said, Lily is still at the house.

Not hysteria. Not exactly. His expression had held the terrible concentration of someone listening for a voice beneath a crowded room.

Mara closed the door and began the cycle.

The chamber heated. A fan started in the venting system. Through the inspection window, the cassette darkened, then softened. The label curled away from the shell. The faint smell of warmed plastic entered the room despite the scrubbers.

Mara stood with her arms crossed, watching.

At 1,100 degrees, the cassette should have collapsed.

At 1,300, it should have burned.

At 1,500, there should have been only a residue of carbon and aluminum.

The shell remained intact.

The furnace alarm began to chirp.

Mara leaned toward the gauge. The temperature had climbed beyond the programmed limit, rising in narrow, impossible increments. 1,612. 1,644. 1,701.

The cassette’s label flattened against the plastic.

The final seven seemed to straighten.

Then the inspection window clouded from the inside.

A child’s hand appeared on the glass.

It was small and wet, five fingers splayed against the furnace window. Water ran from the fingertips in clear lines, though the chamber was dry and blazing. Mara saw the palm, the delicate crease beneath the thumb, the pale crescent of a half-moon nail.

The hand slid down.

Mara stumbled backward.

The furnace door opened.

Not all the way. A single inch of blackness appeared between the seal and the frame. Heat struck her face. The alarm became a shrill, continuous tone.

She reached for the emergency cutoff, but the room had changed.

There was a hallway beside her.

The archive walls were gone. In their place stood pale yellow paint, scuffed at the baseboards. A green door waited at the far end beneath a weak ceiling bulb. The air smelled of rain, old carpet, and canned peaches. Somewhere nearby, a washing machine thudded through an uneven cycle.

Mara was standing beside a child.

The girl’s hand was in hers.

She was perhaps eight. Her brown hair had been cut badly around her ears, and one front tooth was chipped at the upper corner. She wore a red sweater despite the heat of summer. Her fingers were cold and damp.

“Don’t look at the window,” the girl whispered.

Mara looked anyway.

At the end of the hallway, beneath the green door’s frame, was a square of darkness. A basement window. Lightning trembled beyond it.

The girl tightened her grip.

Mara knew, with the unbearable certainty of dreams, that she had promised to watch her. She knew she had failed before. She knew the child had been taken by a family whose name Mara had forgotten, and that her father had spent years trying to find the house where it happened.

Ruth.

The name rose inside her, not as a word but as a wound.

A man called from another room.

“Mara? Keep her upstairs.”

The voice was Elias’s.

She turned, and for one suspended instant saw her father as he had been before the bottles, before the confusion, before his hands began to shake: sober, attentive, kneeling in the hallway with a towel over one shoulder. His expression was frightened but patient. He was waiting for her to do something.

“What do I do?” Mara asked.

The child leaned against her.

“Stay,” she said.

The hallway flickered.

Mara felt the girl’s hand slip from hers.

“No,” she said, and grabbed for it.

The child’s face blurred. The chipped tooth flashed once. The green door became a loading-bay door. The yellow walls became concrete. The smell of rain became hot plastic.

The hand was gone.

Mara struck the floor on one knee.

The furnace alarm had stopped. The chamber door was closed. Through the inspection window, the cassette rested on the ceramic grate, blackened but whole. A thin thread of smoke rose from it and vanished into the vent.

Mara could not breathe.

She pressed both hands to the floor until the concrete steadied beneath her. The grief remained after the vision had gone. It filled her chest with a physical pressure, a mourning so complete that she began to weep before she understood she was doing it.

She had never met Ruth.

There had been no Ruth to lose.

Her father had been sick. Her father had been drunk. Her father had built a daughter out of damaged recollection and asked Mara to help him search for her. That was the explanation she had lived with. It was ugly, but it was solid.

Now the explanation had acquired a hallway.

A chipped tooth.

The weight of a child leaning against her hip.

Mara rose unsteadily and turned off the furnace. The cassette did not cool. When she opened the chamber with tongs, it lay on the grate, its surface unscarred except for a faint rust-colored line along one edge.

She put it in a new evidence bag.

At 2:18 a.m., she sat at her desk and began an incident report.

DATE:  
TIME OF EXPOSURE:  
OBJECT:  
METHOD OF ATTEMPTED DESTRUCTION:

She stopped there.

Her hands were shaking too badly to type. She opened the paper logbook instead, the one required for power failures and network outages. The pen left a wet black line.

At approximately 0118 hours, I attempted mechanical destruction of an anomalous VHS cassette labeled—

She crossed out anomalous.

She wrote damaged.

Then she crossed that out too.

The door opened.

Daniel stood in the corridor wearing the same clothes as earlier, though his shirt was damp at the shoulders. His hair was flattened on one side. He looked as if he had driven through rain with the window open.

Mara stood.

“How did you get in?”

“You left the side door unlatched.”

“I did not.”

He looked past her toward the evidence bags.

“Where is it?”

“Daniel, you need to go home.”

“You said you’d keep it safe.”

“I said I’d keep it isolated.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

His eyes were red, but his expression was alert. Too alert. He had not slept. Mara could see the strain in the small muscles around his mouth.

“I tried to destroy it,” she said.

He stared at her.

“What?”

“The cassette. I tried to shred it. Then I put it in the furnace.”

For a moment he seemed unable to understand the sentence. Then his face changed.

“You played it.”

“No.”

“You saw it.”

“I didn’t play it.”

“You saw Lily.”

Mara felt the word enter the room like a draft.

“Lily is not real.”

Daniel crossed the space between them so quickly that she stepped back. He did not touch her, but his hands closed into fists at his sides.

“Don’t say that.”

“It’s an implanted memory.”

“You don’t know that.”

“The footage shows a child. It doesn’t establish her identity. There are no records of—”

“Records?” His laugh was sharp and breathless. “You think a birth certificate is going to tell you what she sounded like when she was scared?”

“Daniel—”

“She hated chlorine. She had a scar on her knee from falling off Pickle’s food dish. She used to press her face to the basement window because she thought the people outside could see through the glass.”

“Those details are part of the effect.”

“Effect.” He pointed at the bag containing the cassette. “You call her an effect because you can’t stand that she’s there.”

“She isn’t there.”

His expression collapsed into fury.

“You don’t get to decide that.”

“I get to decide what the evidence supports.”

“No, you get to decide what you’re willing to lose.”

The words struck with such precision that Mara stopped.

Daniel’s breathing had become shallow. He looked beyond her, toward the loading bay, toward some house only he could see.

“She’s waiting,” he said. “You know that.”

“No.”

“You were with her.”

Mara’s skin went cold.

“What did you say?”

“In the hallway.”

She held still.

“You were standing beside her,” Daniel said. “She had the chipped tooth. She was holding your hand.”

Mara looked at the sealed evidence bag. The cassette’s label showed through the plastic, pale and crooked.

“That’s impossible.”

“She told me you would say that.”

“Daniel, you have to leave.”

“She said your father called her Ruth because he didn’t know her real name.”

Mara’s throat tightened.

The room seemed to contract around them. The archive’s fluorescent lights buzzed overhead. From the corridor came the faint sound of dripping water.

Daniel turned toward it.

“Lily?”

“Don’t.”

He took one step.

Mara caught his arm. He spun back, and for an instant she saw the child he had been in the yellow-house photograph: thin knees, sunburned cheeks, one hand held out toward a girl just beyond the frame.

“She’s not your sister,” Mara said. “She is something the tape made.”

Daniel tore his arm free.

“You felt her.”

Mara could not answer.

“You felt her hand,” he said. “You felt her disappear.”

The wet sound in the corridor grew louder.

Mara’s desk phone rang.

Both of them flinched.

She snatched up the receiver. “Allegheny Regional Archive.”

“Ms. Venn?” said a woman’s voice. “This is Special Agent June Halpern with the Department of Anomalous Media. Is the object still on the premises?”

Mara looked at Daniel.

“How do you know about the object?”

“We need you to answer the question.”

The hallway light outside the office flickered. A small, wet handprint appeared on the glass of the records-room door.

Daniel whispered, “She found us.”

Mara gripped the phone tighter.

“The object is here,” she said. “There has been an incident.”

“Is anyone exposed?”

Mara looked at Daniel’s exhausted face, at the handprint sliding slowly downward, at the evidence bag containing a cassette that had survived a furnace.

“I don’t know,” she said.

The front doors opened below.

Voices moved through the archive: calm, practiced, already inside.

Halpern said, “Do not touch the object. Do not describe what you have seen. Stay where you are.”

Mara glanced at the report on her desk. The page remained blank except for the crossed-out words.

Behind her, Daniel began to cry.

Not loudly. Not theatrically. He folded over himself, one hand pressed to his chest as if someone had reached inside and taken hold of his heart.

Mara put down the phone.

“Lily,” he said. “She’s still at the house.”

“No,” Mara told him, though she no longer knew whether she meant the house, the girl, or the memory.

The archive doors opened wider below. Footsteps climbed the stairs.

Mara stood beside Daniel and watched the handprint vanish from the glass.

Water sounds grew in the corridor, and a wet handprint appeared on the records-room glass. Daniel said, **“She found us.”** The archive’s front doors opened and practiced voices entered. A caller identifying herself as Special Agent June Halpern of the **Department of Anomalous Media** asked whether the object was still on the premises and whether anyone was exposed. Mara had not contacted the department and does not know how it learned of the tape. Halpern ordered them not to touch the object, not to describe what they had seen, and to remain in place. The callers/agents are now entering the archive.

Daniel began crying and said Lily was still at the house. Mara stood beside him as the handprint vanished. The cassette remains inside the archive, apparently resistant to mechanical shredding and furnace destruction. Formal containment procedures, medical and psychological monitoring, subject testimonies, and a breach incident log are still required.

Current unresolved issues include the tape’s unseen remainder; whether its label, warmth, clicks, print, and unstable provenance indicate agency; the source and nature of Lily/Ruth; the yellow house and Miller Road; Pickle; wet handprints, water sounds, and child laughter; physical alterations to photographs and cards; the anomaly’s ability to affect non-viewers such as Elena and Mara; whether derivative objects propagate exposure; the significance of Elias’s Ruth fixation; the identity and authority of the Department of Anomalous Media; and whether the anomaly can physically displace or manifest its subjects.

chapters.name: AM-97-441
chapters.content:
## AM-97-441

The front doors opened without the alarm sounding.

Mara heard the hydraulic release, then the scrape of grit beneath unfamiliar shoes. Three figures entered beneath the green emergency light. The woman in front wore a charcoal coat and carried a hard-sided case marked with a yellow band. The man behind her shut the doors and wedged them closed.

“Ms. Venn?” the woman asked.

Mara stood beside Daniel near the records-room door. The wet handprint on the glass had vanished, leaving only a cloudy oval.

“I’m Special Agent June Halpern,” the woman said. “Department of Anomalous Media. This is Dr. Irena Vale, clinical containment, and Mr. Tomas Wirth, materials response. Step away from the glass.”

“How did you know it was here?” Mara asked.

“We’ll establish that later. Where is the cassette?”

“In the furnace room. It came out intact.”

Wirth’s expression tightened. “You attempted destruction?”

“I didn’t play it.”

“That wasn’t my question.”

“No,” Mara said. “I didn’t play it.”

Daniel gave a small, exhausted laugh.

“She found us,” he said.

Vale looked at him. She had close-cropped gray hair and a narrow, severe face. Her eyes moved over his hands, his pupils, the damp collar of his shirt.

“Born after the cutoff?” she asked.

“What cutoff?” Daniel said.

“Mr. Reyes, sit down.”

“I need Lily.”

“Sit down.”

“She’s in there.”

Halpern raised one gloved hand. “Nobody touches anything. Nobody describes the image, the sound, or any perceived person. If you’ve experienced a memory that does not belong to you, don’t test it.”

The warning settled over the lobby.

“You already know what it does,” Mara said.

“Yes.”

Halpern removed a card from her coat and held it out. It was blank except for a black designation:

**AM-97-441**

The number stirred no recognition, but Mara felt an involuntary chill.

“That is the object’s designation,” Halpern said. “A cognitohazardous audiovisual medium with a documented autobiographical implantation effect.”

“Current manifestation?” Mara asked.

“Your tape is not unique in every respect.”

Wirth approached the furnace-room door. He pressed a rectangular instrument against the wall. Its lights blinked red, then amber.

“Residual field?” Halpern asked.

“Indeterminate.”

“Proceed.”

Wirth opened the door. From inside came a thin trickle of water.

Daniel flinched.

“Don’t listen,” Mara said.

Vale turned toward her. “Do not instruct him to resist auditory phenomena. That may increase fixation.”

“Then what should I do?”

“Keep him oriented to the present.”

“He’s standing in a dark archive while you tell him his sister isn’t real.”

“I have not told him that,” Vale said. “I will tell him his experience is not evidence.”

Wirth emerged carrying a collapsible table. On it lay the smoke-blackened cassette. Its crooked label remained legible: HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97. The final seven had been retraced until it resembled a hook.

Mara had watched the furnace exceed its limit. She had watched the tape come through untouched.

Wirth opened the case. Inside, nested in gray foam, sat a ceramic-lined metal cylinder. Articulated clamps lowered from the lid, seized the cassette by its edges, and lifted it.

The tape clicked.

From beyond the lobby, a child laughed.

Daniel lunged. Halpern caught him across the chest and turned him aside.

“Lily!” he shouted.

The clamps dropped the cassette into the cylinder. The lid sealed with a hiss. Wirth fitted a second cap over it and rotated the cap until three white marks aligned.

The laugh stopped.

Daniel sagged against Halpern’s arm.

“Is she in there?” he whispered.

“No,” Mara said.

The word hurt her mouth.

Vale clipped a sensor around Daniel’s wrist. “We’re moving you to a controlled medical setting.”

“I’m not going anywhere with you.”

“You are experiencing progressive distortion of autobiographical memory.”

“Lily is my sister.”

“You may continue to feel that she is your sister.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

“No,” Vale said. “It isn’t.”

For a moment Daniel looked like the boy from the tape—or the boy he remembered being—wet-haired, grass-stained, reaching toward someone outside the frame.

Halpern nodded to Wirth. “Seal the building.”

Wirth placed two palm-sized devices on opposite sides of the lobby. Their lights came on. The fluorescent fixtures flickered, and relays snapped throughout the archive.

Mara’s phone vibrated in her coat.

She pulled it out. The screen showed access alerts, failed login attempts, and a message from an unknown number containing a photograph of a yellow-sided house.

Halpern took the phone from her.

“Don’t look at that.”

“I already did.”

“Yes.”

She placed it in a lined pouch and sealed it.

An additional team entered through the side door in disposable coveralls. They photographed the furnace, shredder, corridor glass, and floor. Others bagged every television, monitor, computer, and audio device. The archive’s network was disconnected. Even the staff-room refrigerator was unplugged after a technician reported that its compressor produced a repetitive clicking pattern.

Mara moved toward the furnace room.

A young agent blocked her. “Remain in the lobby.”

“That’s my equipment.”

“It may be contaminated.”

“With what?”

He had no answer.

Vale continued her examination of Daniel. “What year were you born?”

“1994.”

“City?”

“Newark.”

“Your mother’s name?”

“Elena.”

“Occupation?”

“Respiratory therapist.”

“School at age nine?”

“Lincoln.”

“Did you have a dog?”

“Yes.”

“Name?”

“Pickle.”

“What kind?”

“Brown. One white paw. Scar over his left eye.”

“Did Pickle exist in your documented life?”

Daniel looked toward the sealed cylinder. “You’ve seen the records.”

“I’m asking you.”

“No.”

“Did you have a sister?”

“Yes.”

“Name?”

“Lily.”

“Is Lily documented?”

Daniel’s jaw tightened. “She doesn’t need to be.”

Vale paused. “You’ll be sedated for transport.”

“No.”

“It is not punishment.”

“You’ll make me forget.”

“We do not erase memories.”

“Then what do you do?”

“We prevent them from acquiring further structure.”

Daniel turned to Mara. “Tell them I’m not sick.”

“You’re exposed,” Mara said. “That’s different.”

“Tell them Lily is real.”

Mara could not.

His face changed. He understood the silence as betrayal.

Halpern spoke more gently. “Mr. Reyes, this object has caused the same category of injury in other people. We need to separate you from anyone vulnerable, including your mother.”

“You called her?”

“A team is at her residence.”

“What are they telling her?”

“That you’ve been exposed.”

“Does she know about Lily?”

No one answered.

Vale injected a sedative through the sensor port. Daniel jerked, then sagged between the two women. As they lowered him onto a wheeled stretcher, his hand caught Mara’s sleeve.

“Don’t let them take the summer,” he whispered.

She held his fingers until Vale removed them.

The quarantine took less than an hour to become total. Exterior doors were locked and marked. The archive’s water supply to the records wing was shut off. Every object Mara had brought from Daniel’s apartment—the altered photograph, the birthday card, her notes—was placed in separate evidence containers.

She was escorted to a small office overlooking the loading dock. The blinds were closed. On the desk sat a paper cup of water, a sealed bag containing her keys, and several forms printed on gray paper.

Halpern sat opposite her. Vale stood beside the door.

“Before you sign anything,” Halpern said, “you’ll undergo a baseline interview. Blood draw, neurological screening, and memory inventory. We need to determine whether you were exposed directly, indirectly, or through a derivative alteration.”

“Derivative alteration?”

“The photograph. The card. Any object that changed after playback.”

Mara studied her. “You know about the photograph.”

“It was visible through an external security camera at Mr. Reyes’s building.”

“You hacked it?”

“No.”

Mara thought of child Daniel beside Lily, both of them smiling near the pool. She had seen the image change while holding it. She had pretended otherwise.

“Can you restore it?” she asked.

“We don’t know.”

“Daniel?”

“We don’t know.”

Vale’s voice was clinical. “The longer he remains in an ordinary environment, the harder stabilization becomes.”

“Stabilization,” Mara said. “Not recovery.”

“They are not always the same.”

Halpern slid the forms toward her. “You have two options. The first is a standard nondisclosure agreement. You return home under observation, surrender affected materials, submit to scheduled interviews, and have no contact with Mr. Reyes or his family.”

“And the second?”

“Monitored consultant status.”

Mara looked up.

“You remain attached to the investigation as an archival specialist,” Halpern continued. “You’ll be housed under departmental supervision until your exposure status is established. You may assist with provenance, object handling, and records analysis. Contact with Mr. Reyes will be subject to clinical approval.”

“Why offer me that?”

“You handled the object without viewing it, attempted destruction, and did not take it home.”

“I didn’t call you.”

“No,” Halpern said. “You didn’t.”

Mara glanced at the agreement. “How many owners?”

Halpern hesitated.

“You said other people were injured.”

“Seventeen confirmed exposures associated with this designation. Thirty-two probable. The tape has passed through private homes, estate sales, church basements, a school media department, and at least two thrift operations.”

“Since 1997?”

“Since 1997.”

“Where was it before the shop?”

“We have partial records.”

“You tracked it.”

“We tracked events resembling its effects.”

“Why didn’t you intercept it?”

“Sometimes we arrived after the owner died. Sometimes the object changed hands before we identified the pattern. Once, the tape was reported destroyed and resurfaced eleven years later in a box of donated children’s books.”

Mara thought of the shopkeeper’s contradictory stories: the church, the Voss house, Miller Road, a cleanout. None of them necessarily false. All of them perhaps inherited.

“Why AM-97-441?”

“AM is our designation. Ninety-seven is the earliest confirmed production date. Four-four-one is the catalog sequence.”

“Production date,” Mara said. “So it was made.”

“Likely.”

“By whom?”

“That is classified.”

“You want me to sign away my right to speak without telling me what I’m signing about.”

“We want you not to spread a hazard.”

“Those aren’t the same thing.”

“No,” Halpern said. “They aren’t.”

Mara saw the exhaustion beneath the agent’s composure. It was not sympathy, exactly, but the fatigue of someone who had watched people lose arguments with their own minds.

“Can I see Daniel?”

“Not yet.”

“Is he conscious?”

“He will be.”

“Where are you taking him?”

“To a medical observation site. Not a public hospital.”

“His mother?”

“She’s being interviewed by a separate team.”

“Does she know what happened?”

“She knows he has been exposed.”

“Does she know about Lily?”

Halpern’s silence answered.

Mara looked down at the agreements. The nondisclosure form had one signature line and a dozen prohibitions. The consultant contract had six pages of restrictions, but also required psychological care, legal representation, and “reasonable access to affected persons where clinically appropriate.” It permitted her to document non-descriptive factual history and chain-of-custody information.

It was not freedom. It was a door left open by people who had built a room without windows.

“If I refuse both?” Mara asked.

“You remain in quarantine while a determination is made.”

“For how long?”

“That depends on your exposure status.”

“And if I’m considered exposed?”

“You may remain in quarantine indefinitely.”

Vale said, “The restriction is not punitive.”

Mara turned to her. “You keep saying that as if it makes it better.”

“It makes it accurate.”

“Daniel knows his real life. He knows where he grew up, who his mother is, what school he attended. You’re taking him because he loves someone who doesn’t exist.”

“We’re taking him because the distinction between knowing and loving is failing.”

The words found a place in Mara she had been trying not to examine.

Her father had spent years insisting that a missing daughter explained everything: the drinking, the yellow raincoats, his fury when Mara said there had never been a Ruth. If the tape had reached him, then his madness had not been invented. But that did not make Ruth real. It meant only that a false memory could leave a true wound.

She picked up the consultant agreement.

“If I sign this, I want access to the chain-of-custody records.”

“Within clearance.”

“I want Daniel’s interviews preserved.”

“Clinical records are protected.”

“I want them preserved.”

Halpern considered her. “That can be entered as a request.”

“And I want it recorded that I object to destroying testimony.”

Vale’s face hardened. “Testimony can carry the effect.”

“Then redact it. Don’t erase the people.”

“Ms. Venn—”

“I know. You don’t know what’s safe.”

Halpern placed a pen beside the agreement.

“That is the only thing we know.”

Mara signed.

Her name made an ordinary dark line across the page. It looked familiar, but not intimate. She wondered whether that, too, could be altered.

Halpern gathered the forms and sealed them in an envelope. “You’ll be screened now. Blood draw, neurological baseline, memory inventory. No questions about the content of your impressions until Dr. Vale is present.”

“You’re afraid I’ll describe them.”

“We’re afraid description may give them structure.”

“Then how do you know what happened to the other owners?”

“We know enough to contain the damage.”

“That isn’t understanding.”

“No,” Halpern said. “It isn’t.”

Through the closed blinds, dawn began to pale the loading dock. The archive’s windows reflected a building that looked unchanged: brick walls, dusty glass, faded lettering above the entrance. Yet Mara knew it had been closed around her, converted from workplace to evidence.

As Vale opened the door, a faint sound came from the corridor.

Water moving through pipes.

Then, very softly, a child singing:

“Go to sleep, little river stone…”

Mara stopped. “Did you hear that?”
