Vale did not answer. Halpern looked toward the sealed pouch containing Mara’s phone.

The singing ended before the second line.

A technician called for the medical team. Agents moved through the corridor carrying instruments, forms, and sealed containers from one controlled space into another.

Mara followed because Daniel was somewhere beyond the quarantine doors, sedated and dreaming of a sister who had never lived. She followed because her father’s final years had acquired a new shape, and shape was not the same as truth. She followed because the cassette had passed through too many hands, and no one could tell her where it had begun.

At the end of the corridor, the emergency lights made a row of yellow rectangles on the floor.

For one instant, they became the windows of a house. One darkened from within.

Mara kept walking without looking directly at it.
chapters.summary:
Mara Venn, 38, Media Preservation Archivist at the Allegheny Regional Archive, distrusts nostalgia as sanitized distortion. Her father Elias died after dementia and alcohol dependence, obsessed with a nonexistent daughter named Ruth. He bought duplicate yellow raincoats, searched for Ruth, wrote her name compulsively, and spoke of her being taken by “the wrong family.” Mara’s records identify her as an only child, but exposure to the current anomaly has given her vivid, emotionally powerful impressions of Ruth: a chipped-toothed, storm-fearing girl associated with a yellow house, attic or upstairs confinement, and Elias calling from another room. Mara now suspects the anomaly may have shaped or exploited Elias’s fixation without proving Ruth ever existed.

At a failing thrift shop, Mara bought a swollen, mold-clouded VHS labeled **HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97**, its final “7” retraced into a hook. The cassette was warm, clicked inexplicably, bore a rust-colored line and seemingly fresh greasy thumbprint, and had contradictory, unstable provenance stories involving a cardboard box, the Voss house, a church, Miller Road, and a Miller Road cleanout. Mara sealed it under the archive rule **DO NOT PLAY UNCATALOGED MEDIA**, but Daniel Reyes, 26, born in 1994, played roughly ten minutes on a repaired Panasonic television/VCR.

The footage showed a yellow-sided house with white porch rails, green door, browned lawn, blue pool, sprinkler, a woman in a red bathing suit, and two children. Daniel identified the older boy as himself and the girl as his sister Lily, though all records show him as an only child raised by Elena Reyes in a Newark apartment. Playback implanted an emotionally certain alternate childhood: Lily was nearly his twin, eleven months younger, brown-haired, gray/green-eyed, with a summer cowlick and chipped upper tooth. She feared a basement window and thunderstorms, slept with the closet light on, hated peas and chlorine, and warned Daniel not to look at the window. The alternate home included a concrete basement, lightning-cracked window, rusted furnace, canned peaches, yellow-linoleum kitchen, burn mark, pantry floorboard, refrigerator drawing under a lemon magnet, and a pool where Elena wore a red bathing suit.

The implanted history includes Lily’s blue-flowered birthday plate cracked down the middle, her preference for the icing-heavy corner cake piece, an apple/tooth remark, and a brown dog named Pickle with one white paw and a scar over its left eye. Pickle escaped during a storm, died near a drainage ditch, and was buried by Daniel with a spoon. Daniel inconsistently calls these events “the same summer,” sometimes 1997, while remembering being seven. Static and partial footage induced unseen details: a basement, dog-like shape, open door, dirty waving hand, water, dog tags, laughter, and possibly Lily behind the basement window. The cassette became warm after ejection.

Daniel retains documented memories—Newark, Elena, rice dinners during hardship, Lincoln Elementary, and a broken wrist at nine—but experiences them as emotionally flat beside the false childhood, which “has weather.” He physically feels Lily’s hand on his shoulder during thunder and remembers Elena’s incomplete lullaby:

“Go to sleep, little river stone,  
the moon has a house of its own.  
Lie in the dark where the cool reeds grow,  
dream of the places the tide won’t know.”

He initially lied about playing the tape, then demanded to watch the remainder because Lily was still at the house. He briefly grabbed Mara’s wrist and accused her of erasing Lily. Both heard child laughter beneath television static. A wet handprint appeared and vanished on corridor-door glass; similar prints, water sounds, and laughter later manifested around Daniel’s apartment and the archive. Whether transmission occurs through playback, handling, proximity, observation, discussion, or derivative objects remains unknown.

Public records found no yellow house, matching address, second Reyes birth, Lily, infant death, or Pickle. Daniel’s apartment developed anomalous associations: a lemon-shaped refrigerator magnet covered a pale rectangle and pencil marks resembling Lily’s drawing of a house with oversized windows and crooked chimney. A framed photograph altered from Daniel at eighteen outside a brick building in winter to child Daniel beside Lily by the blue pool, marked **DANNY & LILY — JULY 1997** in blue ink; the original remained physically behind it. Daniel associated the image with Lily cutting her foot in grass and refusing to cry, and with an uncertain possible father (“Not ours”). A resealed birthday card appeared in a tax-document shoebox:

**DANNY AND LILY REYES  
YELLOW HOUSE  
MILLER ROAD**

Inside: **TO THE TWO OF YOU—DON’T FIGHT OVER THE CORNER PIECE THIS YEAR.** It smelled of wet cardboard and matched Lily’s remembered preference. Mara bagged the photograph and card separately.

Though Mara never viewed the tape, handling the altered photograph produced an intrusive vision of a yellow-house hallway, child’s hand, chipped tooth, and Elias calling from another room. She briefly saw Lily’s hand move from a red cup to Daniel’s shoulder, then revert, and concealed this from Daniel. This established possible indirect exposure through altered or derivative objects. At Daniel’s door, Mara and Daniel heard pipes and scraping; a wet handprint appeared beneath a broken light and vanished under direct observation. Elena Reyes, 58, initially denied Lily, the yellow house, and Pickle, but became terrified when Daniel supplied details, asked “Is she still there?” and “Is Lily still there?”, warned “Don’t bring her home,” claimed not to know Mara while addressing her by name, and stopped responding to calls. Her knowledge may be genuine, induced, or contaminated.

### Destruction Attempt and First Department Contact

At approximately 23:43, Mara removed the warm cassette from isolation and attempted destruction without playing it. The industrial shredder stalled under motor pressure; reversing it produced a strip of brown-black tape, water sounds, and muffled child laughter, yet the whole cassette appeared in the bolted lower compartment. In the ceramic-lined film furnace, it survived temperatures above 1,700°F. A wet child’s hand appeared on the inspection window, and the chamber briefly transformed for Mara into a yellow hallway with rain, canned peaches, a washing machine, and a basement window. She found herself holding an eight-year-old girl in a red sweater with damp fingers and chipped tooth. The girl said, **“Don’t look at the window,”** then, when Mara asked what to do, **“Stay.”** Elias called, **“Mara? Keep her upstairs.”** The vision ended with the girl’s hand slipping away and left Mara grieving despite knowing she had never met Ruth. The cassette emerged intact except for smoke-blackening.

At about 02:18, Mara began an incident report but could write only crossed-out terms such as “anomalous” and “damaged.” Daniel entered through a side door Mara believed she had secured, demanded the tape, and said Lily had predicted Mara would deny seeing her. He claimed Ruth was a name Elias used because he did not know the girl’s real name. Water sounds and a wet handprint returned. Daniel said, **“She found us.”**

Three people then entered without triggering the archive alarm: Special Agent June Halpern of the **Department of Anomalous Media**, clinical containment specialist Dr. Irena Vale, and materials responder Tomas Wirth. Halpern already knew the object’s location and ordered no one to touch it or describe its image, sound, or perceived people. The department designation is **AM-97-441**, classified as a cognitohazardous audiovisual medium causing autobiographical implantation. AM denotes the department, 97 the earliest confirmed production date, and 441 its catalog sequence. The department states the tape is likely manufactured rather than spontaneously occurring, but its maker is classified.

Wirth’s instruments found an indeterminate residual field. The cassette was transferred into a ceramic-lined metal cylinder with articulated clamps, then sealed under a second cap. It clicked during handling, and a child laughed; Daniel lunged and shouted “Lily!” before Halpern restrained him. Once sealed, the laugh stopped. The department locked down the archive, disconnected its network and water supply to the records wing, removed televisions, monitors, computers, and audio devices, and unplugged even the staff refrigerator after its compressor produced repetitive clicking. Agents photographed the furnace, shredder, corridor glass, and floor; the altered photograph, birthday card, notes, phone, and other potentially contaminated materials were separately contained. Mara’s phone displayed access alerts, failed login attempts, and an unsolicited photograph of a yellow-sided house; Halpern took it before Mara could study it and sealed it in a lined pouch.

Vale evaluated Daniel’s orientation. He correctly supplied his documented birth year, Newark, Elena’s name and occupation, Lincoln Elementary, and other facts, but insisted Pickle and Lily were real despite their absence from records. Vale characterized his condition as progressive autobiographical distortion and said treatment would prevent implanted memories from acquiring further structure, not erase them. Daniel was sedated and transported on a stretcher to a nonpublic medical observation site. He told Mara, **“Don’t let them take the summer.”** A separate team went to Elena’s residence; the department has not disclosed what she was told or whether she knows about Lily.

### Department Disclosure and Mara’s Status

Halpern revealed 17 confirmed exposures associated with AM-97-441 and 32 probable exposures. The tape has moved through private homes, estate sales, church basements, a school media department, and at least two thrift operations. It has been tracked since 1997, though investigators often arrived after owners died or after the tape changed hands. One reportedly destroyed copy resurfaced eleven years later in a box of donated children’s books. The department has only partial chain-of-custody records, and the contradictory thrift-shop accounts may each represent inherited fragments of its history.

Mara underwent quarantine and was offered either a standard nondisclosure agreement with monitored release or monitored consultant status. She chose consultant status, requiring psychological care, legal representation, controlled access to affected persons, archival/provenance work, and clearance-based access to chain-of-custody information. She requested preservation of Daniel’s interviews and testimony rather than destruction, with redaction where necessary, and objected to erasing affected people’s accounts. She remains under departmental supervision pending blood draw, neurological screening, baseline memory inventory, and determination of whether her exposure is direct, indirect, or derivative. The department knows about the photograph’s alteration, likely through external security footage, though Halpern denied hacking the building.

Mara was warned not to describe her impressions before clinical assessment because description may give them further structure. She has not yet formally documented the Ruth vision, the Lily-hand movement, or other subjective events. The department distinguishes stabilization from recovery and has not promised Daniel’s restoration or the photograph’s reversal.

At dawn, while Mara was being escorted for medical screening, water moved through the archive pipes and a child softly sang the first line of Elena’s lullaby. Halpern and possibly Vale heard or registered the event, though Vale did not answer Mara’s question. Emergency lights cast yellow rectangles across the floor; Mara briefly perceived them as windows of the yellow house, one darkening from within, but avoided looking directly.

Unresolved threads: the unseen remainder and apparent agency of AM-97-441; its physical resistance to destruction; unstable provenance and possible manufacture; the yellow house and Miller Road; Lily/Ruth’s status and relationship to Elias, Daniel, Elena, and other victims; Pickle; wet handprints, water, laughter, and singing; alteration or propagation through photographs, cards, phones, and other objects; whether the anomaly can displace or manifest its subjects; Elena’s concealed knowledge; the department’s authority and full history; the fate and treatment of Daniel; Mara’s degree of contamination; and whether preserving testimony itself risks spreading the anomaly.

chapters.name: The Paper Mill
chapters.content:
The road narrowed after Harrisburg and climbed into the hills.

Mara watched it through the darkened windows of the department vehicle: wet pavement, bare trees, collapsed stone walls, mailboxes leaning toward the ditch. Dawn had not yet arrived. A clear partition divided her from Agent Halpern and the driver. Padded polymer cuffs enclosed her wrists, loose enough to flex her fingers.

Dr. Vale sat beside her, reading a paper folder.

“Where are we going?” Mara asked.

“An observation site,” Halpern said from the front.

“That’s not an answer.”

“It’s the answer you’re cleared to have.”

Vale closed the folder. “A containment facility. Medical observation, interviews, provenance consultation.”

“Where?”

“North of here.”

Mara looked at the partition. Halpern’s reflection floated over the road. “And Daniel?”

“Transferred ahead of us,” Vale said.

“Is he awake?”

“For portions of the trip.”

“Did he ask for me?”

“He asked for Lily.”

The name brought thunder with it, chlorine and wet grass, the blue-flowered plate cracked down the middle.

“What did you tell him?”

“That Lily is not a person in the facility.”

“He won’t accept that.”

“No,” Vale said. “He won’t.”

The vehicle crested a ridge. Below, in a valley filled with mist, the paper mill appeared.

Its brick buildings spread beside a hidden river, connected by dark roofs and rusted pipes. A smokestack rose at the center. Floodlights burned along a new perimeter fence. At the entrance, a concrete gatehouse bore no sign.

The vehicle entered three successive gates. Each closed before the next opened.

“Why so many?” Mara asked.

“Compartmentalization,” Halpern replied.

“Against escape?”

“Against information.”

They stopped at a side door. Inside a white vestibule, the cuffs came off. Technicians bagged Mara’s coat, shoes, phone, identification, watch, and the paper folder containing her notes. One drew blood; another took saliva and clipped a pulse monitor to her finger.

A laminated card was held before her.

“What is your full name?”

“Mara Venn.”

“Date of birth?”

“July seventeenth, 1987.”

“Employment?”

“Allegheny Regional Archive.”

“Who is Daniel Reyes?”

“An assistant at the archive. Twenty-six years old. Born in 1994. He watched the tape.”

“Which tape?”

“AM-97-441.”

“Do you hear anything?”

“No.”

“See anything unusual?”

“No.”

“Feel that you have forgotten someone?”

Mara thought of the furnace window, the girl in the red sweater, Elias calling from another room.

“No,” she said.

It was not a lie, exactly. Forgetting implied having once known.

They gave her a gray cotton uniform and led her through the converted administrative wing. The corridor had been built inside the old mill but looked newly made: white walls, seamless rubber floors, doors with small squares of wired glass. Most of the windows had been covered from within.

There were no clocks. No ordinary machinery. No ventilation hum or fluorescent buzz. The building seemed to hold its breath.

At an intersection, a woman with close-cropped white hair waited beside a locked door.

“Saira Okafor,” Halpern said. “Site historian.”

Saira studied Mara. “I know.”

“Mara is consulting on provenance.”

“Then she’ll consult from outside the restricted vault.”

“I understand,” Mara said.

Saira looked at Vale. “Understanding what someone has been told isn’t the same as agreeing.”

They passed through two security doors into a corridor lined with pale ceramic panels. Copper mesh showed beneath transparent strips along the walls, like veins beneath skin. The air smelled of dust, hot metal, and minerals.

At the final door, Halpern placed her palm against a reader, then allowed an eye scan. The door released with a pressure sigh.

Beyond it was another door without a handle. Through a thick observation pane, Mara saw the vault.

It was almost entirely dark. Ceramic tiles covered every wall, ceiling, and floor, their joints sealed in black. Copper mesh formed a continuous lattice. Shelves stood beneath opaque covers. At the center hung a tall rectangular locker, suspended several inches above the floor on four steel supports.

No cables entered it. No pipes touched it.

“What is in the locker?” Mara asked.

“Media,” Saira said.

“How much?”

“Enough.”

Vale stepped beside the pane. “AM-97-441 is kept in a suspension locker. The locker is isolated from the building’s power, network, and environmental systems. The cassette is inside a mechanical inner sleeve, a ceramic pressure vessel, and an external containment cylinder.”

“The cylinder from the archive?”

“Replaced here.”

Mara searched the darkness. Within the locker, she could make out a small shape no larger than a loaf of bread.

“It’s in there now?”

“Yes.”

“I want to see it.”

“No,” Vale said.

“I’ve already seen it.”

“Unsecured contact in an uncontrolled environment is not authorized observation.”

“Then why bring me here?”

“Your expertise is not required for direct access.”

“You said provenance consultation.”

“Provenance can be discussed without visual contact.”

“You have contradictory records. A church, a school, private homes, a historical society—”

“We know.”

“You have fragments.”

“We have enough.”

“Enough to keep it in a box?”

Saira looked through the pane. “Sometimes a box is the most honest answer available.”

A small click came from inside the vault.

Mara’s skin tightened.

The click came again, like plastic teeth engaging.

“What was that?” she asked.

“Thermal contraction,” Vale said.

The temperature display beside the door showed 62 degrees.

Then a child laughed.

It was distant and muffled, two notes rising at the end. Mara recognized it before she heard the sound fully: blue pool, brown grass, a girl turning her head over her shoulder.

Saira closed her eyes.

Halpern touched her earpiece. “Vault status.”

A voice answered from beyond the wall. “Stable.”

“Confirm locker suspension.”

“Stable.”

“Confirm seal integrity.”

“Triple seal intact.”

The laughter ceased.

Mara looked at Saira. “Thermal contraction?”

“That was not an authorized transmission.”

Vale was writing in a small notebook.

“Do you record these events?” Mara asked.

“No recording devices are permitted in the vault zone,” Saira said.

“Then how do you know what happens?”

“People report it.”

“And you preserve the reports?”

Vale looked up. “When preservation does not constitute propagation.”

The answer left a shape around everything unsaid.

A buzzer sounded at the far end of the corridor. Halpern listened to her earpiece.

“Medical wing,” she said.

“Daniel?”

“Your room first,” Vale answered.

“You said he was ahead of us.”

“He is being monitored.”

“I want to see him.”

“Not yet.”

The medical wing occupied the former paper-testing laboratory. Its original windows had been bricked over. Each room held a bed, sink, toilet, and table bolted to the floor. There were no mirrors, exposed pipes, or personal objects.

Daniel lay in the third room with a clear tube in his arm. His hair was damp with sweat. A bruise darkened one side of his jaw.

His eyes opened before the door had fully closed.

“Mara?”

She stepped toward the glass. “I’m here.”

“They said you weren’t coming.”

“I came.”

“Did you bring my things?”

“No. They’re being examined.”

“My wallet’s in my jacket. My keys.”

“I know.”

He turned toward the wall. “I need the photograph.”

Mara glanced at Vale.

“It isn’t safe to return,” Vale said.

“It’s a picture of my family.”

“It’s a contaminated derivative.”

“It’s Lily.”

“It depicts an anomalous construct.”

Daniel sat up. The monitor began to beep faster. “You don’t get to call her that.”

“Daniel,” Mara said.

“No. You keep saying she’s a stain. She’s my sister.”

“You’re here because the tape has changed your autobiographical memory.”

“I remember my life.”

“Which one?”

He looked at her. For a moment his face seemed very young.

“The real one,” he said.

The nurse adjusted the tube. “Your pulse is elevated.”

“She made rice when money was bad,” Daniel said. “My mother. She sang to me.”

“What song?”

“The river one.”

“Tell me something else.”

“She had a scar on her left thumb from a can opener.” He faltered. “I don’t know.”

His face twisted.

Mara pressed her palm to the glass. “You know who you are.”

“I know who I was.”

“You’re still that person.”

“No.” His gaze shifted toward the corridor. “I’m the boy who buried Pickle.”

The monitor quickened.

The nurse put a hand on his shoulder. Daniel flinched so violently that the bed struck the wall.

“Don’t touch me,” he said. “Lily hates when people stand behind her.”

The nurse stepped away.

At the end of the corridor, two orderlies wheeled in a cart covered by a gray sheet. A sealed plastic bin sat beneath it.

Daniel saw it. “Those are mine.”

The orderly checked a tablet. “Personal effects, Reyes.”

“Give them to me.”

“They’re not cleared.”

“My jacket’s in there. The card.”

Mara’s breath caught. The birthday card had been separately contained. She had not known how it reached the department.

Daniel pushed upright. “The card says we’re both still there.”

Vale moved between him and the corridor. “Sedative.”

“Wait,” Mara said.

Daniel fixed his eyes on her. “You saw her.”

Mara said nothing.

“In the furnace,” he whispered. “You saw Lily.”

“I saw something.”

“You saw her.”

“I don’t know what I saw.”

“She told you to stay.”

Mara’s mouth went dry.

“She told me too,” Daniel said. “She said if I stayed upstairs, the window couldn’t take me.”

The nurse injected the sedative.

“No.” Daniel reached toward the glass. “Mara, don’t let them bury the house.”

His fingers touched the window.

Mara placed her hand against his.

The glass was cold.

For an instant something pressed back—not Daniel’s hand, but a smaller palm, wet and narrow, aligned beneath his. Five blurred fingers appeared on the inner surface, then vanished as the drug took hold.

Daniel’s eyes closed.

“Lily?” he murmured.

The nurse drew his hand away.

Mara kept her palm against the glass.

Vale stood beside her. “You are not to touch transparent surfaces in this wing without authorization.”

“Tell me the rule.”

“You don’t touch what may be touching back.”

They left Daniel sleeping under observation.

Mara was taken upstairs to a former office overlooking the river. The window had been replaced by a blank ceramic panel. A bed occupied one corner. On the desk sat a cup of water, two forms, and a pencil without an eraser.

She asked for her clothes.

“Later,” Halpern said.

“My notes.”

“Later.”

“My father’s records were in the archive system. Are they accessible?”

“You’ll receive paper copies.”

“Redacted?”

“Appropriately.”

Halpern stood in the doorway. “Sleep, Ms. Venn.”

“Where is the tape?”

“In the vault.”

“Can it be moved?”

“Yes.”

“Can it be destroyed?”

Halpern’s eyes shifted toward Vale. “No reliable method has been found.”

“The furnace didn’t work.”

“We know.”

“You knew it might not?”

“We suspected.”

“Then why let me try?”

“We didn’t.”

Mara remembered the door she had believed secured, Daniel entering through the side passage, the department arriving before she could complete her report.

“You were watching me.”

“We were tracking the object.”

“Same thing?”

“Not always.”

She sat on the bed. “What happens to Daniel?”

“Observation.”

“For how long?”

“As long as necessary.”

“Will he see his mother?”

“Not until we determine whether contact is stabilizing or transmissive.”

“He’s frightened because he’s alone.”

“He’s frightened because the anomaly is active.”

The distinction felt obscene.

Halpern left. The lock engaged with a soft metallic click.

Mara listened to the building: rain on the roof, a distant pipe settling, muted ventilation. Then water moved through the wall.

She counted the pulses.

One. Two. Three.

A child began to sing, faintly, almost submerged.

“Go to sleep, little river stone…”

Mara crossed to the ceramic panel and pressed her ear against it.

“The moon has a house of its own…”

The song stopped.

Something clicked on the other side.

She held her breath.

In the silence, she understood that the facility had not been built to keep the tape away from people.

It had been built to keep people from bringing the tape home.
chapters.summary:
Mara Venn, 38, Media Preservation Archivist at the Allegheny Regional Archive, distrusts nostalgia as sanitized distortion. Her father Elias died after dementia and alcohol dependence, obsessed with a nonexistent daughter named Ruth. He bought duplicate yellow raincoats, searched for Ruth, wrote her name compulsively, and claimed she had been taken by “the wrong family.” Official records identify Mara as an only child, but exposure to the anomaly has given her vivid impressions of Ruth/Lily-like imagery: a chipped-toothed, storm-fearing girl, a yellow house, an upstairs or attic confinement, and Elias calling from another room. Mara suspects the anomaly may have shaped or exploited Elias’s fixation without proving Ruth ever existed.

## AM-97-441 and Initial Exposure

At a failing thrift shop, Mara bought a swollen, mold-clouded VHS labeled **HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97**, with the final “7” retraced into a hook. The cassette was warm, clicked inexplicably, bore a rust-colored line and apparently fresh greasy thumbprint, and had contradictory provenance stories involving a cardboard box, the Voss house, a church, Miller Road, and a Miller Road cleanout. Mara initially sealed it under the archive rule **DO NOT PLAY UNCATALOGED MEDIA**.

Daniel Reyes, 26, born in 1994, secretly played about ten minutes on a repaired Panasonic television/VCR. The footage showed a yellow-sided house with white porch rails, green door, browned lawn, blue pool, sprinkler, a woman in a red bathing suit, and two children. Daniel identified the older boy as himself and the girl as his sister Lily, despite all records showing him as an only child raised by Elena Reyes in a Newark apartment.

The tape implanted an emotionally certain alternate childhood. Lily was nearly Daniel’s twin, eleven months younger, brown-haired, gray/green-eyed, with a summer cowlick and chipped upper tooth. She feared a basement window and thunderstorms, slept with the closet light on, hated peas and chlorine, and warned Daniel not to look at the window. The alternate home included a concrete basement, lightning-cracked window, rusted furnace, canned peaches, yellow-linoleum kitchen, burn mark, pantry floorboard, refrigerator drawing beneath a lemon magnet, and pool scenes with Elena in a red bathing suit.

Other implanted memories include Lily’s blue-flowered birthday plate cracked down the middle; her preference for the icing-heavy corner cake piece; an apple/tooth remark; and a brown dog named Pickle with one white paw and a scar over its left eye. Pickle escaped during a storm, died near a drainage ditch, and was buried by Daniel with a spoon. Daniel inconsistently dates these events to 1997 while remembering being seven. Static and partial footage induced details of a basement, dog-like shape, open door, dirty waving hand, water, dog tags, laughter, and possibly Lily behind the basement window. The cassette became warm after ejection.

Daniel retains documented memories—Newark, Elena, rice dinners during hardship, Lincoln Elementary, and a broken wrist at nine—but experiences them as emotionally flat beside the false childhood, which “has weather.” He physically feels Lily’s hand on his shoulder during thunder and remembers Elena’s incomplete lullaby:

“Go to sleep, little river stone,  
the moon has a house of its own.  
Lie in the dark where the cool reeds grow,  
dream of the places the tide won’t know.”

He initially lied about playing the tape, then demanded the remainder because Lily was still at the house. He briefly grabbed Mara’s wrist and accused her of erasing Lily. Both heard child laughter beneath television static.

## Propagation and Elena Reyes

Anomalous effects appeared beyond direct playback. A wet handprint appeared and vanished on corridor-door glass; similar prints, water sounds, and laughter manifested around Daniel’s apartment and the archive. Possible transmission routes include playback, handling, proximity, observation, discussion, and derivative objects.

Daniel’s refrigerator acquired a lemon-shaped magnet covering a pale rectangle and pencil marks resembling Lily’s drawing of a house with oversized windows and crooked chimney. A framed photograph altered from Daniel at eighteen outside a brick building in winter to child Daniel beside Lily by the blue pool, marked **DANNY & LILY — JULY 1997** in blue ink; the original remained physically behind it. Daniel associated the image with Lily cutting her foot in grass and refusing to cry, and with an uncertain possible father (“Not ours”). A resealed birthday card appeared in a tax-document shoebox:

**DANNY AND LILY REYES  
YELLOW HOUSE  
MILLER ROAD**

Inside: **TO THE TWO OF YOU—DON’T FIGHT OVER THE CORNER PIECE THIS YEAR.** It smelled of wet cardboard and matched Lily’s remembered preference. Mara separately bagged the photograph and card.

Mara never watched the tape, but handling the altered photograph caused an intrusive vision of a yellow-house hallway, child’s hand, chipped tooth, and Elias calling from another room. She briefly saw Lily’s hand move from a red cup to Daniel’s shoulder, then revert, and concealed this from Daniel. This established probable indirect or derivative exposure. At Daniel’s apartment, Mara and Daniel heard pipes and scraping; a wet handprint appeared beneath a broken light and vanished under direct observation.

Elena Reyes, 58, initially denied Lily, the yellow house, and Pickle. When Daniel supplied details, she became terrified, asked “Is she still there?” and “Is Lily still there?”, warned “Don’t bring her home,” claimed not to know Mara while addressing her by name, and stopped responding to calls. Her knowledge may be genuine, induced, or contaminated. The department later sent a team to her residence; its findings and current status are undisclosed.

## Failed Destruction and Department Intervention

At approximately 23:43, Mara removed the warm cassette from isolation and attempted destruction without playing it. An industrial shredder stalled under motor pressure; reversing it produced a strip of brown-black tape, water sounds, and muffled child laughter, yet the intact cassette appeared in the bolted lower compartment. A ceramic-lined film furnace failed to destroy it at temperatures above 1,700°F. A wet child’s hand appeared on the inspection window, and Mara perceived the chamber as a yellow hallway containing rain, canned peaches, a washing machine, and a basement window. She found herself holding an eight-year-old girl in a red sweater with damp fingers and chipped tooth. The girl said, **“Don’t look at the window,”** then, when Mara asked what to do, **“Stay.”** Elias called, **“Mara? Keep her upstairs.”** The vision ended with the girl’s hand slipping away, leaving Mara grieving despite knowing she had never met Ruth. The cassette emerged intact except for smoke-blackening.

At about 02:18, Mara attempted an incident report but could write only crossed-out terms such as “anomalous” and “damaged.” Daniel entered through a side door she believed secured, demanded the tape, and said Lily had predicted Mara would deny seeing her. Water sounds and a wet handprint returned. Daniel said, **“She found us.”**

Special Agent June Halpern of the **Department of Anomalous Media**, clinical containment specialist Dr. Irena Vale, and materials responder Tomas Wirth arrived before the archive alarm triggered. Halpern ordered everyone not to touch the object or describe its image, sound, or perceived people. The department designated it **AM-97-441**, a cognitohazardous audiovisual medium causing autobiographical implantation. AM is the department prefix, 97 the earliest confirmed production date, and 441 the catalog sequence. The department believes it was manufactured rather than spontaneous, but its maker is classified.

Wirth detected an indeterminate residual field. The cassette was transferred using articulated clamps into a ceramic-lined metal cylinder and sealed under a second cap. It clicked during handling, followed by a child’s laugh; Daniel lunged and shouted “Lily!” before Halpern restrained him. Once sealed, the laugh stopped.

The archive was locked down. Its network and records-wing water supply were disconnected; televisions, monitors, computers, audio devices, and even the staff refrigerator were unplugged after its compressor produced repetitive clicking. Agents documented the furnace, shredder, corridor glass, and floor. The altered photograph, birthday card, notes, phone, and other potentially contaminated materials were separately contained. Mara’s phone displayed access alerts, failed login attempts, and an unsolicited photograph of a yellow-sided house; Halpern seized and sealed it before Mara could examine it.

Vale assessed Daniel as suffering progressive autobiographical distortion. He correctly supplied his documented identity and history but insisted Lily and Pickle were real. Treatment could prevent implanted memories from acquiring further structure but would not necessarily erase them. Daniel was sedated and taken to a nonpublic medical observation site, saying, **“Don’t let them take the summer.”**

## Department History and Mara’s Status

Halpern disclosed 17 confirmed exposures and 32 probable exposures. AM-97-441 has moved through private homes, estate sales, church basements, a school media department, and at least two thrift operations, and has been tracked since 1997. Investigators often arrived after owners died or the tape changed hands. A reportedly destroyed copy resurfaced eleven years later in a box of donated children’s books. Chain-of-custody records are incomplete; contradictory thrift-shop accounts may each preserve fragments of its history.

Mara chose monitored consultant status over a standard nondisclosure agreement with monitored release. Her status includes psychological care, legal representation, controlled access to affected persons, archival/provenance work, and clearance-based access to records. She requested preservation of Daniel’s interviews and testimony, with redaction where necessary, and opposed erasing affected people’s accounts. She remains under departmental supervision for blood draw, neurological screening, baseline memory inventory, and determination of whether her exposure is direct, indirect, or derivative.

The department warned Mara not to describe her subjective impressions before clinical assessment because description may give them further structure. She has not formally documented the Ruth vision, Lily’s apparent hand movement, or other subjective events. The department apparently knows about the altered photograph, likely through external security footage, though Halpern denied hacking the archive. It distinguishes stabilization from recovery and has not promised Daniel’s restoration or reversal of the photograph.

At dawn, water moved through the archive pipes and a child softly sang the first line of Elena’s lullaby. Emergency lights cast yellow rectangles that Mara briefly perceived as windows of the yellow house, one darkening from within, but she avoided looking directly.

## Chapter 6: The Paper Mill / Current Containment

Mara was transported before dawn in a department vehicle to a converted paper mill north of Harrisburg, now an unmarked, heavily compartmentalized containment and medical-observation facility. The vehicle passed three successive gates, each closing before the next opened. Halpern said the compartmentalization was “against information” as much as escape.

On arrival, Mara’s cuffs were removed; technicians confiscated and bagged her coat, shoes, phone, identification, watch, and notes. She underwent blood and saliva collection, pulse monitoring, and a baseline interview. She correctly gave her name, birth date, employment, Daniel’s identity, and AM-97-441’s designation. She denied hearing or seeing anything unusual and denied feeling she had forgotten someone, considering this technically true because forgetting implied once having known.

The facility’s converted administrative and medical wings contain seamless rubber floors, covered or bricked-over windows, no clocks, mirrors, exposed pipes, personal objects, ordinary machinery, or audible ventilation. Mara met Saira Okafor, the close-cropped white-haired site historian, who knows of her and insists that understanding instructions is not the same as agreeing with them.

The restricted vault is lined with sealed ceramic panels and continuous copper mesh. Its isolated environmental and power systems contain a suspended rectangular locker, with no cables or pipes entering it. AM-97-441 is inside a mechanical inner sleeve, ceramic pressure vessel, and external containment cylinder; the cylinder used at the archive was replaced. The locker is isolated from the facility’s power, network, and environmental systems. Direct observation is prohibited. Personnel report anomalous events rather than record them in the vault zone, to avoid possible propagation. Saira stated that sometimes a box is “the most honest answer available.”

During Mara’s escorted viewing through the observation pane, the vault produced repeated plastic-like clicks and then a child’s two-note laugh, despite stable suspension and triple-seal integrity. Halpern confirmed the event was not an authorized transmission. Vale recorded notes; no recording device was used. The incident establishes that AM-97-441 can generate or transmit sound despite isolation, though the mechanism remains unknown.

Daniel had been transferred ahead of Mara and was under medical observation. In a sealed room with a clear observation window, he was sweaty, bruised at the jaw, connected to an IV, and distressed about his confiscated belongings, especially the altered photograph and birthday card. He rejected Vale’s description of Lily as an “anomalous construct,” insisting she was his sister and that he remembered his real life. He recalled Elena’s rice dinners and scarred thumb but faltered when asked for further documented details, then identified himself as “the boy who buried Pickle.” He became agitated when orderlies moved his contained personal effects, saying the card proved they were both still at the yellow house.

Daniel told Mara she had seen Lily in the furnace and that Lily had said staying upstairs would keep the window from taking him. Mara admitted only, “I saw something.” After Daniel pressed his hand to the observation glass, a smaller wet palm briefly appeared aligned beneath his, then vanished as he was sedated. Daniel called “Lily?” before losing consciousness. Vale warned Mara: **“You don’t touch what may be touching back.”**

Daniel’s condition is being monitored for stabilization versus transmissibility; contact with Elena is withheld until the department assesses whether it would help or spread the anomaly. His belongings, including the birthday card, remain uncleared. He remains frightened and objects to being separated from the summer and his family.

Mara was placed in a bare upper-room office with a ceramic-covered window, bed, bolted desk, cup of water, two forms, and an unerasable pencil. Halpern confirmed that AM-97-441 can be moved but that no reliable destruction method exists. Mara realized the department had been tracking her and/or the object before its overt arrival, though Halpern distinguished tracking the object from watching her. Daniel’s fate remains indefinite observation.

Later, water moved through the facility wall and a child sang Elena’s lullaby:

“Go to sleep, little river stone,  
the moon has a house of its own…”

When Mara pressed her ear to the ceramic panel, the song stopped and a click sounded from the other side. The facility’s apparent purpose is not simply to keep the tape away from people, but to keep people from bringing the tape home.

## Unresolved Threads

- The unseen remainder and apparent agency of AM-97-441, including sound generation through multiple containment layers.
- Its resistance to shredding and extreme heat, and whether it can truly be destroyed.
- Its unstable provenance, possible manufacture, original maker, and purpose.
- The yellow house, Miller Road, basement/window, and possible relationship to the Voss and other alleged locations.
- Whether Lily, Ruth, and other perceived children are implanted constructs, displaced real persons, victims, or manifestations of the anomaly.
- The relationship among Lily, Ruth, Elias, Daniel, Elena, and other exposed subjects.
- Pickle and the recurring water, wet hands, laughter, windows, and lullaby.
- Propagation through photographs, cards, phones, testimony, discussion, observation, and other derivatives.
- Elena’s concealed knowledge and the undisclosed outcome of the department’s visit to her.
- Daniel’s treatment, memory stabilization, possible recovery, and whether contact with him or his possessions is transmissive.
- Mara’s degree and route of contamination, including the furnace vision and possible connection to Ruth.
- The department’s complete authority, history, chain of custody, and ethical basis for containment.
- Whether preserving affected people’s testimony protects their identities or gives the anomaly further structure.

chapters.name: Rules for Looking
chapters.content:
The first rule was printed in red.

Mara read it twice before understanding that the sentence was not an instruction but a boundary.

**NO PERSON BORN ON OR AFTER 01 JANUARY 1991 MAY ENTER THE AM-97-441 VAULT ZONE.**

The page lay on the bolted desk beneath the ceramic-covered window. Three sheets, numbered by hand, printed on ordinary paper. No department letterhead, no seal. At the bottom of the first page:

**RULES FOR LOOKING**  
**REVISION 4.3 — CONTROLLED COPY**

Mara touched the corner. The paper was faintly warm.

“Why red?” she asked.

Saira Okafor stood opposite her with a metal tray containing breakfast: sealed oatmeal, two eggs, an orange without a peelable skin, and a bottle of water. Even the spoon was translucent and flexible.

“Because black ink invites interpretation,” Saira said.

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It is the answer we have written down.”

Mara looked at the rule. “Why use a date instead of an age?”

“Because the cutoff is observed by date of birth, not by developmental stage.”

“So someone born December thirty-first, 1990, can enter. Someone born the next day cannot.”

“Correct.”

“And they know why?”

“They know their date of birth. We don’t know whether the boundary is biological, cultural, chronological, or a property of the recording itself. We know everyone born after it who viewed the primary footage developed autobiographical implantation. Several people born before it experienced dreams, false recognition, and emotional bleed-through. None has yet developed a replacement childhood.”

“You use the date as if it were a wall.”

“We use it because pretending not to have a wall would be irresponsible.”

Mara sat on the edge of the narrow vinyl-covered bed. “Daniel was born in ninety-four.”

“Yes.”

“He can’t enter the vault.”

“No.”

“He can’t even be in the same hallway while you move the tape.”

“No.”

“But I can.”

“Under escort.”

“Because I was born in 1988.”

“Because you were born in 1988 and your baseline testing has not shown primary implantation.”

“Has it shown secondary implantation?”

Saira glanced toward the forms on the desk. “Your language has become more image-dependent.”

“That sounds like a yes.”

“It sounds like an observation.”

“Is Lily an image?”

Saira took a moment. “The procedure does not require us to decide what Lily is.”

“No. It only requires us not to say.”

“It requires us to distinguish verified information from subjective experience.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“No,” Saira said. “It isn’t.”

She pushed the tray toward Mara. “Eat before the briefing.”

“I’m not hungry.”

“You’ve been awake for twenty-seven hours.”

Mara drank the water because Saira was watching, and because its passage down her throat felt like a fact her body could still verify.

The formal briefing took place in a room at the end of the medical wing. Four walls, a table, six chairs, and a blank whiteboard. No clock. Dr. Irena Vale sat at the head of the table. Halpern occupied the chair nearest the door. A youngish man with gray at his temples sat beside Vale, a closed folder beneath both hands.

“Mr. Lasker is Security and Compliance,” Vale said.

“Ms. Venn.”

“Archivist,” Mara replied.

“Consultant,” Lasker said.

“Archivist.”

“Your employment classification is suspended pending review.”

“I’m not asking about payroll.”

“No,” Vale said. “You’re asking to retain a category of self that existed before we put you here.”

Mara looked at her. “Is that forbidden too?”

“Nothing is forbidden. Some things are unsafe.”

Lasker opened the folder. “Vault entry is restricted to personnel whose date of birth has been verified through two independent records and one biometric confirmation. Government identification is insufficient. Records and objects can be altered.”

“Biometric confirmation of what?”

“Identity continuity.”

“That isn’t a biometric measurement.”

“It is here.”

Before entry, each person provided fingerprints, retinal pattern, pulse, blood oxygen saturation, and a spoken identity statement: full name, date and place of birth, current assignment, two living people who could verify identity, and one personal fact absent from the personnel file.

“Why the personal fact?” Mara asked.

“Rehearsed facts are vulnerable to substitution.”

“What if I choose a false fact?”

“The discrepancy will be noted.”

“And if I believe it?”

“The discrepancy will still be noted.”

The post-contact statement repeated the questions without prompts or notes. Voice recordings from before and after were compared.

“No cameras?” Mara said.

“No cameras in the vault zone,” Lasker replied. “Verification occurs outside the inner corridor.”

The next section described the vault. It had no direct line of sight from occupied workspaces. The observation pane was layered ceramic composite, with a narrow optical channel that remained shuttered except during authorized transfer. Copper mesh ran continuously through the walls. The floor rested on a vibration-dampening platform. No cable, pipe, duct, or conduit entered the room. Environmental conditions were measured by sacrificial mechanical indicators rather than electronic sensors.

“Sacrificial?” Mara asked.

“Devices destroyed after use.”

“Because they might retain an image?”

“Because we don’t know what retention means.”

The tape would never be handled by a person. It would remain in a mechanical sleeve inside the suspension locker, then be transferred by an articulated arm through a sealed pass-through. The arm had no camera, microphone, wireless component, magnetic motor, or humanlike joint. Its range of motion was limited to the cassette.

“The playback deck is analog,” Mara said.

“Modified Panasonic industrial transport,” Lasker said. “The recording head has been removed and the aperture filled with ceramic resin.”

“So it cannot record.”

“That is the intention.”

“Has it been played?”

“Authorized portions. No full playback since 2014.”

“Who watched?”

“Pre-cutoff personnel.”

“What did they see?”

Vale’s gaze sharpened. “That question is outside your clearance.”

“You want me to enter the vault while refusing to tell me what happened to the last people who did.”

“We want you to enter because your archival expertise is relevant and your birth date makes you less vulnerable than Daniel’s,” Vale said. “We are not asking you to become curious.”

Mara laughed once. “Curiosity is the one thing here that doesn’t require biometric verification.”

“It should,” Halpern said.

Lasker moved to the playback controls. Playback required three operators, all pre-cutoff. One operated the mechanical arm. One monitored analog power draw and deck movement through needle gauges. The third controlled the signal-severance assembly.

“Why three?” Mara asked.

“No single person can decide when the signal has become unsafe.”

“That assumes three people can agree.”

“It assumes disagreement is visible, and delay is measurable.”

The three operators stood in separate control rooms. At any moment, each could pull a mechanical lever. When all three were engaged, the relay physically disconnected the deck from the monitor and grounded the output through a ceramic load. The deck might continue turning for several seconds, but no image or sound should reach the viewing apparatus.

“Should,” Mara said.

“Yes.”

The final page contained prohibitions.

No cameras, wireless devices, magnetic storage, watches, phones, tablets, memory cards, electronic displays, mirrors, photographs, sketches, or diagrams. No unapproved descriptions of the footage: not color, weather, architecture, clothing, faces, animals, voices, or emotional impressions.

Mara read the last category twice.

“Emotional impressions?”

“Those persist longest,” Vale said.

“More than visual details?”

“Visual details tell the mind what to construct. Emotional details tell it why.”

Mara thought of Daniel saying the false childhood had weather.

“What am I allowed to write?”

“Operational observations. Temperature, duration, equipment status, physiological response. You may write that you experienced fear. You may not write what frightened you.”

“That destroys testimony before it’s collected.”

“It delays testimony until we know whether testimony is carrying the anomaly forward.”

“Daniel is a person, not a contaminated document.”

Saira, seated against the wall, spoke quietly. “I know.”

“Do you?”

“Yes.”

“Then why are you helping them lock away everything he says?”

“Because understanding instructions is not the same as agreeing with them.”

Vale pushed a final form across the table. “You will sign that you understand the restrictions.”

“What happens if I break one?”

“Immediate withdrawal,” Lasker said. “Medical isolation. Review of every material you accessed. Possible memory suppression, depending on exposure.”

“Possible?”

“Experimental.”

“And if I refuse?”

“You remain in monitored isolation.”

“For how long?”

“No predetermined duration.”

There it was: the shape beneath every rule. The ability to turn uncertainty into a locked door and call the door compassion.

Mara picked up the pencil. It had no eraser. Her name was already typed on the signature line.

“Before entry,” she said, “I want to see Daniel.”

Vale shook her head. “Not today.”

“He asked me to help him.”

“He asked you to validate an implanted narrative.”

“He asked me not to let you take the summer.”

“Those are not equivalent.”

“They may be to him.”

Vale’s face altered—not into softness, but fatigue. “That is precisely the problem.”

Mara signed.

The entry check took place in a small chamber between two sealed doors. Halpern stood behind a painted line. Lasker operated the equipment.

Mara placed her fingers against a glassless scanner. A green light appeared beneath her skin and vanished. The retinal check required her to look into a black aperture. She saw only darkness.

“Full name.”

“Mara Elise Venn.”

“Date of birth.”

“June fourteenth, 1988.”

“Place of birth.”

“Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.”

“Current assignment.”

“Consultant to the Department of Anomalous Media, media preservation and provenance analysis.”

“Two living people who can verify your identity.”

“My mother and father are dead. Saira Okafor. June Halpern.”

“Personal fact not in your file.”

Mara looked at the sealed door. A yellow rectangle seemed to form beneath the gray, then disappeared.

“I can identify a failing capstan by pitch,” she said. “The pitch drops before the belt slips.”

Lasker recorded it on paper.

“Blood oxygen ninety-eight. Pulse eighty-four. Repeat your name.”

“Mara Elise Venn.”

“Why are you entering the vault?”

“To observe procedure and assist with provenance analysis.”

“Do you expect to see anyone inside?”

“No.”

The answer came too easily. She felt the urge to add: *Not Lily. Not Ruth. Not the girl by the window.*

Instead she said nothing.

The first door opened. Beyond it lay a narrow corridor of gray ceramic, lit by strips at ankle height. At the far end, another door waited.

As Mara crossed the threshold, three soft clicks sounded somewhere beyond the wall.

She stopped.

Halpern’s voice came through the intercom. “Report.”

“Mechanical noise.”

“Location?”

“Unconfirmed.”

“Description prohibited,” Lasker said.

“I didn’t describe it.”

“You classified it.”

“Record the classification.”

The second door opened. The vault remained hidden behind a shuttered observation panel. The mechanical arm was folded against the wall, its dull joints resembling an insect at rest.

Mara stood within the painted square.

“Identity check,” Lasker said.

She repeated her name, birth date, place, assignment, and personal fact.

“Why are you here?”

“To observe procedure.”

“Do you feel you have forgotten someone?”

The question entered her like cold water.

“No,” she said.

The answer was technically true. Forgetting implied once having known. Whatever Ruth was, Mara had no lawful memory of her. Whatever Lily was, Mara had not met her before the tape had begun its work.

The vault shutter opened three inches.

Through the narrow channel, Mara saw the containment locker: a black rectangle suspended in white ceramic. The cassette itself was hidden. The articulated arm unfolded with a faint hydraulic sigh, reached toward the locker, and adjusted by less than a millimeter.

Then something clicked inside the sealed room.

Not the arm. Not the locker.

A plastic button being pressed.

Mara’s hands tightened.

“Report,” Halpern said.

“Unauthorized mechanical sound.”

“Any visual change?”

“No.”

The arm continued. From behind the shutter came a wash of static—not television static exactly, but rain striking a distant roof, with a room listening beneath it.

The three operators remained silent. Mara imagined each waiting beside a lever, waiting for the signal to become something they could name. She understood why descriptions were forbidden. If someone said *house*, another person might see a house. If someone said *child*, the word might arrive carrying a hand, a tooth, a frightened face.

The arm lifted the inner sleeve.

A sound emerged from the vault.

Two notes, descending.

Mara’s breath stopped.

For one impossible instant, the corridor became a yellow hallway. A red cup rested on the floor. Somewhere above her, a child whispered not to look at the window. Her father called from another room, his voice younger and sober.

“Mara?”

The intercom snapped. “Report.”

She forced air into her lungs. “Auditory event. Possible tonal sequence.”

“Physiological response?”

“Elevated pulse.”

“Visual change?”

She looked at the shutter. It showed only the black seam of the vault.

“No.”

Inside, the arm placed the sleeve on the playback deck.

The deck did not activate.

No one moved.

Then the tape clicked once, as if something inside it had shifted its weight.

Mara stared at the narrow opening. She could not see the label, but knew what it said. She knew the final seven had been retraced into a hook. She knew the plastic was swollen from damp and that a greasy thumbprint had appeared where no thumb had touched it.

She knew these things because she had seen them.

Because Daniel had told her.

Because the tape wanted knowledge to feel like inheritance.

“Do not look for an image,” Vale said through the intercom.

Mara realized she had leaned forward.

The shutter closed.

The arm withdrew, carrying the sleeve back toward the locker. When the inner door sealed, the static ceased. The corridor returned to gray ceramic and ankle lights.

“Exit procedure,” Lasker said.

Mara crossed back over the painted line. The outer door opened. She entered the verification chamber and stood before the scanner.

“Full name.”

“Mara Elise Venn.”

“Date of birth.”

“June fourteenth, 1988.”

“Why were you in the vault?”

“To observe procedure and assist with provenance analysis.”

“Did you see a person?”

“No.”

“Did you see a place?”

“No.”

“Did you hear a voice?”

Mara thought of Elias calling from the yellow hallway.

“No,” she said.

Lasker’s machine recorded her pulse.

“Do you feel you have forgotten someone?”

Mara looked at the red revision stamp visible through the partition glass.

“No.”

Only when the door closed between her and the vault did Mara understand that the rules were not meant to tell them what was true.

They were meant to leave enough uncertainty intact that truth, once spoken, could not be used as a mold.
chapters.summary:
## AM-97-441 — Updated Story-So-Far Summary

### Core Anomaly and Initial Exposure
AM-97-441 is a dusty VHS labeled **HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97**, apparently manufactured around 1997 and tracked since then through thrift shops, homes, estate sales, churches, schools, and donated materials. Its provenance is contradictory and incomplete, involving the Voss house, Miller Road, a church, cardboard boxes, and cleanouts. The tape resists shredding and extreme heat and may generate sounds or effects without playback. The Department of Anomalous Media (DAM) classifies it as a cognitohazardous audiovisual medium that implants vivid alternate childhoods, especially in anyone born on or after **1 January 1991**.

Direct footage viewed by Daniel Reyes, born 1994, showed a yellow-sided house, white porch, green door, browned lawn, blue pool, sprinkler, a woman in a red bathing suit, and two children. Daniel identified himself as the older boy and Lily as his younger sister, despite all records identifying him as Elena Reyes’s only child. The implanted childhood includes Lily’s appearance and habits, fear of the basement window and storms, a concrete basement, rusted furnace, canned peaches, yellow kitchen linoleum, a refrigerator drawing, a cracked birthday plate, corner-piece cake preference, and a brown dog named Pickle. Static suggested a basement, water, an open door, a dirty waving hand, dog tags, laughter, and possibly Lily behind the basement window.

Daniel retains verifiable memories of Newark, Elena, rice dinners, Lincoln Elementary, and a broken wrist, but experiences the false childhood as more emotionally vivid and weather-filled. He remembers Lily’s touch during thunder, Pickle’s death and burial, and Elena’s lullaby:

> “Go to sleep, little river stone,  
> the moon has a house of its own.  
> Lie in the dark where the cool reeds grow,  
> dream of the places the tide won’t know.”

### Propagation and Associated Figures
Effects propagate through more than direct viewing. Possible vectors include handling, proximity, discussion, observation, photographs, cards, phones, testimony, and derivative objects.

Daniel’s refrigerator gained a lemon magnet covering a pale rectangle and pencil marks resembling Lily’s drawing. A photograph altered from Daniel at eighteen to child Daniel beside Lily at the blue pool, captioned **DANNY & LILY — JULY 1997**. A birthday card appeared in a tax shoebox:

**DANNY AND LILY REYES / YELLOW HOUSE / MILLER ROAD**

with the message: **TO THE TWO OF YOU—DON’T FIGHT OVER THE CORNER PIECE THIS YEAR.** Both items are separately contained.

Mara Venn, 38, born 1988, Media Preservation Archivist, never viewed the tape directly but was exposed through the altered photograph and other derivatives. She has experienced intrusive imagery of the yellow house, a chipped-toothed girl, Elias calling from another room, and a furnace vision in which she held an eight-year-old girl in a red sweater who said **“Don’t look at the window”** and **“Stay.”** Elias, Mara’s deceased father, had dementia and alcohol dependence and obsessively searched for a nonexistent daughter named Ruth, bought duplicate yellow raincoats, and claimed she had been taken by “the wrong family.” Mara suspects a connection among Ruth, Lily, Elias, and the anomaly but has no proof Ruth existed.

Recurring manifestations include water sounds, wet child handprints, laughter beneath static, dark windows, pipes or scraping, and Elena’s lullaby.

Elena Reyes, 58, initially denied Lily, the yellow house, and Pickle. When Daniel supplied details, she became terrified, asked **“Is she still there?”** and **“Is Lily still there?”**, warned **“Don’t bring her home,”** addressed Mara by name while claiming not to know her, and ceased responding. DAM investigated her residence; the outcome remains undisclosed.

### Destruction Attempt and DAM Containment
Mara’s unauthorized destruction attempt failed: an industrial shredder stalled and returned an intact cassette; a ceramic-lined furnace hotter than 1,700°F failed to destroy it and produced water sounds, laughter, a wet child’s hand, and the yellow-house vision. The tape emerged intact but smoke-blackened.

DAM agents June Halpern, Dr. Irena Vale, and materials responder Tomas Wirth intervened. Wirth detected an indeterminate residual field. The tape was moved by articulated clamps into ceramic and metal containment. The archive was locked down; networks, water, electronics, televisions, monitors, computers, and the refrigerator were disconnected. The altered photograph, card, notes, phone, and other materials were separately contained. Mara’s phone displayed failed login alerts and an unsolicited yellow-house photograph before seizure.

DAM reports 17 confirmed and 32 probable exposures. The anomaly is believed manufactured, but its maker and purpose are classified. No reliable destruction method exists.

Daniel was sedated and taken to a nonpublic medical site. He shows progressive autobiographical distortion while retaining some documented identity and history. He insists Lily is real, objects to the term “anomalous construct,” and remains distressed about separation from her, the “summer,” and his contained photograph/card. His condition is being monitored for stabilization versus transmissibility. Contact with Elena is withheld pending assessment.

Mara chose monitored consultant status rather than a standard nondisclosure agreement. She requested preservation of affected subjects’ testimony and opposed erasing their accounts. Her exposure route and degree of contamination remain under evaluation.

### Paper Mill Facility
Mara was transported to a compartmentalized former paper mill north of Harrisburg, now a DAM containment and medical-observation facility. Three successive gates close before the next opens; Halpern said the design protects against information as much as physical escape.

The facility removes or suppresses ordinary sources of imagery and sound: no clocks, mirrors, exposed pipes, personal objects, ordinary machinery, audible ventilation, electronic devices, or uncovered windows. Saira Okafor, the close-cropped white-haired site historian, told Mara that understanding instructions is not the same as agreeing with them.

The vault is lined with sealed ceramic panels and continuous copper mesh, rests on a vibration-dampening platform, and contains no cables, ducts, pipes, or direct line of sight. AM-97-441 is suspended inside a mechanical inner sleeve, ceramic pressure vessel, and external cylinder within a power- and network-isolated locker. Environmental monitoring uses sacrificial mechanical indicators rather than electronic sensors. Personnel report events rather than recording them in the vault zone.

Despite triple-sealed isolation, the vault previously produced plastic-like clicks and a child’s two-note laugh. The event was not authorized transmission, and no recording device was used.

### Chapter 7 — Rules for Looking
DAM’s controlled document **RULES FOR LOOKING, Revision 4.3** establishes:

- **No person born on or after 1 January 1991 may enter the AM-97-441 vault zone.**
- The cutoff is based on date of birth, not age or development. Post-1990 direct viewers develop autobiographical implantation; pre-1991 personnel have experienced dreams, false recognition, and emotional bleed-through but no confirmed replacement childhood.
- Entry requires dual documentary birth-date verification and biometric identity continuity.
- Personnel must provide fingerprints, retinal pattern, pulse, oxygen saturation, full identity statement, two living identity verifiers, and a personal fact absent from their file.
- Pre- and post-entry statements are compared; discrepancies are recorded even if believed by the subject.
- No cameras, wireless devices, magnetic storage, watches, phones, displays, mirrors, photographs, sketches, diagrams, or unauthorized descriptions of footage are permitted.
- Descriptions of emotional impressions are restricted because emotional details may persist longer than visuals: visuals tell the mind what to construct, emotions tell it why.
- Vault monitoring uses no cameras or electronic sensors. Mechanical equipment is sacrificial where possible.
- The cassette is never handled directly. A nonmagnetic, nonwireless articulated arm transfers it through a sealed pass-through.
- The modified Panasonic industrial deck has its recording head removed and aperture filled with ceramic resin.
- Playback requires three pre-cutoff operators in separate control rooms: one controls the arm, one monitors analog power and deck movement, and one controls signal severance.
- All three must engage before playback; any operator can mechanically disconnect the deck, ground output through a ceramic load, and sever image/sound.
- Post-exposure failure can result in medical isolation, review of all accessed materials, and possible experimental memory suppression. Refusal means indefinite monitored isolation.

Mara challenged the rules as potentially destroying testimony and reducing Daniel to a contaminated document. Vale argued that his request for validation might be validation of an implanted narrative. Saira acknowledged the ethical conflict without resolving it.

### Mara’s Vault Entry
Because Mara was born in 1988 and has shown no confirmed primary implantation, she was permitted escorted entry for procedural observation and provenance analysis. She signed forms despite objecting to indefinite detention and the possibility of experimental memory suppression.

During pre-entry verification she correctly gave her identity, birth date, assignment, and a personal fact: she can identify a failing capstan by pitch before its belt slips. Asked whether she expected to see anyone inside the vault, she answered no, suppressing thoughts of Lily, Ruth, and the girl by the window.

In the gray ceramic corridor, three unexplained clicks occurred. Inside the vault she observed the suspended locker and mechanical arm through a shutter opened only three inches. The arm moved the inner sleeve onto the playback deck, which did not activate. Static resembling distant rain and a listening room emerged, followed by two descending notes. Mara experienced an intense but concealed vision/impression of a yellow hallway, a red cup, a child warning not to look at the window, and Elias calling her name. She reported only an auditory event and elevated pulse, denied visual change, and obeyed the prohibition against describing the content.

The tape clicked as if shifting its weight. Vale warned her not to look for an image. The shutter closed and the sleeve was returned to the locker. During post-entry questioning Mara denied hearing a voice, seeing a person or place, and feeling she had forgotten someone. Her pulse was recorded, but the department did not yet confront her apparent concealment.

The rules’ deeper function is uncertain: they may not determine truth but preserve enough ambiguity to prevent spoken descriptions from becoming templates for further implantation. Mara now knows that DAM’s containment strategy seeks not only to keep AM-97-441 away from people, but to prevent people from carrying its images, emotions, and narratives back into the world.

### Unresolved Threads
- Whether AM-97-441 can truly be destroyed, and how it produces sound through isolated containment.
- Its maker, original purpose, manufacture date, and contradictory chain of custody.
- The yellow house, Miller Road, Voss property, basement/window, and possible real-world location.
- Whether Lily, Ruth, Pickle, and other figures are implanted constructs, displaced persons, victims, or manifestations.
- The relationship among Lily, Ruth, Elias, Daniel, Elena, and other exposed subjects.
- Elena’s concealed knowledge and current condition.
- Daniel’s treatment, transmissibility, possible recovery, and the fate of his photograph/card.
- Mara’s indirect contamination, her concealed vault vision, and possible connection to Ruth.
- Whether testimony, photographs, cards, phones, discussion, and observation propagate the anomaly.
- DAM’s full history, authority, ethics, and possible prior knowledge of Mara.
- Whether containment protects affected identities or erases them—and whether silence itself allows the anomaly to retain control.

chapters.name: The Interview Schedule
chapters.content:
The first thing Dr. Vale gave Mara was a clock.

It was a small mechanical timer with a red hand and a brass bell. The bell had been removed, leaving two empty screw holes in the casing. Without the bell, the device could measure a period but could not announce its end.

“Why no digital display?” Mara asked.

“Because you would look at it.”

“I need to know the time.”

“You need to know the intervals. Those aren’t the same thing.”

Vale wound the timer. The spring made a dry, insectlike sound. They sat in an interview room on the medical side of the paper mill, though the room contained nothing Mara associated with medicine. The walls were gray ceramic beneath paint. A table and two chairs were bolted to the floor. A third chair stood empty against the wall, its back facing them.

Mara had been told the room was not electronically monitored. Someone waited beyond the sealed door, listening through a tube microphone or perhaps only watching for the agreed signals. She had not asked which. Every unanswered question in the facility seemed to acquire weight.

Vale set a paper folder on the table. It had no title, no stamped number, and no identifying mark except a narrow blue thread sewn through the upper corner.

“Exposure protocol,” she said. “This applies to direct viewers and to anyone with probable secondary exposure. Sedation, isolation, removal of personal objects, then interviews at six hours, twenty-four hours, seventy-two hours, and thirty days.”

“Sedation first?”

“Usually.”

“Usually?”

“We sedate before the subject can tell us what they saw. The first account is important, but it’s also the most transmissible.”

“Transmissible isn’t the right word.”

“It is when a person hears a description and begins remembering it.”

“Then call it memetic.”

“Memetic suggests we understand the mechanism.”

“And transmissible suggests we understand it less?”

“Correct.”

Vale opened the folder. The pages had been printed on heavy, uncoated stock. Mara noticed that even the staples had been removed. The papers lay in a stack held together by a strip of linen.

“At six hours, the subject remains in a bare room under constant light,” Vale said. “No windows, reflective surfaces, recognizable packaging, or personal clothing. Phones, wallets, photographs, jewelry, books, keys, and anything carried during exposure are removed before waking. Food and water are served in unlabeled containers.”

“Why remove personal objects?”

“Objects become anchors.”

“Or evidence.”

“Both.”

“You take their clothes?”

“Hospital garments without seams, pockets, logos, or color distinctions.”

“Shoes?”

“If medically necessary, plain disposable footwear.”

“What about wedding rings?”

“Removed.”

“That must be difficult for people.”

“The ring may be difficult for them.”

“You’re assuming the object is contaminated.”

“We’re assuming we don’t know what it is.”

Vale continued. “At the first interview we ask for orientation and immediate experience. Name, date of birth, present location, last verified memory before exposure. Then we ask whether the subject has acquired a person, place, event, object, or obligation.”

“Acquired?”

“Subjects often describe memories as if they’ve found something. We don’t correct them.”

“Why not?”

“Correction creates conflict. Conflict makes the implanted material defensive.”

Mara thought of Daniel in the medical wing. She had seen him once through the observation panel, seated on a bed in a pale blue shirt with the pockets removed. His hair had been cut short. He had been staring at the blank wall, smiling with an exhausted tenderness that did not belong in that room.

He had asked whether anyone had found Lily.

The nurse had said no one had been looking.

“At twenty-four hours,” Vale said, “we repeat the questions and ask for sensory detail, but not narrative detail.”

“What’s the distinction?”

“‘The floor was cold’ is sensory. ‘My sister slept in the room below me because she was afraid of the storm’ is narrative.”

“You ask them to separate perception from interpretation.”

“We ask them to separate what they experienced from what the memory explains.”

“That’s a reasonable clinical method.”

“It’s also containment.”

The timer ticked between them. Its red hand had moved less than a minute, but Mara had the impression that the room was getting smaller.

“At seventy-two hours, we test contradiction. We present verified facts from the subject’s life and ask whether they recognize them. We avoid images when possible. Images are too efficient.”

“Daniel knows his mother.”

“Does he?”

“He knows her name. He knows where he grew up.”

“Those are data points.”

“He knows she burned rice when she was tired.”

“Did he say that before discussing Elena’s lullaby?”

Mara said nothing.

Vale turned a page. “At thirty days, we assess whether the memories have stabilized into an alternate autobiographical structure. Functional identity, emotional allegiance, and transmissibility.”

“Emotional allegiance.”

“To the people inside the memory.”

“Do you ask whether they love the invented people?”

“We ask whether they would harm a real person to protect them.”

“Has anyone?”

“Not yet.”

The answer left a cold place in the room.

Mara rested her hands flat on the table. “And if the answer is yes?”

“Then we assess capacity, access, intent, and likelihood of repetition.”

“You isolate them.”

“We isolate anyone whose memories remain actively generative.”

“That’s a phrase.”

“It’s a clinical category.”

“It sounds like a way to avoid saying prison.”

“Prison has a sentence. These cases do not.”

Mara looked at the empty chair. “How long was the longest?”

Vale did not consult the folder. “Nine years.”

“Where is the subject now?”

“Dead.”

“From the anomaly?”

“From pneumonia.”

“Did she ever leave?”

“She was released twice.”

“And?”

“Both times she attempted to locate a house that did not exist.”

“Did she hurt anyone?”

“Not physically.”

“What does that mean?”

“She entered other people’s homes.”

The timer continued ticking.

Vale removed another sheet from the folder. “You will be given a statement form after this. It concerns your vault entry.”

“I already gave a statement.”

“You gave the statement we asked for.”

“That sounds like an accusation.”

“It is a discrepancy.”

Mara felt pressure gather behind her eyes: the beginning of the yellow hallway again. She saw, or almost saw, a red plastic cup on a floor painted the color of old cream. Somewhere beyond a wall, water struck glass.

“What discrepancy?”

“You reported an auditory event. Your pulse rose during the interval in which the mechanical system produced no measurable sound.”

“The equipment is imperfect.”

“Not in that way.”

“Then your instruments are.”

Vale regarded her. “The protocol assumes subjects may conceal information.”

“Why would they?”

“Because they know we will remove it.”

Mara looked at the empty chair. “You make concealment rational.”

“We make it survivable.”

A knock sounded beyond the door. Three taps, evenly spaced.

Vale answered with two.

A nurse entered carrying a tray. She wore gray clothing without a collar or pockets. No name badge, only a white strip of tape bearing a number. The tray held a glass of water, a paper cup, and a sealed packet of crackers with the wrapper removed. She set it down, checked the timer, and left.

“What’s in the cup?” Mara asked.

“Nothing for you.”

“It’s for Daniel?”

Vale did not answer.

“Where is he now?”

“Interview room three.”

“May I observe?”

“No.”

“May I hear?”

“No.”

“May I read the interview afterward?”

“No.”

“Then what exactly am I doing here?”

“Learning why you cannot.”

Vale gathered the folders and left.

Mara remained beneath the fixed light, listening to the timer tick toward a bell that could never sound. She imagined the spring running down. She imagined the red hand reaching its mark and continuing past it, because nothing in the mechanism knew that the interval was over.

After several minutes, the door opened again. This time Saira Okafor stood in the threshold.

“Come with me,” Saira said.

“Where?”

“To the archive room.”

“Is that where the testimonies are?”

“It is where the testimonies that are permitted to remain are kept.”

Saira did not wait for an answer. Mara followed her through two corridors. The facility’s silence changed from room to room. In one passage, it seemed soft and padded; in another, it pressed against the ears like deep water. There were no clocks, mirrors, exposed pipes, personal objects, ordinary machinery, audible ventilation, or uncovered windows. Every doorway had a number, but the numbers were painted on the floor rather than mounted at eye level.

The archive room was not an archive in any recognizable sense. Shelves held sealed envelopes instead of books. Each had been wrapped in translucent paper and tied with thread. Some bore dates. Others had only a black line. A steel cabinet occupied the center of the room, its doors secured by three different locks.

Saira sat at the central desk and read a document through a magnifying lens.
