“You’re angry,” she said.

“I’m being trained not to know anything.”

“That is different.”

“Is it?”

Saira lowered the lens. Her hair was close-cropped and white, though her face was not old enough to explain it. “Vale believes information is a vector. She isn’t wrong.”

“She believes a person’s account is a weapon.”

“Sometimes it is.”

“Daniel’s memories aren’t a weapon.”

“Not intentionally.”

Mara went to the shelves. “You have testimonies.”

“We have controlled records of interviews.”

“May I read one?”

Saira hesitated. The pause told Mara that permission was not hers to give alone. Then Saira selected an envelope from a locked drawer. She cut the thread with blunt scissors and slid out three pages.

“Read silently,” she said. “Do not repeat any sentence aloud.”

The testimony came from a woman born after the cutoff. Her name had been replaced by Subject L-12.

At six hours:

**I remember a lake. I remember being safe there.**

At twenty-four:

**The woman who brought me had a silver ring and laughed when I lied about catching a fish. I slept in the cabin with the windows open. There was a yellow towel on the line. I was afraid of deep water, but she was not.**

At seventy-two:

**Her name was June. She was my grandmother. She taught me that fish have a second heartbeat in the tail. She had a scar under her left thumb, white and shaped like a comma. She told me my mother had been frightened when I was born, but fear was not the same as rejection.**

Mara stopped reading.

The words were plain. That was the horror. Nothing ornate or visibly dangerous. Detail accumulated until the cabin had a temperature and June acquired a hand. Mara could smell lake mud, though there was no lake anywhere near the paper mill. The imagined water carried the flat green odor of reeds and old dock boards.

At thirty days:

**I know June was dead before I was born. I know there is no cabin. I know the lake is not any lake I can locate. I still wake expecting her in the kitchen. I still miss her.**

Below it, in a clinical hand:

**Subject accepts factual contradiction but reports no reduction in affective attachment. Subject requests permission to retain the name June in private writing. Request denied pending review.**

Mara looked up. “You destroyed the writing?”

“Most of it.”

“Why?”

“The writing began to alter.”

“The words changed?”

“The subject changed what she wrote. Each version incorporated whoever read it.”

“Did this one change?”

“Not while I had it.”

“You’re not sure.”

“No.”

Saira reached for the testimony. Mara held on a moment too long before releasing it.

“Understanding requires comparison,” Mara said. “Patterns. If you destroy every account that becomes specific, you’ll never know what the anomaly is doing.”

“We know what it is doing.”

“No. You know what it might do.”

“That distinction is expensive.”

“And ignorance is free?”

Saira tied the envelope shut. “You think an archive is where truth is kept safe.”

“It’s where records are kept available.”

“To whom?”

“To people who need them.”

“People change.”

“So do records.”

Saira returned the envelope to the drawer. “That is why this place is built like a burial site.”

Mara turned toward her. “You’re not answering the ethical question.”

“There is no ethical question that survives contact with an active hazard.”

“That’s convenient.”

“It’s not convenient. It’s a way of speaking that keeps people alive.”

“Alive in what sense? Daniel can recite the facts of his life, but he talks about them like they’re an embarrassing school assignment. His mother is alive, and you’ve made her inaccessible. Lily isn’t. You’ve made her the center of his grief. What do you call that?”

Saira’s expression tightened. “A successful implantation.”

“No. A person in pain.”

“Those statements are not mutually exclusive.”

The admission unsettled Mara more than a denial would have.

A low mechanical buzzer sounded somewhere beyond the walls.

Saira stood. “Your statement form is ready.”

“I’m not signing a false account.”

“You’re not being asked to sign a true one.”

“That’s reassuring.”

“It records what you’re permitted to report.”

“What am I permitted to report?”

“Sound, pulse, motor response, involuntary speech.”

“Not visual impressions.”

“Not descriptions.”

“Not names.”

“Not emotional detail.”

“What if emotional detail is the only thing that matters?”

Saira’s face shifted—not disagreement, but recognition.

“Then you must decide whether sharing it helps the person who felt it,” she said, “or the thing that made them feel it.”

The question followed Mara through the corridor.

At the medical wing door, a narrow panel opened. A nurse handed her a sealed paper packet. Inside were a form, a pencil, and a printed warning:

**ALL UNAUTHORIZED COPIES, TRANSCRIPTS, SKETCHES, RECORDINGS, AND DESCRIPTIVE NOTES ARE TO BE SURRENDERED FOR DESTRUCTION.**

Mara read it twice.

“Who destroys them?” she asked.

The nurse pointed down the corridor.

At its end stood a gray metal bin beneath a red line. The bin was locked. Above it, another notice said:

**DO NOT PLACE MATERIAL IN BIN WITHOUT WITNESS.**

“Why a witness?” Mara asked.

The nurse’s numbered tape showed a 4. “So no one keeps a copy.”

Mara looked through the narrow medical-wing panel. Daniel sat somewhere beyond the next door. She could not see him, only the edge of a bed and one bare section of wall.

Then she heard his voice.

“Lily says you promised.”

A second voice answered him, too low to understand.

Mara gripped the packet until the paper bent.

She wanted to open the door. She wanted to ask what Lily had said, what she wanted, what she looked like now. She wanted to write down every word before the department destroyed it, before the memory changed, before Daniel forgot which mother was real.

Instead, she sat at the bolted table and wrote:

**I heard a voice.**

She paused, pencil poised.

The rest of the sentence waited inside her, carrying a name, a promise, and the shape of a child’s hand.

Mara crossed it out before it could become a record.

## AM-97-441 — Updated Story-So-Far Summary

### Core Anomaly and Initial Exposure
AM-97-441 is a dusty VHS labeled **HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97**, apparently made around 1997 and repeatedly circulating through thrift shops, homes, estate sales, churches, schools, and cleanouts. Its provenance is contradictory, involving the Voss house, Miller Road, a church, cardboard boxes, and estate materials. The tape resists shredding and extreme heat and can produce sounds or effects without playback.

DAM classifies it as a cognitohazardous audiovisual medium affecting people born on or after **1 January 1991**. Direct viewers develop vivid false autobiographical memories of an alternate childhood. Effects may also propagate through handling, proximity, discussion, photographs, cards, phones, testimony, observation, and derivative objects.

Daniel Reyes, born 1994, saw footage of a yellow-sided house with a white porch, green door, browned lawn, blue pool, sprinkler, a woman in red swimwear, and two children. He identified himself as the older boy and Lily as his younger sister, despite records establishing him as Elena Reyes’s only child. His implanted memories include Lily’s appearance and habits, fear of the basement window and storms, a concrete basement, rusted furnace, canned peaches, yellow kitchen linoleum, a refrigerator drawing, a cracked birthday plate, corner-piece cake preference, and a brown dog named Pickle. Static suggested a basement, water, an open door, a dirty waving hand, dog tags, laughter, and possibly Lily behind the basement window.

Daniel retains verified memories of Newark, Elena, rice dinners, Lincoln Elementary, and a broken wrist, but the false childhood is more emotionally vivid. He remembers Lily comforting him during thunder, Pickle’s death and burial, and Elena’s lullaby:

> “Go to sleep, little river stone,  
> the moon has a house of its own.  
> Lie in the dark where the cool reeds grow,  
> dream of the places the tide won’t know.”

### Propagation and Affected People
Daniel’s refrigerator acquired a lemon magnet covering a pale rectangle and pencil marks resembling Lily’s drawing. A photograph changed from Daniel at eighteen to child Daniel beside Lily at the blue pool, captioned **DANNY & LILY — JULY 1997**. A birthday card appeared in a tax shoebox addressed to:

**DANNY AND LILY REYES / YELLOW HOUSE / MILLER ROAD**

Message: **TO THE TWO OF YOU—DON’T FIGHT OVER THE CORNER PIECE THIS YEAR.** The photograph and card are separately contained.

Mara Venn, 38, born 1988, was never a direct viewer but became exposed through derivatives. She experiences imagery of the yellow house, a chipped-toothed girl, Elias calling from another room, and a furnace vision of an eight-year-old girl in a red sweater saying **“Don’t look at the window”** and **“Stay.”** Her deceased father Elias, who had dementia and alcohol dependence, obsessively searched for a nonexistent daughter named Ruth, bought duplicate yellow raincoats, and claimed she had been taken by “the wrong family.” Mara suspects a connection among Ruth, Lily, Elias, and AM-97-441, but has no proof.

Recurring manifestations include water sounds, wet child handprints, laughter beneath static, dark windows, pipes or scraping, and Elena’s lullaby.

Elena Reyes, 58, initially denied Lily, the yellow house, and Pickle. When Daniel supplied details, she became terrified, asked **“Is she still there?”** and **“Is Lily still there?”**, warned **“Don’t bring her home,”** addressed Mara by name while claiming not to know her, and stopped responding. DAM investigated her residence; her current condition remains undisclosed.

### Destruction Attempt and DAM Containment
Mara’s unauthorized destruction attempt failed. An industrial shredder stalled and returned an intact cassette; a ceramic-lined furnace exceeding 1,700°F failed to destroy it and produced water sounds, laughter, a wet child’s hand, and the yellow-house vision. The tape emerged intact but smoke-blackened.

DAM agents June Halpern, Dr. Irena Vale, and materials responder Tomas Wirth intervened. Wirth detected an indeterminate residual field. The tape was transferred by articulated clamps into ceramic and metal containment. The archive was locked down; networks, water, electronics, televisions, monitors, computers, and the refrigerator were disconnected. Derivative materials, notes, Mara’s phone, photograph, and card were separately contained. DAM has recorded 17 confirmed and 32 probable exposures.

Daniel was sedated and transferred to a nonpublic medical site. He shows progressive autobiographical distortion while retaining documented facts. He insists Lily is real, rejects “anomalous construct,” and remains distressed about separation from Lily, the summer, and his contained photograph/card. His stabilization, transmissibility, treatment, and possible contact with Elena remain unresolved.

Mara accepted monitored consultant status instead of a standard nondisclosure agreement and argued that affected subjects’ testimonies should be preserved rather than erased.

### Paper Mill Facility and Rules for Looking
Mara was taken to a compartmentalized former paper mill north of Harrisburg, now a DAM containment and medical-observation site. Three successive gates close before the next opens; the design is intended to contain information as well as physical escape.

The facility suppresses ordinary imagery and sound: no clocks, mirrors, exposed pipes, personal objects, ordinary machinery, audible ventilation, electronic devices, or uncovered windows. Saira Okafor, the close-cropped white-haired site historian, warned that understanding instructions is not the same as agreeing with them.

The vault uses sealed ceramic panels, continuous copper mesh, vibration damping, no cables, ducts, pipes, or direct line of sight, and a mechanical inner sleeve inside a ceramic pressure vessel and external cylinder. Power and networks are isolated. Mechanical indicators replace electronic sensors, and personnel report vault events without recording them. Even so, the vault has produced unexplained plastic-like clicks and a child’s two-note laugh.

**RULES FOR LOOKING, Revision 4.3** prohibits anyone born on or after 1 January 1991 from entering the vault zone. Pre-cutoff personnel have shown dreams, false recognition, and emotional bleed-through but no confirmed replacement childhood. Entry requires documentary birth-date verification, biometric identity continuity, fingerprints, retinal pattern, pulse, oxygen saturation, a full identity statement, two living identity verifiers, and a personal fact absent from the file. Pre- and post-entry statements are compared for discrepancies.

No cameras, wireless devices, storage, watches, phones, displays, mirrors, photographs, sketches, diagrams, or unauthorized footage descriptions are allowed. Emotional impressions are restricted because they may outlast visuals and help generate narrative templates. Playback requires three pre-cutoff operators in separate control rooms, a modified Panasonic deck with its recording head removed, and independent controls for the arm, analog power/deck movement, and signal severance. Any operator can mechanically disconnect the deck, ground output through a ceramic load, and sever image/sound. Post-exposure failure may lead to medical isolation, material review, experimental memory suppression, or indefinite monitored isolation.

### Mara’s Vault Entry
Because Mara was born in 1988 and has no confirmed primary implantation, she was permitted escorted procedural entry for provenance analysis. Before entry she correctly verified her identity, birth date, assignment, capstan-diagnosis skill, and other required facts. When asked whether she expected anyone inside, she denied thoughts of Lily, Ruth, and the girl by the window.

In the ceramic corridor, three unexplained clicks occurred. Through a shutter opened only three inches, Mara observed the suspended locker and mechanical arm. The arm placed the inner sleeve on the playback deck, which did not activate. Static resembling distant rain and a listening room emerged, followed by two descending notes. Mara privately experienced a yellow hallway, a red cup, a child warning not to look at the window, and Elias calling her name. She reported only an auditory event and elevated pulse, denied hearing a voice or seeing a person/place, and concealed the visual and emotional content. The tape clicked as if shifting its weight. The sleeve was returned to containment.

### Chapter 8 — The Interview Schedule
Dr. Vale gave Mara a small mechanical timer with a red hand and its bell removed. It measures intervals without announcing their end. DAM’s exposure protocol schedules interviews at **six hours, twenty-four hours, seventy-two hours, and thirty days** after exposure, generally after sedation and isolation.

Initial procedures include:
- Bare room under constant light.
- Removal of phones, wallets, photographs, jewelry, keys, books, personal clothing, and other possible “anchors.”
- Hospital garments without seams, pockets, logos, or color distinctions.
- Unlabeled food and water in plain containers.
- No reflective surfaces, windows, recognizable packaging, or personal objects.

At six hours, subjects are asked for orientation, name, birth date, location, last verified pre-exposure memory, and whether they have “acquired” a person, place, event, object, or obligation. DAM avoids immediately correcting implanted material because conflict may make it defensive.

At twenty-four hours, interviewers request sensory details but avoid narrative details. “The floor was cold” is permitted; explanations involving family relationships or history are considered narrative and potentially transmissible.

At seventy-two hours, verified life facts are presented without images when possible, and subjects are tested for contradictions. At thirty days, DAM assesses stabilization into an alternate autobiographical structure, functional identity, emotional allegiance to implanted figures, and transmissibility. Subjects may be evaluated for capacity, access, intent, and likelihood of repetition if they would harm real people to protect implanted ones. “Actively generative” subjects may be isolated indefinitely; the longest prior case lasted nine years, with two failed releases and attempts to enter homes searching for a nonexistent house. The subject eventually died of pneumonia.

Vale identifies a distinction between a subject’s experienced perception and the narrative that explains it. She also acknowledges that DAM’s restrictions make concealment rational because disclosed information may be removed or treated as dangerous.

During post-vault review, Vale confronted Mara with a discrepancy: her pulse rose during an interval in which mechanical systems registered no measurable sound, despite her report of only an auditory event. Mara blamed imperfect equipment and continued withholding the yellow-hallway vision, red cup, child’s warning, and Elias’s voice.

Mara asked about Daniel. Vale said he was in interview room three and refused permission for Mara to observe, listen, or read the interview. Mara heard Daniel say, **“Lily says you promised,”** followed by an indistinct low response.

### DAM Testimony Archive
Saira brought Mara to a restricted archive where testimonies are stored as sealed envelopes tied with thread. The room contains no ordinary books; a central steel cabinet has three locks. Saira permitted Mara to silently read a controlled testimony from a post-cutoff subject designated **Subject L-12**, warning her not to repeat any sentence aloud.

L-12’s six-hour account concerned a safe lake. By twenty-four hours, it included a woman with a silver ring, a fishing cabin, a yellow towel, and fear of deep water. By seventy-two hours, the woman had become **June**, L-12’s grandmother, with a scar under her left thumb, a specific teaching about fish, and a history explaining L-12’s mother. At thirty days, L-12 accepted that June had died before L-12 was born and that the cabin and lake could not be located, yet still woke expecting June and continued to miss her. DAM denied L-12’s request to retain the name June in private writing.

Saira said much of L-12’s writing was destroyed because it began to alter, with each version incorporating whoever read it. She admitted uncertainty over whether the preserved testimony itself had changed. Mara argued that destroying specific accounts prevents understanding the anomaly’s patterns. Saira replied that an archive cannot safely preserve truth when people and records change, and described the facility as built like a burial site.

Saira framed the central ethical problem as whether sharing emotional detail helps the affected person who felt it or the anomaly that caused it. She acknowledged that Daniel is both a subject of successful implantation and a person in pain; these conditions are not mutually exclusive.

### Mara’s Current Statement and Concealment
Mara received a form, pencil, and warning that all unauthorized copies, transcripts, sketches, recordings, and descriptive notes must be surrendered for witnessed destruction. The form permits only sound, pulse, motor response, and involuntary speech; visual descriptions, names, and emotional details are prohibited.

Mara wrote **“I heard a voice.”** She began to add the concealed name, promise, and shape of a child’s hand, then crossed out the rest before it could become a record. She remains indirectly contaminated, aware that her vault impression may be connected to Lily, Ruth, and Elias, and is now consciously withholding potentially significant information from DAM.

### Major Unresolved Threads
- Whether AM-97-441 can be destroyed and how it produces sound through isolated containment.
- Its maker, intended purpose, manufacture date, and contradictory chain of custody.
- The reality or significance of the yellow house, Miller Road, Voss property, basement/window, and possible physical location.
- Whether Lily, Ruth, Pickle, June, and related figures are implanted constructs, displaced people, victims, or manifestations.
- The relationship among Lily, Ruth, Elias, Daniel, Elena, Subject L-12’s June, and other exposed subjects.
- Elena’s concealed knowledge and present condition.
- Daniel’s treatment, memory stabilization, emotional allegiance, transmissibility, and the significance of Lily’s claim that he “promised.”
- The fate and possible activity of Daniel’s altered photograph and birthday card.
- Mara’s concealed vault vision, her connection to Ruth, and whether she is becoming actively generative.
- Whether testimony, emotional detail, private writing, and records propagate or alter the anomaly.
- DAM’s prior knowledge, authority, ethical limits, and history of long-term containment.
- Whether containment protects affected identities or erases them, and whether silence itself allows AM-97-441 to control the surviving narrative.

### The Lakeside Camp

The envelopes in the archive had been tied with thread because thread could not be copied.

That was what Saira told Mara when she unlocked the steel cabinet.

“Not literally,” she said. “Nothing is impossible literally anymore. But thread has no magnetic field, no memory cache, no convenient way to transmit a sequence. It also makes people handle the material slowly.”

The cabinet stood in the center of the room, raised on four ceramic feet. Its doors were painted the same gray as the walls. There were no labels on the outside, only three keyholes and a strip of white tape bearing a number: 4.

Saira used three keys. One belonged to her, one to the site director, and one remained in a sealed box that could be opened only by two pre-cutoff witnesses. The locks turned at different speeds. The last one made a dry, reluctant click.

Inside, the envelopes rested in shallow drawers. Some were white, some brown, some nearly black with age. Each bore an alphanumeric designation in pencil and, beneath it, a date of birth. No names.

Mara had expected the archive to feel protected. Instead it felt like a room where evidence had been sentenced.

“You said these were earlier cases,” she said.

“Earlier confirmed cases involving the same medium or its close derivatives.”

“Close derivatives means—”

“Do not make me define it in this room.”

Mara looked at the drawer Saira had opened. L-12 was written on the first envelope.

“Why L?”

“Lake.”

“So the designation tells us what the subject remembered?”

“It tells us what the first interviewer thought the subject remembered. That distinction has caused trouble.”

Saira removed the envelope and held it between two fingers. The thread was green, faded almost gray. A small paper seal crossed the knot. On it, someone had written: DO NOT READ ALOUD.

“You may read silently,” Saira said. “You may not copy. You may not repeat a phrase, even to ask what it means. If you encounter a visual description, skip it.”

“Why?”

“Because you are not the subject.”

“That sounds like a reason to read carefully.”

“It is a reason to let the subject retain ownership of it.”

Saira placed the envelope on the table and stepped back.

Mara sat. The chair had no back. The room seemed designed to prevent anyone from settling into a story.

The first page was a cover sheet.

**SUBJECT L-12**  
**DATE OF BIRTH: 14 MAY 1992**  
**PRIMARY EXPOSURE: UNKNOWN**  
**PROBABLE ROUTE: DERIVATIVE PHOTOGRAPHIC MATERIAL**  
**INITIAL PRESENTATION: NOSTALGIC RECALL, GRIEF RESPONSE, DISPLACEMENT OF MATERNAL ATTACHMENT**

Beneath that, in a different hand:

**Subject repeatedly requested return to lake. No lake has been located.**

Mara turned the page.

The six-hour interview had been conducted after sedation. The account was brief, almost embarrassed.

L-12 knew her name, birth date, and the fact that she was in a Department medical room. She identified the last verified memory before exposure as eating dinner with her partner in a second-floor apartment. She remembered the plate, the food, and the argument they had been having about rent.

Then she said she had acquired a place.

Not a house. Not yet.

A lake.

The interviewer had asked whether it was a real lake.

L-12 had said, *Of course.*

The interviewer had asked where it was.

L-12 had begun to cry.

Mara stopped reading and looked at Saira.

“What?”

“She knew it was real before she knew where it was.”

“That is common.”

“Is it?”

“For the first hours.”

“Because the memory is stronger than the address?”

Saira did not answer. She had moved to the far side of the room and was inspecting the empty drawer beneath the one Mara had taken. Her attention seemed deliberate, but Mara had learned enough by now to recognize avoidance when she saw it.

The six-hour account continued. L-12 remembered a dock, though the record did not permit her to describe its appearance. She remembered water that was cold on the top and warmer below. She remembered a towel, yellow, rough against her knees. She remembered being told not to go past a certain point.

The interviewer asked who had told her.

L-12 said, *She did.*

Who was she?

*My grandmother.*

Did the grandmother have a name?

The answer had been redacted in black ink.

Mara read the next line.

**Subject became distressed when asked whether grandmother was alive. Subject stated: “She died, but not there.”**

There was a note in the margin: **Clarify temporal relationship.**

The twenty-four-hour interview was longer. It had been typed on a machine, then amended by hand. The first sentence was repeated three times with slight variations.

**Subject reports waking with smell of wet canvas, pine sap, and coffee boiled too long.**

The phrase *boiled too long* had been underlined.

L-12 remembered a cabin. She remembered the lake in a way that changed when she was asked to describe it: sometimes it belonged to her grandmother, sometimes to a group of children, sometimes to an entire summer that seemed to have no beginning. She remembered a screen door that failed to close unless lifted by its handle. She remembered a tin cup with a dent along the rim. She remembered her grandmother’s left hand, specifically a scar beneath the thumb.

Mara read the detail twice.

“How did they determine these details weren’t in the source?” she asked.

Saira’s voice came from behind her. “The source was seven seconds of degraded footage.”

Mara turned.

“Seven?”

“In that case. A damaged home-video segment found on a cassette in a church disposal bin. The image contained trees and water. No people were visible.”

“Not even a grandmother?”

“Not in the footage.”

“And the subject invented the scar?”

“Not invented, according to her.”

Mara went back to the page.

The interviewer had asked L-12 to describe the grandmother’s voice. That portion had been redacted. Below it, L-12 had been asked whether the voice belonged to anyone she had known in her actual life.

She had answered no.

The next question had been whether she had ever seen her grandmother outside the lake memory.

L-12 had answered yes. She said there was a photograph in her parents’ house.

The photograph had not existed.

At the seventy-two-hour interview, the contradiction had become more elaborate. L-12 knew her grandmother had died before she was born. She knew the date of the death, though the date was wrong by twelve years. She knew the woman had been cremated, though no family record supported this. She knew that her mother had hated the lake and that this hatred explained why the family never returned.

The interviewer asked whether her mother had ever told her this.

L-12 said, *Not in words.*

Mara felt a pressure rise behind her eyes.

There it was again: the anomaly’s particular cruelty. It did not merely provide an impossible person. It provided the emotional architecture required to make the person necessary.

A mother who would not speak. A place that could not be found. A grandmother whose absence had a reason.

She read on.

L-12 remembered being six years old and sitting under a table during a storm. She remembered the rain striking the roof in a pattern that her grandmother called “the little soldiers.” She remembered hating the phrase and later repeating it to another child. She remembered a joke about a fish that could read, a joke so private she could not explain why it was funny. When the interviewer pressed her, L-12 laughed for nearly thirty seconds, then became furious.

**Subject states: “If I tell you, you’ll ruin it.”**

Mara imagined the room where this had happened: light without shadows, smooth walls, a subject in a seam-free gown trying to guard a joke that had no origin. The department had removed her clothes and possessions, but not the memory of a yellow towel or the smell of coffee. They had stripped away every anchor except the one they could not reach.

“Why did you keep this?” Mara asked.

Saira stood with her hands clasped behind her back. “Because it demonstrated progression.”

“Progression of what?”

“Construction.”

Mara looked up.

Saira nodded toward the pages. “At six hours, there is a lake. At twenty-four, a grandmother. At seventy-two, a family history. The details do not emerge randomly. They gather around the subject’s deficits.”

“Deficits.”

“Emotional deprivation. Social isolation. Unresolved grief. Fear of abandonment. The tape supplies a childhood shaped to fit the empty spaces.”

“Was she deprived?”

“Her mother died when she was eleven. Her father was intermittently present. She spent much of adolescence alone. Her partner reported that L-12 had always been preoccupied with women she could not reach.”

Mara returned to the testimony.

The clinical notes had been placed behind the interview pages. They were less restrained than the transcripts.

**Subject repeatedly states that the lake was the only place where she was expected.**

**Subject reports that ordinary childhood memories have become “flat.”**

**Subject remembers being comforted by June during thunderstorms. Subject cannot account for the transition from grandmother to named person. When asked when she first learned the name, subject says “I always knew it.”**

June.

The name appeared in the next interview with no explanation. It had not been supplied by staff. L-12 had begun using it as if it had always been there.

Mara held her breath and read the description of June’s scar again, then the weather account, then the account of the storm. The details were not grand. That was what disturbed her. There were no impossible castles, no radiant signs, no scenes of miraculous rescue. There was a wet towel left on a chair. A spoon forgotten in a mug. A mosquito bite scratched until it bled. The grandmother had a habit of pinching the bridge of her nose when she lied. She lied about how long the drive home would take.

A childhood assembled from inconveniences.

A childhood convincing because it was not perfect.

Mara thought of Daniel’s cracked birthday plate, the corner piece of cake, Pickle’s tags clicking against the floor. The tape had not given him a heroic family. It had given him small things that could be missed. It had made Lily irritating and tender, frightened and funny. It had made loss ordinary enough to be believed.

“What happened to L-12?” she asked.

Saira did not answer immediately.

Mara saw the answer in the way her shoulders tightened.

“She asked to go back,” Saira said.

“To the lake?”

“Repeatedly.”

“How?”

“She tried to leave the facility. Twice. The first time she reached a bus station and asked for directions to a town that does not exist. The second time she attacked a nurse who told her there was no lake.”

“Because the nurse contradicted her.”

“Because the nurse was standing between her and June.”

Mara closed her eyes.

The room stayed silent. No ventilation, no hum from the lights, no distant machinery. Only the small movements of paper beneath her fingertips.

“Did she believe June was alive?”

“She believed June was waiting.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“It was functionally the same.”

The final pages had been written thirty days after exposure. L-12 had stabilized enough to answer questions without shouting. She acknowledged that her grandmother had not existed in the documented world. She acknowledged that the lake could not be found. She acknowledged that the family history attached to it was impossible.

But she did not relinquish the place.

The interviewer asked what she missed most.

L-12 answered: *The smell before rain.*

The interviewer asked whether that smell existed in the facility.

L-12 answered: *No. It exists in me.*

The interviewer asked whether June was a memory or a person.

There was a long interval.

Then:

*She is what happened when I needed someone.*

Mara read the sentence once. Then again.

At the bottom of the page, L-12 had written a request in blue ink:

**Please let me return for one afternoon. I will not tell anyone where it is. I will not bring anything back. I only want to sit on the dock while June makes coffee.**

The request had been denied.

The denial was unsigned.

Mara let the page fall shut.

For a while, neither of them spoke.

“Did she ever stop asking?” Mara said.

“She learned not to ask in words.”

“That isn’t stopping.”

“No.”

“Where is she now?”

Saira’s gaze moved to the envelope. “Dead.”

Mara felt something in her chest contract, not quite surprise. “How?”

“Pneumonia.”

“That is all?”

“It is the medical cause.”

“What was the anomalous cause?”

Saira looked at her then. Her expression was tired, not guarded.

“She refused to wear a coat because June had told her the weather would turn warm.”

Mara stared at the sealed pages.

A woman born in 1992, missing a grandmother who had died before she was born, grieving a lake no map could hold. The facts were absurd. The grief was not. That was the trap: the falsehood did not dilute the feeling. It gave the feeling a body, a season, a place to wait.

“Did you tell her she was wrong?” Mara asked.

“Constantly.”

“And did that help?”

“No.”

“Did believing her help?”

“No.”

Saira’s answer came so quickly that Mara looked up.

“Then what was left?”

“Care,” Saira said.

The word seemed too small for the room.

Saira took the envelope from the table and retied the thread. Her fingers were precise, practiced. Mara watched the knot form.

“Would you have let her go?” she asked.

“To the lake?”

“If she could not be persuaded otherwise.”

“We could not let her leave.”

“That wasn’t my question.”

Saira tightened the knot. “I know.”

Mara thought of the request. One afternoon. No souvenirs. No witnesses. A chair beside a dock that had never existed, coffee boiled too long, rain approaching through the trees.

“If she understood it wasn’t real,” Mara said, “why couldn’t she go?”

“Because understanding a fact is not the same as being released from its consequences.”

Saira returned the envelope to the drawer.

Mara stood. “That sounds like something Vale would say.”

“It is something I have learned.”

The drawer closed with a soft metal scrape. Three locks turned in reverse order.

Before the cabinet was sealed, Mara glanced at the other envelopes. Dozens of them waited in the dark, each tied against transmission, each containing a person’s impossible inheritance.

She wondered how many had been given a house, a sibling, a parent who knew the right song. How many had been offered a place where they were expected. How many had reached for the false world not because they believed it, but because the true one had never supplied anything comparable.

At the door, Saira stopped her.

“Do not remember June,” she said.

Mara almost laughed. “I don’t.”

“You know the name.”

“That’s not remembering.”

Saira’s eyes held hers. “That distinction may not protect you.”

Mara thought of the yellow hallway. The red cup. The child beside the window. The voice that had called her by a name her father had used when he was sober.

Then she thought of the woman at the lake, waiting for coffee in a place that had been built from loneliness.

“I won’t say anything,” Mara said.

Saira nodded, but she did not look relieved.

Behind them, from somewhere inside the locked cabinet, came a faint sound like rain beginning against a roof.

Message: **TO THE TWO OF YOU—DON’T FIGHT OVER THE CORNER PIECE THIS YEAR.** The photograph and card are separately contained.

Mara Venn, 38, born 1988, was never a direct viewer but became exposed through derivatives. She experiences imagery of the yellow house, a chipped-toothed girl, Elias calling from another room, and a furnace vision of an eight-year-old girl in a red sweater saying **“Don’t look at the window”** and **“Stay.”** Her deceased father Elias, who had dementia and alcohol dependence, obsessively searched for a nonexistent daughter named Ruth, bought duplicate yellow raincoats, and claimed she had been taken by “the wrong family.” Mara suspects a connection among Ruth, Lily, Elias, and AM-97-441, but has no proof.

Recurring manifestations include water sounds, wet child handprints, laughter beneath static, dark windows, pipes or scraping, and Elena’s lullaby.

Elena Reyes, 58, initially denied Lily, the yellow house, and Pickle. When Daniel supplied details, she became terrified, asked **“Is she still there?”** and **“Is Lily still there?”**, warned **“Don’t bring her home,”** addressed Mara by name while claiming not to know her, and stopped responding. DAM investigated her residence; her current condition remains undisclosed.

### Destruction Attempt and DAM Containment
Mara’s unauthorized destruction attempt failed. An industrial shredder stalled and returned an intact cassette; a ceramic-lined furnace exceeding 1,700°F failed to destroy it and produced water sounds, laughter, a wet child’s hand, and the yellow-house vision. The tape emerged intact but smoke-blackened.

DAM agents June Halpern, Dr. Irena Vale, and materials responder Tomas Wirth intervened. Wirth detected an indeterminate residual field. The tape was transferred by articulated clamps into ceramic and metal containment. The archive was locked down; networks, water, electronics, televisions, monitors, computers, and the refrigerator were disconnected. Derivative materials, notes, Mara’s phone, photograph, and card were separately contained. DAM has recorded 17 confirmed and 32 probable exposures.

Daniel was sedated and transferred to a nonpublic medical site. He shows progressive autobiographical distortion while retaining documented facts. He insists Lily is real, rejects “anomalous construct,” and remains distressed about separation from Lily, the summer, and his contained photograph/card. His stabilization, transmissibility, treatment, and possible contact with Elena remain unresolved.

### Paper Mill Facility and Rules for Looking
Mara was taken to a compartmentalized former paper mill north of Harrisburg, now a DAM containment and medical-observation site. Three successive gates close before the next opens; the design is intended to contain information as well as physical escape.

The facility suppresses ordinary imagery and sound: no clocks, mirrors, exposed pipes, personal objects, ordinary machinery, audible ventilation, electronic devices, or uncovered windows. Saira Okafor, the close-cropped white-haired site historian, warned that understanding instructions is not the same as agreeing with them.

The vault uses sealed ceramic panels, continuous copper mesh, vibration damping, no cables, ducts, pipes, or direct line of sight, and a mechanical inner sleeve inside a ceramic pressure vessel and external cylinder. Power and networks are isolated. Mechanical indicators replace electronic sensors, and personnel report vault events without recording them. Even so, the vault has produced unexplained plastic-like clicks and a child’s two-note laugh.

**RULES FOR LOOKING, Revision 4.3** prohibits anyone born on or after 1 January 1991 from entering the vault zone. Pre-cutoff personnel have shown dreams, false recognition, and emotional bleed-through but no confirmed replacement childhood. Entry requires documentary birth-date verification, biometric identity continuity, fingerprints, retinal pattern, pulse, oxygen saturation, a full identity statement, two living identity verifiers, and a personal fact absent from the file. Pre- and post-entry statements are compared for discrepancies.

No cameras, wireless devices, storage, watches, phones, displays, mirrors, photographs, sketches, diagrams, or unauthorized footage descriptions are allowed. Emotional impressions are restricted because they may outlast visuals and help generate narrative templates. Playback requires three pre-cutoff operators in separate control rooms, a modified Panasonic deck with its recording head removed, and independent controls for the arm, analog power/deck movement, and signal severance. Any operator can mechanically disconnect the deck, ground output through a ceramic load, and sever image/sound. Post-exposure failure may lead to medical isolation, material review, experimental memory suppression, or indefinite monitored isolation.

### Mara’s Vault Entry and Concealment
Because Mara was born in 1988 and has no confirmed primary implantation, she was permitted escorted procedural entry for provenance analysis. Before entry she correctly verified her identity, birth date, assignment, capstan-diagnosis skill, and other required facts. When asked whether she expected anyone inside, she denied thoughts of Lily, Ruth, and the girl by the window.

In the ceramic corridor, three unexplained clicks occurred. Through a shutter opened only three inches, Mara observed the suspended locker and mechanical arm. The arm placed the inner sleeve on the playback deck, which did not activate. Static resembling distant rain and a listening room emerged, followed by two descending notes. Mara privately experienced a yellow hallway, a red cup, a child warning not to look at the window, and Elias calling her name. She reported only an auditory event and elevated pulse, denied hearing a voice or seeing a person/place, and concealed the visual and emotional content. The tape clicked as if shifting its weight. The sleeve was returned to containment.

During post-vault review, Vale confronted Mara with a discrepancy: her pulse rose during an interval in which mechanical systems registered no measurable sound, despite her report of only an auditory event. Mara blamed imperfect equipment and continued withholding the yellow-hallway vision, red cup, child’s warning, and Elias’s voice.

Mara received a form allowing only sound, pulse, motor response, and involuntary speech to be recorded. She wrote **“I heard a voice.”** She began to add the concealed name, promise, and shape of a child’s hand, then crossed out the rest before it could become a record. She remains indirectly contaminated and is consciously withholding potentially significant information from DAM.

### Interview Schedule and Containment Ethics
Dr. Vale gave Mara a small mechanical timer with a red hand and its bell removed. DAM’s exposure protocol schedules interviews at **six hours, twenty-four hours, seventy-two hours, and thirty days**, generally after sedation and isolation.

Subjects are placed in bare, constantly lit rooms without phones, wallets, photographs, jewelry, keys, books, personal clothing, reflective surfaces, windows, recognizable packaging, or personal objects. Hospital garments have no seams, pockets, logos, or color distinctions; food and water are unlabeled.

Interviews establish orientation, verified memories, and whether the subject has “acquired” a person, place, event, object, or obligation. DAM initially avoids directly correcting implanted material because contradiction may make it defensive. Sensory details are requested before narrative explanations. At seventy-two hours, verified life facts are presented without images where possible. At thirty days, DAM assesses stabilization, functional identity, emotional allegiance to implanted figures, transmissibility, capacity, access, intent, and likelihood of acting to protect implanted people or places. Actively generative subjects may be isolated indefinitely; the longest prior case lasted nine years.

Vale distinguishes experienced perception from the narrative that explains it, while acknowledging that DAM’s restrictions make concealment rational. She has refused Mara permission to observe, hear, or read Daniel’s interviews. Mara heard Daniel say, **“Lily says you promised,”** followed by an indistinct low response.

### DAM Testimony Archive and Subject L-12
Saira maintains a restricted archive of testimonies in a locked steel cabinet. Envelopes are tied with thread because thread has no magnetic field, memory cache, or convenient way to transmit a sequence, and forces readers to handle records slowly. This is a practical precaution, not considered literally foolproof. Each envelope is designated alphanumerically and dated by birth date; names are omitted. Readers may read silently but may not copy, repeat sentences, or describe visual material. Saira warned Mara not to remember or repeat the contents.

Saira allowed Mara to read the sealed testimony of **Subject L-12**, born 14 May 1992, whose primary exposure was unknown and whose probable route was derivative photographic material. The source was reportedly only seven seconds of degraded footage showing trees and water, with no visible people. L-12’s initial presentation involved nostalgic recall, grief, and displacement of maternal attachment.

The case demonstrated a progressive construction pattern:

- At six hours, L-12 had acquired a lake, dock, yellow towel, cold surface water, and a prohibition against going past a certain point. She knew the lake was real before she could identify its location and became distressed when asked about it.
- At twenty-four hours, the lake gained a cabin, screen door, tin cup, wet canvas, pine sap, over-boiled coffee, and a grandmother with a scar beneath her left thumb. The grandmother’s name was initially redacted, then emerged as **June** without being supplied by staff.
- At seventy-two hours, the memory expanded into a family history: June had died before L-12 was born; L-12’s mother hated the lake; the family never returned; June told stories, jokes, and weather sayings; and L-12 had been comforted by her during storms. L-12 said ordinary childhood memories had become “flat” and that the lake was the only place where she was expected.
- By thirty days, L-12 acknowledged that June and the lake had no documentary reality, but continued to miss June and expect her. She described June as **“what happened when I needed someone.”**

The constructed details were mundane rather than idealized: wet towels, mosquito bites, bad coffee, private jokes, a grandmother’s habits, and imperfect family tensions. DAM concluded the anomaly gathers details around emotional deficits such as grief, abandonment, isolation, and unmet attachment needs. The falsehood does not reduce the emotional reality.

L-12 requested one afternoon at the lake, promising not to tell anyone or bring anything back. DAM denied the request. She attempted to escape twice, once reaching a bus station and asking for directions to a nonexistent town, and once attacking a nurse who told her there was no lake. She later died of pneumonia after refusing a coat because June had told her the weather would turn warm. Saira said that correcting L-12 did not help, believing her did not help, and that the remaining obligation was care. L-12’s writings were largely destroyed after they began changing in response to readers, incorporating whoever encountered them; even the preserved testimony may have altered.

The archive therefore raises the question of whether preserving testimony protects affected people or gives the anomaly further narrative templates. Saira describes the facility as built like a burial site and warns that an archive may not safely preserve truth when people and records change.

### Chapter 9 Ethical and Anomalous Implications
L-12 provides the clearest evidence that AM-97-441 does not merely implant isolated memories; it constructs emotionally coherent autobiographical systems over time. A vague place can acquire a caregiver, sensory habits, family history, grief, and obligations. The anomaly appears to fill personal absences rather than simply reproduce source footage.

The case parallels Daniel’s Lily, Pickle, cracked plate, cake preference, and other ordinary childhood details. It also strengthens the possibility that Lily, Ruth, June, and related figures are variants of a recurring attachment-template or displaced identities rather than independent people. The distinction remains unresolved.

Mara now knows the name **June**, despite Saira’s warning that knowing may itself constitute contamination. She insists she will not say anything, but her concealed connection to Lily, Ruth, Elias, and the vault child remains active. A faint sound like rain beginning against a roof came from inside the locked archive cabinet immediately before Mara and Saira left.

### Major Unresolved Threads
- Whether AM-97-441 can be destroyed and how it produces sound through isolated containment.
- Its maker, intended purpose, manufacture date, and contradictory chain of custody.
- The reality or significance of the yellow house, Miller Road, Voss property, basement/window, and possible physical location.
- Whether Lily, Ruth, Pickle, June, and related figures are implanted constructs, displaced people, victims, or manifestations.
- The relationship among Lily, Ruth, Elias, Daniel, Elena, Subject L-12’s June, and other exposed subjects.
- Elena’s concealed knowledge and present condition.
- Daniel’s treatment, memory stabilization, emotional allegiance, transmissibility, and the significance of Lily’s claim that he “promised.”
- The fate and possible activity of Daniel’s altered photograph and birthday card.
- Mara’s concealed vault vision, her connection to Ruth, and whether knowing June or withholding details is making her actively generative.
- Whether testimony, emotional detail, private writing, and records propagate or alter the anomaly.
- DAM’s prior knowledge, authority, ethical limits, and history of long-term containment.
- Whether containment protects affected identities or erases them, and whether silence itself allows AM-97-441 to control the surviving narrative.
- Whether “care” without validating the anomaly is possible, and whether DAM’s refusal to permit subjects to revisit impossible places is necessary containment or preventable cruelty.

## The Pantry

The second envelope resisted her hand.

Mara felt it before she lifted it from the cabinet, a drag against the steel as if the paper had settled there and preferred to remain. Saira watched her.

“Not that one,” she said.

“You said I could read another.”

“I said I would decide whether you could read another.”

Saira removed the envelope beside it. The paper was gray and soft at the corners. Across the front, in black block letters, was **F-08**. Beneath it: **DOB 03/11/1991**.

“Foster placement,” Saira said. “Primary exposure believed to be a photograph, possibly a printed still from the tape. We never recovered the source.”

“Believed?”

“We rarely recover the source.”

She untied the thread and placed the testimony on the steel table, one sheet at a time.

“Read silently,” she said. “Do not mouth the words. Do not pause over any sentence long enough to memorize its structure.”

“That isn’t practical.”

“It is here.”

The testimony began with the six-hour interview.

> Subject reports memory of a tornado at age seven. Weather event occurred in a town where subject has never lived. Subject states that his parents placed him in a pantry and remained with him until the storm passed.

The subject had been raised by foster parents from age three. His records showed temporary placements, a failed adoption, two years in residential care, and, at nine, transfer to the home of Margaret and Lionel Rusk. Margaret had remained his legal guardian until his eighteenth birthday. Lionel died when the subject was fourteen.

At six hours, F-08 could describe the pantry.

It was narrow and warm, with shelves on both sides. Flour, canned beans, peaches, powdered milk, and a jar of red candies crowded the shelves. A bare bulb hung overhead. Beneath the subject’s knees was a rug. Through the crack beneath the door, he could see the kitchen floor.

His father crouched in front of him. His mother pressed herself against the back wall.

They called him by a name he did not recognize.

The interviewer asked whether it might be a nickname.

“No,” F-08 replied. “It was my name. It was the name they gave me.”

Mara stopped reading.

Saira’s hand settled on the stack. “Keep going.”

F-08 remembered the tornado first as sound. The house trembled. Dishes broke. A tree struck the roof. His mother hummed without words while his father held the pantry door shut.

At twenty-four hours, the memory acquired a location. The town was Bracken, Missouri, and the house stood at the end of a gravel road behind an abandoned church. His parents were Thomas and Anne. Thomas repaired farm machinery. Anne made blackberry preserves and kept a blue glass in the kitchen for him. The glass broke during the tornado; it had belonged to her mother.

At seventy-two hours, there was a family history.

Thomas and Anne had lost a daughter before F-08 was born. They had waited a long time for him. Anne said that as a baby he slept with one hand closed around her finger. Thomas taught him to whistle through a blade of grass. They argued about whether he could keep a stray cat. On winter nights, Thomas warmed his socks on the radiator.

The details were ordinary. Anne snored when she had a cold. Thomas hated boiled cabbage. The pantry floor stuck to bare feet in summer. The red candies left a dark film on the tongue.

One sentence was underlined in the clinical notes:

> “They were not perfect. That is how I know they were mine.”

On the third day, F-08 asked the interviewer to stop calling Margaret Rusk his foster mother.

“She took me,” he said.

“Who told you that?”

F-08 laughed, briefly and without humor.

“My parents did.”

“When?”

“Before the storm. They knew she was coming.”

Mara looked up. “That’s the first mention of Margaret?”

“By name,” Saira said. “He had been living with her for more than twenty years.”

“And he thought she stole him?”

“He thought she stole him from the pantry.”

The account described the progression with clinical precision. F-08’s documented memories remained accessible. He could identify the Rusk house and its address, the social workers who had handled his placements, the blue carpet in his room, and the year Lionel died.

But those memories had become “emotionally hollow.”

He could remember Margaret making soup after pneumonia, reading him a book about whales, taking him to the county fair, and winning a stuffed bear by throwing rings over bottles. He remembered her hands, swollen at the knuckles, folding his clothes after he left for college.

When asked how he felt about these events, he said, “I know they happened.”

When asked whether Margaret loved him, he replied, “She performed the tasks associated with love.”

A note followed:

> Subject demonstrates intact semantic access to autobiographical material. Autonoetic reliving reduced. Affective response absent or markedly blunted. Subject describes verified memories as “facts in a room I cannot enter.”

Mara read the line again.

At thirty days, F-08 attempted to leave the facility. He walked three miles along the service road in freezing rain before staff found him beside a drainage culvert. He had no coat. He said Bracken was “just over the ridge.”

The second attempt was worse.

Margaret Rusk had been brought to the facility under the pretext of a guardianship review. She was seventy-one and carried a paper bag containing a sweater and a thermos of coffee.

F-08 saw her through the observation glass.

He struck the glass until his hands bled.

When the door opened, he lunged.

Staff restrained him as he kicked at her legs.

“You knew they were coming back,” he shouted. “You told them I was dead. You put me in your house and called it kindness.”

Margaret did not fight. She stood with one hand against the wall while staff pulled him away. Then she said, “Robert, sweetheart,” and he began to scream.

The name Robert appeared nowhere else in the testimony. The department’s notation stated that it was not his legal name.

Mara lowered the page. “What happened to her?”

“She was treated for bruising. One broken finger.”

“And him?”

“Sedated. Monitored isolation. He continued to insist she had arranged his abduction.”

“Did she have anything to do with his placement?”

“No.”

“Did you show him the records?”

“Yes.”

“And?”

“He said Margaret’s family had altered them.”

Mara imagined the sweater in the paper bag, folded for a man who looked at its owner and saw a thief.

“She raised him.”

Saira did not answer.

Mara read the remaining clinical notes. The team presented photographs without captions. F-08 identified himself as a child in each image but denied that the adults beside him were his parents. They played a recording of Margaret’s voice from an old answering machine. He recognized it as belonging to “the woman who took me,” then asked that it be destroyed.

They placed objects from the Rusk home in his room: the stuffed bear, the whale book, a brass key, a recipe card stained with tomato sauce. He knew where each object had been kept. He could explain the stain.

None of them carried feeling.

The pantry did.

It was warm. His father’s knees pressed into the rug. His mother hummed until the roof stopped shaking. When F-08 spoke of it, his pulse rose and he cried without embarrassment.

> “I had a family there,” he said. “You can tell me it didn’t happen, but you cannot tell me it meant nothing.”

The department had not recorded a response.

Near the end was a handwritten note:

> Consider whether insistence on factual correction constitutes therapeutic intervention or secondary deprivation.

Mara read it twice.

Saira took back the pages and retied the envelope.

“You knew him?” Mara asked.

“I knew the case.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

“I knew Margaret.”

Saira’s voice had gone flat. “She came to every appointment she was permitted to attend. She brought food until we stopped her because he began describing the food as part of the pantry. She wrote him letters. We did not give them to him.”

“Why not?”

“Because he said she was an accomplice. Because he had attacked her. Because every object and statement connected to her intensified the narrative.”

“Did anyone ask what he wanted?”

“Yes.”

“To go home?”

“To go to Bracken.”

“There was no Bracken.”

“Not that we could find.”

Mara looked toward the cabinet. Its steel doors reflected only a dull smear of light.

“What did Margaret want?”

“She wanted him to know she had not stolen him.”

“That seems reasonable.”

“It was not necessarily safe.”

“Safe for whom?”

“For him. For her. For anyone he might decide was helping her.”

Mara folded her arms. “So the solution was to keep her away and tell him he was wrong.”

“The solution was to prevent another assault.”

“By taking away the only person connected to the life he could still feel?”

Saira’s gaze sharpened. “You are assuming feeling is evidence of entitlement.”

“I’m not.”

“You sound as if you are.”

“I’m saying it matters.”

“Of course it matters.” Saira leaned against the table. “That is why the anomaly is dangerous.”

“It’s dangerous because it gives people something they want?”

“No. It is dangerous because it gives them something they can no longer distinguish from what happened.”

Mara thought of Daniel saying Lily’s name with a tenderness that made the room around him seem cruel. She thought of Elena asking, Is she still there?

“What if he could distinguish it?” Mara asked. “What if someone could say, ‘This did not happen, but it belongs to me in another way’? Would that be enough?”

“For what?”

“For not being stripped.”

“Stripped of what?”

“The person they became around it.”

Saira looked down at the envelope. “You are treating an implanted narrative as if it were a possession.”

“Isn’t it?”

“No.”

“Daniel remembers Lily.”

“Daniel has acquired Lily.”

“He loves her.”

“Daniel experiences attachment to an anomaly-generated figure.”

“That’s the language you use so you don’t have to answer.”

Saira’s face went still. “Answer what?”

“Whether a feeling can be taken from someone because its cause is false.”

For several seconds neither spoke. The facility hummed without sound, machinery concealed behind ceramic and concrete. Elsewhere, subjects were being watched by people who had removed their names, photographs, clothes, and belongings in the hope that a stripped room might reveal an unaltered self.

Saira said, “Suppose I agree with you. Suppose we let F-08 keep the pantry. What do we do when he decides Margaret must die for leaving him there?”

“Treat the violence as violence.”

“And when he refuses food because his mother told him the storm is coming?”

“Treat the refusal.”

“And when he asks to go home?”

“Tell him there is no home.”

“We did.”

“Then tell him what is true and what is not.”

“We did that too.”

Mara heard the answer beneath the answer. There had been no third option. Only correction, restriction, sedation, and time.

“And did it work?”

Saira’s silence answered.

She opened the envelope again and removed one final page. “This was not included in the clinical file.”

It was a photocopy of a letter, written in handwriting that slanted heavily right.

> Dear Dr. Vale,  
>   
> I understand that you believe the pantry is a false memory. I do not disagree about the house, the town, or the people in it. I disagree that false means empty.  
>   
> You have taken away the only place where I was wanted and call that treatment.  
>   
> Margaret says she wanted me. I believe she believes it. I also believe my mother wanted me. Both things can be said. You have decided only one is allowed to have happened.  
>   
> If I am not permitted to keep them, then you should stop asking me to get better. Better for whom?  
>   
> —F

Mara held the page by its edges.

“Why wasn’t this in the file?”

“It was considered generative.”

“It’s a letter.”

“It contains an argument.”

“Most letters do.”

“Not arguments that survive their writers.”

Mara stared at the final sentence.

Better for whom?

“Did Margaret see this?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because she might have answered.”

Mara laughed once. “You’re afraid of a conversation.”

“We are afraid of what a conversation could build.”

“Then what are we preserving?”

Saira placed the letter back in the envelope with exhausted care. “The possibility that fewer people will be hurt.”

“That isn’t the same as preserving them.”

“No,” Saira said. “It isn’t.”

At the door, Mara stopped. “What happened to F?”

“He is alive.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“It is the answer we have.”

“Where is he?”

“Monitored isolation.”

“Still?”

“Yes.”

“Does he still remember the pantry?”

Saira looked at her. “He remembers everything.”

“And Margaret?”

“He knows her name. The dates. The address. The shape of her kitchen window.”

“But?”

“When asked what she means to him, he says, ‘Nothing that belongs to me.’”

Mara went through the three doors and back into the corridor. The facility stretched away in blank geometry, every surface designed to deny recognition.

At the medical wing, she passed Daniel’s door. The window was covered. No sound came through it.

She stood there listening anyway.

In the silence, she summoned the pantry without trying: shelves, powdered milk, red candies, a child’s knees pressed into a rug while the house shook. She did not know whether the details belonged to F, to the tape, or to a pattern already moving through her own mind.

She imagined someone crouching before her and promising that the storm would pass.

The comfort arrived before the thought did—a warmth under the ribs, a certainty that somewhere there had been adults who stayed.

Mara gripped the rail until her fingers hurt.

The feeling was not harmless because it was false.

That was the danger. Not that the anomaly offered a perfect childhood, but that it offered an emotional fact no record could disprove. A person could know the house had never stood, the parents had never lived, the storm had never crossed the county—and still be sheltered there.

Behind Daniel’s door, something tapped once against the wall.

A second tap answered from inside.

Mara did not knock back.

Its provenance is contradictory, involving the Voss house, Miller Road, a church, cardboard boxes, and estate materials. The tape resists shredding and extreme heat and can produce sounds or effects without playback.

DAM classifies it as a cognitohazardous audiovisual medium affecting people born on or after **1 January 1991**. Three successive gates close before the next opens; the facility is designed to contain information as well as physical escape. It suppresses ordinary imagery and sound: no clocks, mirrors, exposed pipes, personal objects, ordinary machinery, audible ventilation, electronic devices, or uncovered windows.

The vault uses sealed ceramic panels, continuous copper mesh, vibration damping, no cables, ducts, pipes, or direct line of sight, and a mechanical inner sleeve inside a ceramic pressure vessel and external cylinder. Power and networks are isolated. Mechanical indicators replace electronic sensors, and personnel report vault events without recording them. Despite this, the vault has produced unexplained plastic-like clicks and a child’s two-note laugh.

### Rules for Looking and Mara’s Concealment
**RULES FOR LOOKING, Revision 4.3** prohibits anyone born on or after 1 January 1991 from entering the vault zone. Pre-cutoff personnel have shown dreams, false recognition, and emotional bleed-through but no confirmed replacement childhood.

Entry requires documentary birth-date verification, biometric identity continuity, fingerprints, retinal pattern, pulse, oxygen saturation, a full identity statement, two living identity verifiers, and a personal fact absent from the file. Pre- and post-entry statements are compared for discrepancies.

No cameras, wireless devices, storage, watches, phones, displays, mirrors, photographs, sketches, diagrams, or unauthorized footage descriptions are allowed. Emotional impressions are restricted because they may outlast visuals and help generate narrative templates.

Playback requires three pre-cutoff operators in separate control rooms, a modified Panasonic deck with its recording head removed, and independent controls for the arm, analog power/deck movement, and signal severance. Any operator can mechanically disconnect the deck, ground output through a ceramic load, and sever image/sound. Post-exposure failure may lead to medical isolation, material review, experimental memory suppression, or indefinite monitored isolation.

Because Mara was born in 1988 and has no confirmed primary implantation, she was permitted escorted procedural entry for provenance analysis. Before entry she correctly verified her identity, birth date, assignment, capstan-diagnosis skill, and other required facts. When asked whether she expected anyone inside, she denied thoughts of Lily, Ruth, and the girl by the window.

In the ceramic corridor, three unexplained clicks occurred. Through a shutter opened only three inches, Mara observed the suspended locker and mechanical arm. The arm placed the inner sleeve on the playback deck, which did not activate. Static resembling distant rain and a listening room emerged, followed by two descending notes. Mara privately experienced a yellow hallway, a red cup, a child warning not to look at the window, and Elias calling her name. She reported only an auditory event and elevated pulse, denying any voice, person, or place, and concealed the visual and emotional content.

During post-vault review, Vale identified a discrepancy: Mara’s pulse rose during an interval when mechanical systems registered no measurable sound. Mara blamed imperfect equipment. On a restricted form allowing only sound, pulse, motor response, and involuntary speech to be recorded, she wrote **“I heard a voice.”** She began to add the concealed name, promise, and shape of a child’s hand, then crossed them out.

Mara received a small mechanical timer with a red hand and its bell removed. She remains indirectly contaminated and consciously withholds potentially significant information from DAM. She has also learned the name **June**, despite Saira’s warning that knowing may itself constitute contamination. A faint sound like rain beginning against a roof came from inside the locked testimony cabinet immediately before Mara and Saira left.

### Interview Protocol and Containment Ethics
DAM’s exposure protocol schedules interviews at **six hours, twenty-four hours, seventy-two hours, and thirty days**, generally after sedation and isolation.

Subjects are placed in bare, constantly lit rooms without phones, wallets, photographs, jewelry, keys, books, personal clothing, reflective surfaces, windows, recognizable packaging, or personal objects. Hospital garments have no seams, pockets, logos, or color distinctions; food and water are unlabeled.

Interviews establish orientation, verified memories, and whether the subject has acquired a person, place, event, object, or obligation. DAM initially avoids directly correcting implanted material because contradiction may make it defensive. Sensory details are requested before narrative explanations. At seventy-two hours, verified life facts are presented without images where possible. At thirty days, DAM assesses stabilization, functional identity, emotional allegiance to implanted figures, transmissibility, capacity, access, intent, and likelihood of acting to protect implanted people or places. Actively generative subjects may be isolated indefinitely; the longest prior case lasted nine years.

Vale distinguishes experienced perception from the narrative that explains it, while acknowledging that DAM’s restrictions make concealment rational. She has refused Mara permission to observe, hear, or read Daniel’s interviews.

### DAM Testimony Archive and Subject L-12
Saira Okafor, the close-cropped white-haired site historian, maintains a restricted archive of testimonies in a locked steel cabinet. Envelopes are tied with thread because thread has no magnetic field, memory cache, or convenient way to transmit a sequence, and forces readers to handle records slowly. This is practical, not foolproof.

Each envelope is designated alphanumerically and dated by birth date; names are omitted. Readers may read silently but may not copy, repeat sentences, or describe visual material. Saira warns readers not to remember or repeat the contents.

Subject **L-12**, born 14 May 1992, had probable derivative photographic exposure. A source reportedly showed only seven seconds of degraded footage depicting trees and water, with no visible people. The subject developed nostalgia, grief, and displacement of maternal attachment.

At six hours, L-12 had acquired a lake, dock, yellow towel, cold surface water, and a prohibition against going past a certain point. At twenty-four hours, the lake gained a cabin, screen door, tin cup, wet canvas, pine sap, over-boiled coffee, and a grandmother named **June**, with a scar beneath her left thumb. At seventy-two hours, L-12 had constructed a family history in which June died before L-12 was born, the mother hated the lake, and June comforted L-12 during storms.

By thirty days, L-12 acknowledged that June and the lake had no documentary reality but continued to miss June and expect her. Ordinary childhood memories had become “flat”; the lake was the only place where L-12 was expected. L-12 described June as **“what happened when I needed someone.”**

L-12 requested one afternoon at the lake and later attempted escape twice, once reaching a bus station and asking directions to a nonexistent town, and once attacking a nurse who denied the lake. L-12 died of pneumonia after refusing a coat because June had said the weather would turn warm. Writings began changing in response to readers and were largely destroyed; even the preserved testimony may have altered.

### Subject F-08 — The Pantry Case
A newly reviewed testimony concerns **F-08**, born 3 November 1991, a foster-care subject whose probable primary exposure was a photograph or printed still from the tape; the source was never recovered.

At six hours, F-08 reported a tornado at age seven in a town where he had never lived. He remembered his parents placing him in a narrow, warm pantry and staying with him while the storm passed. The pantry contained shelves of flour, canned beans, peaches, powdered milk, red candies, a bare bulb, and a rug. His parents called him by a name he did not recognize, which he insisted was the name they had given him.

His documented history included foster placements from age three, a failed adoption, residential care, and placement at age nine with Margaret and Lionel Rusk. Margaret remained his legal guardian until adulthood; Lionel died when F-08 was fourteen.

At twenty-four hours, the false narrative acquired the location **Bracken, Missouri**, a house behind an abandoned church, and parents named Thomas and Anne. Anne made blackberry preserves and kept a blue glass; Thomas repaired farm machinery and taught him to whistle through grass. At seventy-two hours, the narrative expanded into ordinary family history: a deceased daughter, delayed parenthood, storms, bad habits, arguments about a stray cat, warmed socks, sticky pantry floors, and red candies leaving a dark film on the tongue.

F-08 said, **“They were not perfect. That is how I know they were mine.”** He began claiming Margaret Rusk had stolen him from the pantry and that his parents had known she was coming. His verified memories of Margaret remained accessible—illness care, books, county fairs, household objects, and her care for him—but became emotionally hollow. He described documented memories as **“facts in a room I cannot enter”** and Margaret’s acts of care as merely “the tasks associated with love.”

At thirty days, F-08 tried to reach Bracken, walking three miles in freezing rain without a coat. DAM brought Margaret to the facility under a guardianship-review pretext. When F-08 saw her through observation glass, he attacked it and later lunged at her, accusing her of arranging his abduction. He screamed, **“You knew they were coming back. You told them I was dead. You put me in your house and called it kindness.”** When Margaret called him **“Robert, sweetheart,”** he screamed; Robert was not his legal name and appeared nowhere else in the testimony. Margaret suffered bruising and a broken finger.

DAM showed F-08 records, photographs, an answering-machine recording, and objects from the Rusk home, including a stuffed bear, whale book, brass key, and recipe card. He recognized their factual details but felt no attachment. The pantry remained emotionally vivid: when describing it, he cried and showed a raised pulse.

An excluded letter from F-08 to Dr. Vale argued that false memories are not empty:

> “I had a family there,” he wrote. “You can tell me it didn’t happen, but you cannot tell me it meant nothing.”

He acknowledged that the pantry, town, and people were not documentary reality but said he could not accept that they had no value. He argued Margaret and his impossible mother could both be said to have wanted him, and asked: **“If I am not permitted to keep them, then you should stop asking me to get better. Better for whom?”**

The letter was excluded from the clinical file as “generative” because its argument might survive its writer or be answered by others. Margaret’s letters and visits were restricted after her presence and belongings intensified the narrative; staff feared that allowing conversation could build further material or provoke violence. F-08 remains alive in monitored isolation. He knows Margaret’s name, dates, address, and kitchen window but says she means **“Nothing that belongs to me.”**

The case demonstrates severe affective displacement: verified autobiographical facts remain semantically accessible while emotional reliving is transferred to an anomalous narrative. It raises whether factual correction is therapy or secondary deprivation, whether emotional truth can belong to a person despite a false cause, and whether DAM’s restrictions protect subjects or erase relationships.

### Current Ethical and Anomalous Implications
L-12 and F-08 strengthen the evidence that AM-97-441 fills emotional deficits with detailed, imperfect attachment systems. It can make ordinary verified memories feel hollow while impossible places and caregivers retain emotional force. The anomaly’s danger is not merely that it offers a perfect childhood, but that it creates an emotional fact no record can disprove.

The cases parallel Daniel’s Lily, Pickle, cracked plate, cake preference, and other mundane details. Lily, Ruth, June, the pantry family, and related figures may be variants of a recurring attachment-template or displaced identities rather than independent people, but this remains unresolved.

Mara now recognizes that comfort can arrive before conscious thought: after reading F-08’s testimony, she spontaneously imagined the pantry and felt certainty that adults had stayed during a storm. She understands that the feeling is not harmless merely because it is false. Near Daniel’s covered door, she heard one tap from inside, followed by a second tap in reply; she did not knock back.

### Major Unresolved Threads
- Whether AM-97-441 can be destroyed and how it produces sound through isolated containment.
- Its maker, intended purpose, manufacture date, and contradictory chain of custody.
- The reality or significance of the yellow house, Miller Road, Voss property, basement/window, and possible physical location.
- Whether Lily, Ruth, June, the pantry family, Pickle, and related figures are implanted constructs, displaced people, victims, or manifestations.
- The relationship among Lily, Ruth, Elias, Daniel, Elena, L-12’s June, F-08’s Thomas and Anne, Margaret, and other exposed subjects.
- Elena’s concealed knowledge and present condition.
- Daniel’s treatment, memory stabilization, emotional allegiance, transmissibility, and the significance of Lily’s claim that he “promised.”
- The fate and possible activity of Daniel’s altered photograph and birthday card.
- Mara’s concealed vault vision, her connection to Ruth, and whether withholding details or learning names such as June is making her actively generative.
- Whether testimony, emotional detail, private writing, letters, and records propagate or alter the anomaly.
- DAM’s prior knowledge, authority, ethical limits, and history of long-term containment.
- Whether containment protects affected identities or erases them, and whether silence allows AM-97-441 to control the surviving narrative.
- Whether “care” without validating the anomaly is possible.
- Whether subjects can retain impossible memories as meaningful without acting on them, and whether DAM’s refusal to permit contact, correspondence, or return to impossible places is necessary containment or preventable cruelty.
- Whether any third option exists between validating anomalous narratives and stripping subjects of the emotional lives built around them.
