### The Summer Archive

The first lie Mara told about her father was that he had begun disappearing at the end.

It was a useful lie because it gave the disappearance a direction. Elias had been present, then less present, then absent, as if dementia were a tide drawing him out from the shore of the family. Alcohol had made the process visible: bottles in the recycling bin, receipts folded into his shirt pocket, the sour sleep of a man who had lost an argument with his own body. By the last year, he misplaced names and dates. He called Mara by her mother’s name. He asked the same question three times in one afternoon.

He had not vanished, Mara told herself. He had deteriorated.

The file drawer in the Department of Anomalous Media was labeled MEDICAL—V and locked with a key that was not supposed to exist.

Mara found it on a ring in Saira Okafor’s office, beneath a brass tag marked HISTORICAL MATERIALS. Saira had gone to the medical wing to argue against moving Daniel into deeper isolation. Vale was in a meeting with the directorate. The mill, for once, had no alarms in it. No laughter. No running water. Only the dull shudder of the building settling around its buried machinery.

Mara stood in the doorway of Saira’s office, the key warm from her palm.

She had asked Saira two nights before whether the department had known her father.

Saira had looked at her for a long time and said, “Known him how?”

That was answer enough.

The cabinet was not digital. Nothing important in the facility was digital anymore. Its drawers held folders bound with cotton tape, microfilm sleeves, carbon copies, receipts, photographs sealed in waxed envelopes. The records had been transferred, Saira had told her, from institutions that no longer existed and from departments that had changed names to make their histories harder to follow.

Mara inserted the key.

The lock opened with a small, embarrassed click.

Inside, the files were arranged by surname. Venn occupied a single gray folder, thinner than she expected. It had no red stripe, no current hazard notation. On its tab someone had written, in block capitals:

**VENN, ELIAS—EXPOSURE, PROBABLE**  
**STATUS: NONCOMPLIANT / CLOSED**

Mara read the second line twice.

Noncompliant.

She slid the folder free.

The first document was a one-page intake form dated October 4, 2008. The agency listed at the top was not DAM but the Office of Media Irregularities, a predecessor Mara had never heard named except in footnotes. Subject birth date: March 2, 1957. Occupation: archivist, historical consultant. Exposure site: Pennsylvania Historical Society, Mercer County collection annex. Object: consumer VHS cassette, handwritten label. Duration of viewing: approximately forty-three seconds.

Mara’s breath shortened.

Forty-three seconds.

She looked toward the office door, though no one stood outside it. The mill’s corridor remained blank and gray, its white walls designed to deny the eye anything it could hold. Even the light fixtures were covered in opaque ceramic housings. There were no shadows except her own.

She returned to the page.

**Subject reports no nausea, seizure, or visual distortion. Subject insists recording depicts “the summer archive.” Repeatedly asks whether the children were recovered. Subject has supplied multiple contradictory locations for residence depicted.**

The next line had been crossed out in black ink.

**Subject claims a daughter named Ruth.**

Mara put one hand flat on the desk.

The paper did not change.

She had learned to distrust that relief.

Under the intake form was a field report from the historical society, written by someone named C. Wirth. The name made her pulse trip. Wirth had been the technician who measured the residual field after the furnace failed to destroy the tape. This could have been coincidence. Wirth was not an uncommon name in Pennsylvania. But the report’s phrasing was unmistakable.

“Material presented as routine family-film accession. No source chain available. Cassette swollen, label adhered with household tape. Surface markings consistent with heat damage or prolonged storage in damp conditions.”

Mara stopped reading.

The current tape had been swollen. Its label had been damp at the edges. The shopkeeper had not remembered where it came from. She had told herself those similarities were the anomaly’s signature, not evidence of a single object.

The report continued.

“Playback commenced on institutional deck. Subject Venn entered room during third minute and viewed monitor without warning. Initial image described by subject as yellow-sided residence, female adult in red swimwear, two children near ground-level pool. Subject remained in room after operator stopped tape. Subject later stated that the recording had shown his daughter at approximately age seven.”

Mara closed her eyes.

For an instant she smelled wet grass.

Not the sterile dampness of the mill, not the mineral odor that sometimes rose from the old paper vats. This was summer grass crushed under bare feet. Chlorine. Warm plastic. Somewhere beyond the office wall a woman called a child inside.

Mara bit the inside of her cheek until the smell broke apart.

She opened her eyes and read on.

The report said Elias had not viewed the tape again. He had requested access to the historical society’s accession files, then attempted to remove three boxes of unsorted home movies. When staff refused, he became verbally aggressive. He had returned the following morning with a camera, a flashlight, and a map of Mercer County. Security had escorted him from the building.

The map was mentioned twice. So was a girl in an attic.

**Subject maintains that the tape is incomplete. States that “the summer was archived in pieces,” and that one child remains above the house in a room not shown on the recording. Subject requests permission to retrieve “the attic reel.”**

Mara stared at the words until the letters blurred.

There had been no attic in her father’s stories. Not exactly. There had been a house, though he never agreed where it stood. Sometimes it was in Mercer County, sometimes near the Susquehanna, sometimes “past Miller Road.” He had said Ruth was waiting upstairs. Once, during the winter he stopped sleeping, he had stood at the bottom of their staircase and told Mara not to open the door at the top.

She had assumed he meant the bathroom.

The folder held no recording, only copies of notes and a chain-of-custody report. The cassette had been collected from the historical society after Elias left. It was assigned an inventory number, placed in a temporary evidence locker, and then—according to the next page—lost during a departmental consolidation.

Lost.

Mara laughed once, softly. It was an ugly sound.

The report listed three other cassettes in the same shipment. Two had been destroyed after producing “unaccountable domestic audio.” The third had been transferred to an unnamed federal partner. No partner’s name appeared.

The tape had not merely circulated through thrift shops and estates. It had passed through the hands of people who knew enough to be afraid and not enough to stop it.

She turned to the medical notes.

The first physician had written that Elias’s neurological examination was unremarkable. His blood alcohol level was negative. Toxicology showed no hallucinogens, sedatives, or unusual compounds. He was oriented to person and place but not date. He correctly identified his wife’s death, Mara’s occupation, and the address of his home.

Then came the clinical summary.

**Subject’s factual recall remains intact but is subordinated, in his language, to an emotionally privileged narrative. He rejects the term “hallucination.” He states: “You’re calling it false because you weren’t there.”**

Mara sat down.

The sentence felt like something he had said to her.

Not those words. Something close enough that she had filed it under his ordinary stubbornness. Her father had always treated disagreement as a moral defect in the other person. If he said the roof leaked, and it did not leak, the problem was not his observation but your failure to respect water.

She read the next paragraph.

**Subject repeatedly describes a girl named Ruth, age indeterminate, located in an upper room of a yellow residence. Reports auditory contact through walls and vents. Reports that girl is not “dead,” but “waiting for the archive to finish.” Subject has drawn the same architectural arrangement nineteen times despite no prior training in drafting. Drawings depict enclosed stairwell, narrow hall, attic door, and window facing a tree with a split trunk.**

Nineteen drawings.

Mara thought of the yellow hallway she had seen in the furnace reflection. The red cup. The child behind the door. She thought of the page from Breach Log 97-6, the warning that had changed when she read it:

Why are you punishing a child for remembering?

No. Why are you punishing me for remembering?

She pulled her sleeve over her wrist.

The department had known.

Not just that he had been strange, or drunk, or grieving. They had known he had handled the same kind of object. They had documented Ruth. They had documented the yellow house. They had documented the attic.

And none of this had reached Mara.

There was an attached letter from the Office of Media Irregularities to Elias’s primary physician. It recommended “continued clinical observation without disclosure of anomalous-media involvement,” because informing the subject could encourage “narrative consolidation and retaliatory acquisition behavior.”

Narrative consolidation.

The phrase had the bloodless precision of a scalpel. It meant that when Elias said Ruth, they heard a vector. When he looked at Mara and insisted she had helped the wrong family, they heard contamination.

Mara placed the letter beside the intake form.

He had been a patient, a source, a threat, and a problem to be closed. He had also been her father. The department had managed to preserve all the categories except the last one.

A sound came from the wall.

Three knocks.

Mara froze.

A pause.

Two knocks.

The office seemed to contract around her. She could feel the pulse in her fingertips. The folder lay open like a mouth.

“Not now,” she whispered.

The wall gave no answer.

She gathered the papers, then stopped herself. Taking them would be a breach. Leaving them was a kind of surrender. The distinction had grown increasingly difficult to maintain. They had told her not to make copies, not to repeat descriptions, not to carry the affected material beyond approved rooms. But the department had already carried its silence into her childhood and called that protection.

She read the final medical note.

It was dated January 11, 2009, six months before Elias died.

**Subject demonstrates persistent fixation on “summer archive.” Believes personal records have been altered to remove daughter. Has attempted to contact historical society, county assessor, and local property owners. Subject states that the recording does not show the past but “the part of the past that was saved.” When asked who saved it, subject became tearful and replied, “The people who wanted us to forget we were related.”**

Below that, in a different hand:

**No further interviews recommended. Family not to be informed unless necessary for safety.**

Mara felt the old shape of her anger, familiar as a scar.

For years she had thought the hospital had failed him. Then she had thought he had failed himself. She had not considered the possibility that someone had watched him fracture and chosen not to tell the person standing closest to him.

The file did not say whether she had been interviewed. It did not say whether the department had observed her. There was no record of a home visit, no notation of her age, no mention that she had been born in 1988 and therefore considered resistant.

Perhaps they had believed she was safe.

Perhaps they had known she was not.

She replaced the documents in the folder, but before closing it she noticed a smaller envelope tucked beneath the back flap. It was unmarked except for a date: **06/17/09**.

Inside was a photocopy of one of Elias’s drawings.

The original had been made in pencil on lined paper. The house was a rough rectangle with a peaked roof and a second, smaller peak above it. A staircase rose through the center. At the top, a door opened inward. A girl stood behind it, or perhaps in front of it; the lines were too heavy to tell. Her hand was a dark oval.

At the bottom of the page Elias had written:

**SUMMER ARCHIVE / ACCESS THROUGH CHILD’S ROOM**

Mara’s skin prickled.

The girl’s face was blank.

Not erased. Never drawn.

A note on the photocopy said: **Subject refuses to assign facial features. States “she changes when named.”**

Mara thought of Daniel describing Lily’s chipped tooth, her lighter hair, the way she held her breath. Details gave the shape a place to live. Names gave it a door.

The girl in Elias’s drawing had no name.

Except Ruth.

Except perhaps not.

She returned the copy to its envelope. On the reverse side, nearly invisible beneath the copier’s gray haze, was a stamped accession mark:

**PHS—BOX 44—HOME FILMS—SUMMER 1997**

Mara’s hand went cold.

She knew the current tape had been labeled HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97. She knew the label was not proof of identity. She knew the anomaly could reproduce conventions, dates, houses, children. She knew that a record written by a frightened archivist might be only another surface waiting to be completed.

But the historical society had possessed a tape with the same date, the same yellow house, and the same impossible promise of a missing child.

The coincidence was not comforting. It was an invitation.

She shut the folder.

The knock did not return.

Mara carried the Venn file to the doorway and paused before putting it back. On the other side of the corridor, a maintenance light flickered once. For a moment the blank wall seemed to have a window in it: black glass, wet with rain. A child’s palm rested against the other side.

Mara did not look directly at it.

She placed the file in the drawer, locked the cabinet, and returned Saira’s key to the ring.

Then she went to the records room.

The historical society’s accession material was kept in a locked steel cabinet separate from the testimony archive. Mara had access to it under her consultant credentials, though Vale had suspended all provenance work after the breach. She entered her birth date, gave her full identity statement, and supplied the personal fact the machine requested.

“My father bought two yellow raincoats in the same size,” she said. “One in 2007, one in 2008. He claimed the first had been stolen, but the receipt for the second was from a store in Altoona.”

The machine clicked.

The drawer opened.

Box 44 had been reduced to a single inventory card. Its contents were listed as “miscellaneous domestic media, unstable provenance,” followed by nine accession numbers, seven crossed out. The card had been handled often; the edges were dark with fingerprints.

At the bottom, in Elias’s handwriting, someone had written:

**Ask where the summer goes when no one is watching.**

Mara read the sentence once.

Then she turned the card facedown.

Behind her, the records room door closed by itself.

On the steel cabinet, a pale patch of condensation formed in the shape of a child’s hand. Five fingers. A narrow palm. The impression remained for several seconds, then began to slide downward, slowly, as though the child on the other side were losing strength.

Mara did not touch it.

She stood with the file against her chest and understood, with a clarity more painful than fear, that her father had not been the first person in the family to enter the archive.

He had only been the first one who came back talking.
chapters.summary:
## AM-97-441 — Updated Story-So-Far Summary

### Anomaly and Exposure
AM-97-441 is a dusty VHS labeled **HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97**, apparently from 1997 but circulating through contradictory chains involving the Voss house, Miller Road, a church, thrift shops, estate materials, schools, cleanouts, and now a Pennsylvania historical society collection. It resists destruction, produces sound or effects without playback, and can generate images through unrelated or damaged surfaces.

It primarily affects people born on or after **1 January 1991**, though pre-cutoff individuals can become exposed through derivatives, attention, handling, discussion, photographs, testimony, inference, and emotional completion. It constructs vivid, internally coherent false autobiographies around perceived absences—siblings, families, caregivers, homes, grief, promises, sensory details, and attachment. Verified memories remain factually accessible but often become emotionally flat.

AM-97-441 can use any surface capable of holding attention and exploits curiosity, longing, inference, or willingness to supply missing names and relationships. Derivative media may activate independently and recruit multiple mutually contradictory identities. Confirmed and probable case counts remain unstable.

### Daniel Reyes
Daniel Reyes, born **17 October 1994**, directly viewed the tape and developed an alternate childhood centered on a yellow-sided house on **Miller Road**. He remembers a sister, **Lily**, an alternate mother in a red bathing suit, a brown dog named **Pickle**, a possible father called Dad, a blue pool, basement window, yellow kitchen linoleum, storms, and leaking water.

Lily has a chipped tooth, lighter hair, hates peas, sleeps with one foot outside the blanket, and can hold her breath longer than Daniel. Daniel’s verified life—his mother Elena Reyes, Newark, Lincoln Elementary, friend Marcus Bell, medical care, graduation, birth date, and work at DAM—remains semantically available but emotionally hollow. He insists Lily exists and that officials use the wrong tense. He has asked Mara to tell Lily he is sorry; voices have answered through walls and moisture has appeared beneath verified photographs.

During restricted interviews, Daniel correctly identified Newark, Elena, his birth date, and other factual anchors, but visual questions—especially Elena’s face—triggered anomalous completion. He said he knew Elena had brown eyes but could no longer see her face; attempts to do so produced the yellow kitchen and Pickle. He remains able to name Elena, Newark, and his factual history, but his emotional and visual access to Elena is deteriorating.

Daniel continues to hear or attribute messages to Lily, including that she is angry and that Mara is making him choose between realities. In the latest incident, he pressed his hand to the wall while a basin-like water sound and the recurring knock pattern—**three knocks, pause, two knocks**—came from inside it. He was sedated after asking Mara to help him find Lily. The water sound continued for eleven seconds after he became unconscious. He remains in Medical Isolation Room Seven, with transfer to indefinite neurological isolation proposed.

### Elena Reyes and Related Figures
Elena, 58, initially denied Lily, Miller Road, and Pickle, but became terrified when Daniel supplied details. She asked **“Is she still there?”** and **“Is Lily still there?”**, warned **“Don’t bring her home,”** addressed Mara by name despite claiming not to know her, and then stopped responding. Her condition, prior knowledge, and possible exposure remain unknown. Under the long-term plan, she may also be isolated.

Mara’s deceased father **Elias Venn**, born 2 March 1957, repeatedly searched for a nonexistent daughter named **Ruth**, bought duplicate yellow raincoats, and claimed she had been taken by “the wrong family.” He had long described a yellow house, an upper room or attic, and a child waiting behind a door. He died in 2009 after years of fixation, with factual recall intact but subordinated to an emotionally privileged narrative.

Ruth, Lily, June, and Miri may be related manifestations of a recurring attachment template, but no identity has been established.

### Mara Venn
Mara, born in **1988**, was never a confirmed direct viewer but became exposed through derivatives. She has mechanical expertise and escorted vault access for provenance analysis. She concealed an early vision of a yellow hallway, red cup, child’s warning, and Elias calling her name, reporting only an auditory event and elevated pulse.

She learned the name **June**, and reading F-08’s testimony caused her to imagine a pantry and feel certainty that adults had stayed with a child during a storm. She suspects comfort may arrive before conscious thought and may itself be anomalous. She recognizes recurring images and emotional structures but actively interrupts completion, including by biting her cheek when nearly supplying a child’s name.

After Breach Log 97-6, Mara read the incident report and saw its warning change from **“Why are you punishing a child for remembering?”** to **“Why are you punishing me for remembering?”** She saw a yellow hallway, red cup, and child beyond a door, heard a hand sliding down glass, and wrote that the log might itself be unsafe. Vale crossed out the warning and sealed the page.

Mara has challenged Vale’s prohibition on descriptions and names, arguing that factual memory and anomalous attachment must be held together rather than forcing subjects to choose. She increasingly distrusts procedures that preserve official identity by erasing personhood. Her own identity-continuity verification is becoming uncertain: when asked for a personal fact absent from her file, she first gave a fact already documented about Elias’s raincoats, then supplied an additional detail about the receipt’s actual store.

In Daniel’s room, Mara resisted his demand to validate Miller Road or Lily but assured him that Elena and his first life were real. She did not reveal her own vision of the child behind glass. The recurring smell of wet grass and knocking appeared during the encounter. She now openly opposes the plan to bury the tape and place affected people in permanent isolation.

### Elias Venn and the Summer Archive
Mara secretly accessed a historical medical file on Elias from Saira’s office. The file, marked **“VENN, ELIAS—EXPOSURE, PROBABLE / STATUS: NONCOMPLIANT / CLOSED,”** documents that Elias viewed approximately forty-three seconds of a VHS at the **Pennsylvania Historical Society, Mercer County collection annex**, on 4 October 2008. The cassette had a handwritten label, swollen damp storage, unstable provenance, and imagery described as a yellow-sided residence, a woman in red swimwear, and two children near a ground-level pool—closely matching Daniel’s Miller Road memories and AM-97-441.

Elias insisted the recording depicted **“the summer archive,”** repeatedly asked whether the children had been recovered, and supplied contradictory locations for the house. He claimed a daughter named Ruth remained in an upper room or attic and requested an “attic reel.” He described auditory contact through walls and vents and said Ruth was waiting for the archive to finish. He made nineteen consistent drawings of a yellow residence with a central stairwell, narrow hall, inward-opening attic door, split-trunk tree, and a faceless girl with a dark hand. He said her face changed when named.

Elias attempted to obtain the historical society’s unsorted home movies and later sought maps and property records. The agency recommended that his family not be informed of the anomalous-media involvement, fearing narrative consolidation and retaliatory acquisition behavior. His clinical statement—**“You’re calling it false because you weren’t there”**—resembles the current ethical dispute over whether anomalous emotional realities can be dismissed as false.

The historical society’s records identified a shipment containing several domestic-media cassettes. Two were destroyed after producing “unaccountable domestic audio”; a third was transferred to an unnamed federal partner. Elias’s cassette was later listed as lost during departmental consolidation. Box 44 was associated with **PHS—BOX 44—HOME FILMS—SUMMER 1997**, creating a direct but not yet proven connection to the current tape.

The surviving inventory card contains Elias’s handwritten note: **“Ask where the summer goes when no one is watching.”** A condensation handprint formed on the card’s steel cabinet and slid downward as if a child were losing strength behind the surface. Mara did not touch it. She now believes Elias was not the first family member to enter the “archive,” only the first to return speaking about it.

### Containment Facility and Procedures
DAM operates a containment and medical-observation site in a former paper mill north of Harrisburg. Three successive gates close before the next opens. The facility suppresses ordinary imagery and sound: no clocks, mirrors, exposed pipes, personal objects, ordinary machinery, audible ventilation, electronic devices, or uncovered windows.

The vault uses sealed ceramic panels, continuous copper mesh, vibration damping, no cables, ducts, pipes, or direct line of sight, and a mechanical inner sleeve inside a ceramic pressure vessel and external cylinder. Power and networks are isolated. Mechanical indicators replace electronic sensors, and vault events are reported without recording them. The vault has nevertheless produced plastic-like clicks and a child’s two-note laugh.

No one born after the cutoff may enter the vault zone. Pre-cutoff entry requires birth-date verification, biometric identity continuity, fingerprints, retinal pattern, pulse and oxygen readings, a full identity statement, two living identity verifiers, and a personal fact absent from the file. Cameras, wireless devices, storage, watches, phones, displays, mirrors, photographs, sketches, diagrams, and unauthorized footage descriptions are prohibited.

Playback requires three pre-cutoff operators in separate control rooms, a modified Panasonic deck with its recording head removed, independent mechanical controls, and immediate manual signal severance. Exposed subjects may receive sedation, medical isolation, experimental memory suppression, or indefinite monitored isolation.

Following Breach Log 97-6, whiteboards were turned to face walls, including an evacuation diagram outside Medical Isolation; “C-4” was scrubbed from it, and writing supplies were treated as contaminated. Vale’s interim directive prohibits discussion of visual content, use of personal names for exposed subjects, repetition of narratives, unauthorized questions about identities or sensory details, and unapproved notes. Dreams, intrusive imagery, emotional displacement, or unexplained recognition trigger isolation. **“Unauthorized curiosity”** is classified as a breach precursor.

### Indefinite Isolation Proposal
A gray, unsigned departmental packet proposed burying the source object beneath the facility at a depth of at least **forty meters**, inside a ceramic pressure vessel, poured concrete, and continuous copper mesh, with access discontinued after emplacement. Burial is scheduled to begin **tomorrow night** and is expected to take place within seventy-two hours if the vault remains quiet.

The same proposal recommends **indefinite neurological isolation** for subjects who prefer constructed autobiographical material over verified identity. Treatment would consist of sensory minimization, pharmacological dampening, restricted interpersonal contact, periodic identity verification, and sedation as needed. It contains no provision for family visits, appeals, or an endpoint. Vale has approved the plan in principle and intends, according to Saira, to place all active subjects under deep sedation until the source is declared inert.

Mara objects that this is permanent containment without ethical review, burying both the cassette and the people it changed. Vale argues that exposed subjects are simultaneously people and potential vectors who cannot reliably consent to the narratives or relationships they express. Saira confirms that four rooms are suitable for at least seventeen subjects, implying that some may be made to share isolation space.

### Keller Secondary Exposure
Junior records assistant **E. Keller**, born **9 September 2001**, reportedly never saw the monitor, entered Wing C, or read the breach log. She overheard an unidentified technician’s account of Owen Bell’s event and developed a narrative involving an enclosed agricultural structure, an unnamed child, responsibility for the child’s confinement, an older male outside, a quilt with a geometric green marking, and an inward-opening window. She asked, **“Is she still in there?”** and **“Who is the little one?”** She remains under observation after attempting to break through a partition with her hands.

### Failed Destruction and Derivatives
Mara’s unauthorized destruction attempt failed. An industrial shredder returned an intact cassette. A ceramic-lined furnace exceeding 1,700°F produced water sounds, laughter, a wet child’s hand, and a yellow-house vision before yielding a smoke-blackened tape. Wirth detected an indeterminate residual field.

The cassette, derivative materials, notes, Mara’s phone, altered photograph, birthday card, monitor, cable, photographs, testimony, furnace, and other media are separately contained or destroyed as circumstances permit. Their current activity remains uncertain. Inert or destroyed surfaces may retain or generate domestic and child-associated manifestations.

### Owen Bell and Breach Log 97-6
Owen Bell’s records are inconsistent. Earlier material classified him as a pre-cutoff guard, but Breach Log 97-6 records his birth as **4 May 1993**, making him post-cutoff. Near a monitor transfer, he initially denied seeing or hearing its output but accurately referenced the hand and laugh, asked whether it was trying to get out or in, and whispered a name ending in **“Miri”** while claiming to be an only child.

He illegally entered Maintenance Office C-4 at 02:17 and activated a disconnected monitor. He developed an alternate autobiography centered on hiding with a dark-haired girl named **Miri** in an apple shed during summer 1999. Miri wore a yellow ribbon, had a scarred knee, hated apples with their skin on, and could whistle through her teeth. The narrative included promises to return, a green-square quilt, an older boy or brother with a bad knee, a feared father, wasps, apples, wet rope, and an inward-opening shed window. Owen shifted among child, older brother, outside watcher, and person behind the glass.

He identified Dr. **Irena Vale** as Miri, accusing her of abandoning him. An archival photograph transformed under his touch into a yellow-house/apple-shed scene; the corridor fragmented into multiple settings. A red-sweatered, chipped-toothed girl warned **“Don’t look at the window.”** Owen concluded that he was simultaneously victim, older brother, and threat, shouting that Miri was afraid of him. The photograph showed a dirty hand pointing toward Vale.

Technicians **Jessa Harlan** (born 1992) and **Minh Dao** (born 1994) developed contradictory secondary narratives after viewing or inspecting C-4. Harlan remembered Bell as a childhood acquaintance linked to a yellow house and apple shed; Dao remembered him as a school-bus classmate associated with a blue marble. Both forgot meeting Bell at DAM. Harlan wrote **Miri** on her arm; Dao wrote **Owen Bell—1999** on his palm.

Bell alternated identities, told Vale **“You left me in the shed,”** and said **“Tell Miri the window opens from inside.”** Before sedation he said **“I’m sorry, Owen,”** apparently addressing another self. He was transferred to Medical Isolation Room Seven; his current stability is unknown. Harlan and Dao were sedated and removed from Wing C.

The monitor activated without power during transport, showing static, yellow light, a dark figure, and a child’s laugh. Furnace destruction at 1,900°F failed to prevent running-water sounds for eleven seconds. Other Wing C monitors produced a closing door, a woman calling a name, and a dog bark. Ceramic foam filled the corridor; one worker claimed it covered a bedroom door. The incident log may itself be an unsafe derivative.

### Testimony Archive and Affected Subjects
Saira Okafor maintains a restricted testimony archive in a locked steel cabinet. Envelopes are tied with thread to force slow handling. Readers must read silently, may not copy or repeat sentences, and may not describe visual material. Testimonies can alter in response to readers.

**L-12**, born 14 May 1992, developed a lake, dock, yellow towel, cold water, cabin, and grandmother named **June** after probable derivative photographic exposure. June comforted L-12 during storms and was described as “what happened when I needed someone.” Verified memories became emotionally flat; escape attempts, violence toward a nurse, refusal of protective clothing, pneumonia, and death followed.

**F-08**, born 3 November 1991, developed a false childhood involving a tornado, pantry, and parents named Thomas and Anne in Bracken, Missouri. His foster-care history and attachment to guardian Margaret Rusk remained factual but emotionally hollow. He attacked Margaret through observation glass and argued that false memories are not empty, asking whether forced recovery is **“better for whom?”** He remains isolated, and contact with Margaret is restricted because it intensifies the narrative.

Saira previously saw a lake in a photograph from her grandmother’s effects, despite her grandmother living in Queens. She developed memories of skipping stones and a drowned boy. After describing the lake to her husband, he dreamed it, stopped recognizing their apartment, and believed the kitchen was filling with water. He supplied the name **Peter** for the boy; the boy was not real, and the lake acquired a dock afterward. Saira concludes that silence slows transmission but does not heal existing subjects.

### Water and Knock Manifestations
Mara and Saira have heard a child’s laugh and the squeak of a hand sliding down glass in the boiler room. Saira officially described the sound as a “ventilation fault,” although the facility has no ventilation.

Saira burned a note reading **“Emotion supplies architecture”** in a dead furnace. It ignited immediately, and the furnace produced running-water sounds like a child’s bath followed by **three knocks, pause, two knocks**. The same pattern later sounded inside Daniel’s medical-isolation wall and recurred after Daniel was sedated. The facility may be generating or hosting a domestic space behind sealed surfaces.

At the end of the latest incident, the knocking stopped and a child laughed somewhere below the medical wing, as if someone had finally opened a door.

### Current Ethical and Anomalous Implications
DAM distinguishes experienced perception from the story explaining it, but factual correction may destroy meaningful emotional attachments. Silence may limit spread while encouraging subjects and staff to privately complete the anomaly’s fragments. The revised policy risks erasing affected people’s identities and isolating them from ordinary human response.

Mara argues for preserving both verified facts and anomalous emotional realities. Vale prioritizes identity continuity, source burial, sedation, and preventing narrative completion. The discovery that DAM’s predecessor documented Elias’s exposure—and concealed it from Mara—has deepened Mara’s distrust of the department and suggests DAM has knowingly suppressed family connections and prior cases.

Elias’s records indicate that AM-97-441 or a closely related cassette existed in institutional custody as early as **2008**, with earlier provenance possibly extending to the historical society’s **1997 summer archive**. The agency’s loss of the cassette and destruction or transfer of related tapes suggest a much longer history of failed containment than DAM has disclosed.

### Major Unresolved Threads
- Whether the original cassette can be destroyed, safely buried, or declared inert.
- The maker, purpose, manufacture date, and contradictory chain of custody.
- Whether the historical-society cassette viewed by Elias was the current tape, an earlier instance, or a related object.
- The physical or narrative reality of Miller Road, the yellow house, basement window, pool, Voss property, attic, and apple shed.
- Whether Lily, Ruth, June, and Miri are constructs, displaced people, victims, or manifestations of one attachment template.
- The relationship among Daniel, Elena, Elias, Mara, Owen, and Dr. Vale.
- Elena’s concealed knowledge and current condition.
- Daniel’s loss of Elena’s face, his stabilization, Lily’s promise, the father figure, and the continuing water effects.
- The altered photograph, birthday card, monitor, cable, testimony, furnace, walls, furnaces, and other derivative objects.
- Whether Mara’s withheld knowledge and Owen’s inferential exposure make them generative.
- Owen’s current state, the source and identity of Miri, and the recursive child behind the glass.
- Dr. Vale’s possible connection to Miri, her silence about the red-sweatered girl, and the meaning of the hand pointing toward her.
- The status of Harlan, Dao, Keller, Elena, the removed worker, and other probable secondary exposures.
- Whether photographs, archival media, logs, walls, furnaces, unrelated hardware, and institutional records can function as active surfaces.
- DAM’s prior knowledge, authority, ethical limits, and history of long-term containment, including the concealment of Elias’s case from Mara.
- Whether silence prevents spread or merely delays completion.
- Whether any viable alternative exists between validating anomalous narratives and stripping subjects of the emotional lives built around them.
- The meaning of the “summer archive,” the missing attic reel, the faceless child whose appearance changes when named, and the question of where the summer goes when no one is watching.
- Whether the condensation hand on the records-room cabinet indicates an active child or merely another architectural manifestation.

chapters.name: The Wrong Family
chapters.content:
The first receipt was for a yellow raincoat.

Mara found it inside an envelope from a hardware store in Carlisle, the paper softened at the creases and freckled brown where someone’s thumb had worried it. The date was October 11, 2008. One child’s raincoat, size small. One adult poncho. Two pairs of rubber boots.

At the bottom, in Elias’s handwriting, were the words:

**For Ruth. Do not let her go outside alone.**

Mara sat beneath the dead fluorescent tubes and read the sentence until the letters ceased to mean anything.

Outside the archive’s sealed room, the paper mill gave its usual noises: a distant metal knock, a settling groan, the slow shudder of old ductwork that no longer connected to anything. She had been told the building had no audible ventilation. The sound had been classified as structural movement.

She placed the receipt in a clear sleeve, then took it out again.

These were not restricted materials, technically. They were her father’s belongings, transferred to the department because the department had already opened his life and labeled it **EXPOSURE, PROBABLE**. The letters, receipts, and appointment notes had been stored in a gray evidence carton in Saira’s office. Mara had waited until Saira went to the medical wing and used the key she had left in the lock.

She had told herself she wanted provenance.

She wanted to know when Elias had begun to disappear.

For most of Mara’s childhood, his disappearances had been ordinary. He disappeared into the garage with a bottle wrapped in newspaper. He disappeared into the television room, watching old weather reports with the sound turned off. He disappeared from conversations by turning his head toward some point just beyond the speaker, as though a second conversation were taking place there.

After Mara’s mother left, he disappeared into Ruth.

Ruth had not arrived in a single declaration. First she was a child who had been expected and never born. Then she was a daughter lost in a hospital mix-up. Then she was a girl who had lived with another family before someone took her again. By the time Mara was twenty, Ruth had a chipped tooth, a yellow coat, and a habit of hiding beneath the back stairs.

Mara had known she was not real.

Knowing had not protected her.

Elias asked about Ruth at breakfast, in the car, beside the washing machine. He asked why Mara was letting the wrong family keep her. Once, after she came home from college, he blocked the front door.

“You know what they’ve done,” he said. “Don’t pretend you don’t.”

“Who?”

He looked over her shoulder.

“The family.”

The word carried such complete accusation that Mara apologized before she knew what she was apologizing for.

Now she opened the next envelope.

There were letters from Elias to the Mercer County Historical Society, all addressed to a curator whose name had been crossed out in black marker. The first was dated November 2008.

**Dear Mr. Pell,**

**I am not asking you to confirm the girl. I am asking you to confirm the house. There is a distinction, and I hope the society understands it. A house can be located even if a person cannot. You have the maps. You have the tax records. You have the films.**

**The house is on Miller Road, or it was. Yellow siding. Split-trunk tree near the side yard. A low window below grade. The pool is not permanent. The children use a plastic one.**

Mara stopped reading.

The children.

Not Ruth alone.

She continued.

**The girl says the family changed the room. This is why the photographs may not agree. Please look for the stairwell. Central stairwell, narrow hall, door opening inward. If there is an attic, do not enter it.**

The letter ended with a request for property maps and “any home-media inventory connected with the summer of 1997.”

There were seven more. Elias wrote every few weeks, then every few days. He offered money, threatened legal action, apologized for threatening legal action. He claimed to have found the house near a cemetery, then in a development outside Mechanicsburg, then behind a church that had burned in 1983. In one letter the Voss family had changed its name. In another, there had never been a Voss family, only “the people who took the place over.”

The language was paranoid, but not random.

The earliest letters were controlled, almost bureaucratic. Elias listed dates, addresses, names, and measurements. He corrected his spelling. He underlined words only once.

By January, the handwriting leaned.

**Ruth was in the upstairs room during the thunderstorm. I heard her.**

By February:

**Mara has spoken to them. She believes them because they have taught her the words.**

By March:

**You are helping the wrong family erase her.**

That sentence appeared three times, in three different letters, each sent to a different recipient: the historical society, the county assessor, and Mara herself.

The letter to Mara was undated. It had been folded into quarters, then unfolded, then folded along new lines.

**Mara,**

**You know the difference between a locked door and a door that has been made to look locked. Do not let them tell you that absence is proof. Ruth is not gone. She is where they put the part of the summer they could not keep.**

**You have always been good at finding things. Find the house.**

There was no signature.

Mara remembered receiving it. She had been thirty, living in Philadelphia, working in a museum basement and sleeping badly. Elias had called at two in the morning and said he needed her to come home. She refused. He said, “They’re using your voice now,” and hung up.

The letter arrived three days later. She read it on the train and felt irritation, then shame for feeling irritated, then a tenderness so vast it frightened her. She put it in a drawer and never answered.

The receipt beneath it was from a liquor store.

October 2008 again.

One bottle of bourbon. One bottle of vodka. Two packs of cigarettes.

The next receipt was from a motel in New Castle, paid in cash for three nights. The address written on the back was not in New Castle but near the historical society’s collection annex.

A second motel receipt, two weeks later, showed one night.

A third showed four.

Mara knew this period as the drinking years. She knew the story because she had repeated it until it became almost comforting in its ugliness. Her father had lost his job. Her mother was gone. He drank. He developed dementia early. He became obsessed with a daughter who had never existed. He died in a hospital with restraints around his wrists because he kept trying to leave and “go upstairs.”

The story had edges and causes. It allowed Mara to be angry without being cruel.

The new documents took the edges away.

She found an appointment slip from a Pittsburgh neurologist dated April 2009. The appointment had been crossed out in red. Beneath it, someone had written:

**Patient refuses assessment. States physician is not Elias’s doctor.**

A photocopy of the intake form was attached. In the section asking for immediate concerns, the nurse had written:

**Reports hearing child through walls. Reports family photographs have “wrong people” in them. Oriented to date and location. Denies alcohol use today.**

The word **today** had been circled.

Another page, partly erased by chemical solvent, listed cognitive tests. Elias had scored poorly on visual recall but perfectly on orientation. He knew the year, month, day, building, and reason for the appointment. He could name the president and subtract serial sevens.

When asked to draw a clock, he had drawn a square house.

Mara stood so abruptly that her chair struck the wall.

For a moment the papers became a second floor plan: Miller Road, yellow siding, central stairwell, a child below ground, a door opening inward.

She thought of Daniel’s voice through the intercom, saying Lily had a chipped tooth.

She thought of her father saying Ruth had been taken.

The words were not proof. The anomaly could supply details across people, make one person’s longing resemble another’s. It could turn a stranger’s yellow house into the architecture of her own childhood.

But what if the resemblance came from somewhere else?

At the bottom of the carton was a small spiral notebook. Its cover had been torn off. Most pages contained addresses, property-tax numbers, and directions. One had been blackened at the edges.

**11/14 — house not there.**

**11/15 — house there, but wrong.**

**11/16 — window under kitchen. Water sound.**

**11/17 — Ruth says I brought the wrong girl.**

Mara read the last line twice.

The next page was blank except for a thumbprint.

In the evidence photograph, the print looked gray and dry. In front of her, moisture gathered along one ridge and slid toward the torn edge.

Mara withdrew her hand.

A knock sounded inside the wall.

Three times.

A pause.

Two.

The room held its breath.

She stared at the ceramic panel beside the cabinet. Its surface was seamless and pale, faintly reflective—not enough to show her face, only the suggestion of person-shaped darkness. For one instant the darkness seemed smaller than she was.

A child standing on the other side.

Mara bit the inside of her cheek until she tasted blood.

“What did you see?” she asked herself.

The question was forbidden. Not because questions created answers, exactly, but because an answer invited a second question, and the second question supplied a room.

She closed the notebook.

The knock did not come again.

The last documents were hospital billing statements, pharmacy receipts, and a death certificate. The official cause of death was aspiration pneumonia. Contributing factors included alcohol dependence, malnutrition, and “progressive cognitive impairment.”

The pharmacy receipts showed something else.

For six weeks before his hospitalization, Elias had filled prescriptions for an antipsychotic and a seizure medication. He had also stopped drinking. The blood panels attached to his final admission showed an elevated liver count but no alcohol.

He had been sober when he told them about Ruth.

Mara looked again at the clinical note.

**Oriented to date and location.**

Not cured. Not well. But present.

She remembered the last time she saw him conscious.

He was in the hospital’s locked ward, his wrists bruised where he had pulled against the restraints. Mara stood outside the room because he had accused her of being one of them. Through the glass, he pointed toward the corner behind her.

“She’s waiting,” he said.

“Who?”

He turned his head, listening.

“Ruth.”

“There is no Ruth.”

His expression changed. Not anger. Hurt.

“You know there is.”

“I know you believe there is.”

“No.” He pressed his palm against the glass. “You know where she is.”

Mara had left.

For years, she remembered this as the moment she stopped trying to rescue him. She remembered the ward smelling of disinfectant and burnt toast, her father’s hospital bracelet, the conviction that love could not require her to enter his delusion.

But another detail rose, unwanted and precise.

His hand had been wet.

Not sweaty. Wet enough that, when he lowered it, five narrow trails remained on the glass.

Mara shut her eyes.

The image persisted: a child’s hand sliding down a window.

She opened them. The wall was blank.

The door opened, and Saira entered. She stopped when she saw the documents.

“You found it.”

Mara’s anger steadied her.

“You knew.”

“I knew there was an exposure file.”

“You knew it was him.”

“I knew it was likely him.”

“You let me spend two days thinking my father was a drunk with dementia.”

“He was also a man with alcohol dependence and cognitive impairment.”

“Was he exposed?”

“Yes.”

The word seemed too small.

Mara rose. “Why wasn’t I told?”

“Because family members are not briefed until they need to know.”

“I’m his daughter.”

“Which is precisely why you weren’t briefed.”

“You had his records. You had the tape. You had the same yellow house.”

“We don’t know that the current tape is the one he viewed.”

“You knew enough.”

Saira looked at the raincoat receipt. Her face tightened, not with surprise but recognition.

“Elias was exposed for approximately forty-three seconds,” she said. “He never watched a full sequence. He saw enough to construct a narrative, then spent the rest of his life trying to locate it.”

“He spent the rest of his life trying to find his daughter.”

“Those may not be different statements to him.”

Mara pushed the letter toward her. “He knew details Daniel knows.”

“Daniel may have supplied them because the anomaly supplied them.”

“That’s circular.”

“It’s the only honest explanation we have.”

“Then what are the wrong family and the yellow coat?”

Saira was silent for a moment.

“Emotional architecture,” she said. “The anomaly doesn’t give everyone the same family. It gives them a structure that accommodates the absence they already carry. A missing sister. A grandmother who died too soon. A parent who never protected them. Details converge because the structures converge.”

“My father didn’t have a missing sister.”

“No. He had a daughter he believed he had failed.”

Mara looked at the letter.

**You have always been good at finding things. Find the house.**

“He was delusional.”

“Yes.”

“He was telling the truth.”

Saira’s eyes lifted to hers.

“About what?”

Mara had no answer that could survive the room.

Elias had been wrong about Ruth as a factual person. Wrong about the family, the house, the theft. Yet he had encountered something. He had seen a tape that made a child’s absence feel like an injury inflicted by strangers. It had given him a place to put his guilt and a daughter shaped from it.

Could a person be both delusional and right?

She thought of Daniel, who could recite his birth date but could not see Elena’s face. The memory was invented. The grief was not.

Saira gathered the papers into a careful stack.

“We should return these.”

“Not yet.”

“Mara.”

“Not yet.”

Saira’s gaze moved to the ceramic wall. “Did it activate?”

“No.”

The lie left a metallic taste.

Saira seemed to hear something anyway. She turned toward the panel, listening.

Nothing came.

Mara slid Elias’s letter beneath her coat. The paper was warm from the table, though the room was cold.

She did not know whether she was stealing evidence or taking back a piece of her father. She did not know whether Ruth had ever existed, whether Elias had seen her, or whether the anomaly had found the oldest wound in him and taught it to speak.

But she knew the department had called his case closed while keeping every object that proved it had never understood what happened.

At the door, Saira said, “If you begin seeing the house, report it.”

Mara looked at her.

“What if I already have?”

Saira’s expression changed.

Behind the wall, far below them, water began to run.
