chapters.content:
The first irregularity was a door that had opened without a hand.

At 02:13, Vault Access recorded the inner seal disengaging for four seconds. No operator badge had been presented. No biometric authorization appeared beside the event. The system logged only a pressure change and, beneath it, a line of corrupted characters resembling the teeth of a comb.

At 02:17, the same thing happened again.

At 02:21, the vault’s mechanical counter advanced by one.

Mara was shown the report at 06:40 in a room without windows, clocks, or a table large enough to suggest anyone might stay. The pages carried a red seal: INTERNAL—NO DUPLICATION.

Dr. Vale stood at the far end of the room with her hands clasped behind her back.

“You were in the library at 19:08,” she said.

Mara looked down at the access log. “Yes.”

“Your badge was used at 19:08.”

“I was in the library.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It’s the answer to the question you asked.”

Vale slid another page toward her. “Your badge opened the personnel door to the relay annex. At 19:12, a maintenance override was entered from the same terminal. At 19:16, it was canceled. At 19:18, the motion sensor registered a person moving toward the vault. At 19:19, it registered a person moving away.”

“Who?”

“We don’t have an image.”

“You don’t have cameras.”

“We don’t have images,” Vale repeated.

There were seven minutes between the first access and the last motion reading. Seven minutes in which someone—or something—had crossed a controlled boundary. The report did not say whether the vault itself had opened. It said inner seal, not door. The distinction comforted no one.

Mara touched the edge of the paper. It felt faintly damp.

“Did anyone see the person?”

“Two staff members heard footsteps.”

“Names?”

“Pre-cutoff personnel. They were not exposed.”

“Names, Irena.”

Vale’s eyes sharpened. “Do not use my first name in this room.”

Mara withdrew her hand.

The last page carried a typed recommendation:

**ACCESS IRREGULARITY MAY REPRESENT PRECURSOR EVENT TO TRANSFER. RECOMMEND IMMEDIATE BURIAL.**

Beneath it, in Vale’s handwriting:

**No further delay is operationally defensible.**

“What does immediate mean?” Mara asked.

“Tomorrow.”

The word altered the room. Friday had been a date on a schedule, an approaching event they might still change. Now it was an order.

“You’re accelerating.”

“I’m responding to an unauthorized access event.”

“You said the vault didn’t open.”

“I said the seal disengaged.”

“For four seconds.”

“Four seconds is sufficient.”

“For what?”

Vale did not answer.

A knock sounded at the door.

Three. Pause. Two.

Neither woman moved.

The intercom crackled. “Doctor? Reyes is ready for transfer.”

Mara stood so quickly her chair struck the wall. “No.”

Vale turned toward the speaker. “Proceed.”

“You can’t move him now.”

“Mr. Reyes is being transferred to Neurological Isolation Two.”

“He agreed to the controlled exposure.”

“He is not competent to consent to exposure.”

“He is competent enough to tell you what he wants.”

“He believes a fabricated child is communicating through the walls.”

“So did Owen.”

“Owen is also being moved.”

Mara felt pressure gather behind her eyes: a yellow hallway, a red cup on a sill, someone small waiting beyond a door. She bit the inside of her cheek until the room returned.

“Where are you taking them?” she asked.

“Separate isolation suites.”

“For how long?”

“Until transfer.”

“That isn’t a duration.”

“It is the duration of the emergency.”

“Which is convenient.”

Vale’s face went pale. “You think I want this?”

“I think you want it finished.”

“Yes,” Vale said.

The admission entered the room with the quiet weight of a body.

“I want the object buried,” she continued. “I want every derivative destroyed. I want the staff returned to work without wondering which wall will become a door. I want the subjects protected from another escalation.”

“That isn’t the same as helping them.”

“No. It is what we can do.”

“You’ve had weeks.”

“We have had decades.”

“Not with Daniel.”

“No,” Vale said. “With people like Daniel.”

The intercom clicked again.

“Move him,” Vale said.

Mara reached the door before the guards did.

Two security officers waited in the corridor, both born before the cutoff. Behind them stood Pell, one hand near the restraint case.

“Daniel is not a package,” Mara said.

“No one said he was,” Vale replied.

“Then let me speak with him.”

“You may speak with him in Isolation Two.”

“That is not what I meant.”

Vale stepped close. Mara smelled bitter coffee on her breath. “You are not to interfere with this transfer.”

“You’re removing Saira too.”

That stopped her.

Mara had seen Saira in the medical wing at dawn, speaking with Harlan through the observation window. Now a guard waited at the far end of the hall beside the access lift.

“Dr. Okafor has been reassigned,” Vale said.

“To where?”

“Administrative review.”

“For participating in the library meeting?”

“For violating subject-separation protocol.”

“She was trying to keep Owen from hurting himself.”

“She was creating an unauthorized emotional group.”

Mara stared at her. “You hear yourself, don’t you?”

“I hear the same thing I have heard since 1976.”

The number came without explanation. Vale’s eyes went elsewhere: a white farmhouse, green shutters, a shed whose window opened inward. For an instant Mara saw the child behind the doctor.

Then Vale returned.

“Take Reyes to isolation,” she said.

Daniel’s room was at the end of the medical wing. His possessions had been arranged on the floor: shoes, shirt, paperback book, toothbrush, plastic cup, and the photograph that had changed in his apartment.

It showed two children beside the yellow house.

Daniel sat on the edge of the bed, his bandaged hand in his lap. “They’re taking me downstairs.”

“Isolation.”

“I know.”

“Daniel—”

“Lily says not to go.”

Pell entered behind her. “Stand up, please.”

Daniel looked at him. “You don’t remember me.”

“I’m security.”

“You were at the library. You kept shaking your hand because you had water on it.”

Pell’s face tightened.

Mara saw the water: a dark smear across the floor, running from the bed toward the wall. She blinked. It was gone.

Daniel noticed. “She’s been talking to you too?”

“No.”

“You don’t have to be embarrassed.”

“Daniel, listen to me. They’re moving you because of the access irregularity.”

“The tape didn’t open.”

“I know.”

“It can open without opening.”

Pell stepped forward.

Daniel picked up the photograph. “What happens to this?”

“We’ll secure it.”

“Where?”

Mara glanced toward the corridor. “It can’t go with you.”

He held the photograph against his chest. “It’s my family.”

“It’s an altered image.”

“You keep saying that like altered means empty.”

“No. I’m saying we have to be careful.”

“You said Lily could matter even if she wasn’t real.”

“I said your attachment could matter.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

“No.”

Daniel’s mouth trembled. He looked younger than twenty-nine, younger even than the boy in the footage, though Mara had never seen that face clearly enough to know whether the thought was hers.

“Then what am I supposed to do?” he asked. “Keep all the facts and lose everything they mean?”

No one answered.

From inside the wall came a soft, tuneless hum.

Daniel turned toward it.

The guards moved. Pell took the photograph from his hands. Daniel did not resist. He only listened.

“It’s the song,” he whispered.

Mara recognized none of the melody, but its cadence entered her body as if it had been waiting there: a mother singing in a kitchen, a child answering upstairs, the last note held too long.

“Don’t follow it,” Mara said.

Daniel looked at her. “You know where it goes.”

“I don’t.”

“You do.”

Pell sealed the photograph in a gray evidence sleeve. The plastic clouded from the inside.

Daniel was escorted into the corridor. As he passed Mara, he touched her shoulder with his unbandaged hand.

“If Lily asks,” he said, “tell her I didn’t leave because I stopped loving her.”

Mara could not speak.

They took him through a steel door marked **N-2**. It shut with a sound like a book closing.

Saira was still in the corridor. The guards had not yet removed her. She watched the sealed door.

“What is Neurological Isolation Two?” she asked.

Mara shook her head.

“That means you don’t know.”

“I know the words.”

“Do you know what they mean?”

Before Mara could answer, Saira pulled a folded packet from beneath her sweater.

“I found this in the clinical planning archive.”

“You weren’t authorized to access it.”

“Neither was the tape.”

She opened the packet. The first page was headed **POST-EXPOSURE MANAGEMENT: ACTIVE SUBJECTS**.

Below it were columns for **acute stabilization**, **long-term disposition**, and **contingency**.

The acute procedures were familiar: sedation, isolation, object removal, identity checks, neurological observation.

The long-term column was nearly blank.

Under **Daniel Reyes**:

**Continue observation.**

Under **L-12**:

**No appropriate family reintegration pathway identified.**

Under **F-08**:

**Guardian contact contraindicated pending emotional restoration.**

Under **Owen Bell**:

**Persistent alternate identity; indefinite supervision recommended.**

The contingency field repeated one phrase:

**If subject demonstrates irreversible displacement, consider permanent neurological isolation.**

Mara read it twice.

“What does irreversible mean?”

“It means they haven’t decided,” Saira said.

“It means they’ve decided. They just haven’t written the duration.”

At the bottom of the packet was a **FAMILY CONTACT WAIVER**. It offered no option for a subject to request contact with a relative while retaining anomalous attachments. There was no provision for counseling over grief directed toward an impossible person, no distinction between literal belief and emotional construction.

There was, however, a checkbox for **TRANSFER TO PERMANENT CARE FACILITY**.

The box was premarked.

“Where is the permanent care facility?” Mara asked.

Saira gave a humorless laugh. “There isn’t one.”

“Then why is it here?”

“To make the absence look like a plan.”

A guard approached. “Dr. Okafor, you need to come with us.”

Saira folded the pages. “Mara.”

“I’m here.”

“If they separate us, don’t let them call the burial treatment.”

“What should I call it?”

“Containment. If that’s what it is.”

“And if it isn’t?”

Saira looked toward N-2. “Then call it what it is.”

The guard took her arm. She did not struggle.

“Ask Vale who receives the patients after the ground closes,” Saira said.

Then the lift doors swallowed her.

Mara found Vale in the transfer office, standing before a wall-mounted schedule. The ordinary calendar had been removed. In its place was a white board marked with colored lines. The burial route ran in red from the vault to the north service yard.

“Who receives them?” Mara asked.

Vale did not turn. “You’ve read the disposition files.”

“Who receives Daniel?”

“Medical personnel.”

“After tomorrow?”

“He remains under DAM custody.”

“In isolation.”

“Under observation.”

“For how long?”

Vale faced her. “You are asking a question that assumes recovery.”

“I’m asking one that assumes he is alive.”

“He is alive.”

“Then what does care look like?”

Vale glanced at the board. “We prevent him from exposing anyone else.”

“That’s containment.”

“Yes.”

“Not care.”

“Care is a word people use when they want to make risk emotionally negotiable.”

Mara placed the disposition packet on the desk. “You can’t hold people indefinitely because you don’t know how to help them.”

“We can if the alternative is allowing them to alter everyone around them.”

“Then build a program.”

“With what staff? Which families? What therapists can sit with someone mourning a sister who never existed without reinforcing the delusion or humiliating the patient? What hospital admits a man who may make nurses remember him as their brother?”

“You’re describing reasons to develop one.”

“I’m describing the world we have.”

“The world we have is the result of decisions like this.”

Vale’s hand tightened against the desk.

“You think the burial is about ending an argument,” she said.

“It is.”

“It is about ending a source.”

“And preventing anyone from studying it again.”

“Yes.”

“And preventing the subjects from having a say.”

“Yes.”

The answer was immediate.

Vale opened a locked cabinet and removed a blue folder. “Every delay creates another opportunity for a derivative. Every interview becomes a possible carrier. Every attempt to understand the structure gives it more material. We have seen photographs change. We have seen people acquire childhoods from descriptions. We have seen a monitor produce a hand where no hand was recorded.”

“Owen saw Miri because someone left a fragment unsecured.”

“Owen saw Miri because he was vulnerable.”

“He was curious.”

“Curiosity is one form vulnerability takes.”

Mara looked at the red route. It passed through the relay chamber, across the service yard, and into a square labeled **B-4 / BURIAL VESSEL**.

“You’re removing the possibility of research,” she said.

“I’m removing the possibility of recurrence.”

“You don’t know that burial will work.”

“No.”

“You said it survived furnaces.”

“I know.”

“You said it may relocate through emotional material.”

“I know.”

“Then this is not a solution.”

“It is a boundary.”

“Between what?”

Vale looked toward the corridor, where Daniel had disappeared behind N-2.

“Between the people we can still protect and the questions we cannot afford to ask.”

For a moment Mara saw Vale as the girl she had been: thirteen years old, standing before an inward-opening window, waiting for a sister no adult could follow. The image was not a vision exactly. It was an arrangement of details Mara had never been told, fitted together with such ease that she could not tell whether she had remembered them or invented them.

Dark hair. Yellow ribbon. Scarred knee.

Mara bit her cheek.

Vale noticed. “You’re completing.”

“I’m resisting.”

“There’s no difference once the detail arrives.”

“There is if I don’t accept it.”

Vale’s gaze lowered to the blood at Mara’s lip. “That is what everyone says before the detail becomes more important than the person.”

The facility speakers clicked.

A voice announced that the north service yard had been cleared for burial preparation. The announcement repeated once, but on the second pass the words distorted beneath a wash of static. Mara heard running water.

Vale turned toward the speaker.

The sound stopped.

“Tomorrow,” Mara said.

“Tomorrow,” Vale replied.

“And the subjects?”

“Confined.”

“And Saira?”

“Removed from the wing.”

“And if Daniel asks for Lily?”

Vale opened the blue folder. Inside was a transfer order bearing her signature.

“Then he will be reminded that Lily is not real.”

Mara stared at the signature.

“That’s all?”

“It has to be.”

“No,” Mara said. “It only has to be simple.”

Vale closed the folder.

Beyond the office wall, something knocked three times, paused, and knocked twice.

This time, the sound came from inside the floor.

Neither woman moved toward it.

The burial crew continued preparing the ground.

## AM-97-441 — Updated Story-So-Far Summary

### Anomaly
AM-97-441 is a dusty VHS labeled **HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97**, inventory designation **M-97-4B**, with contradictory provenance involving the Voss house, Miller Road, churches, thrift shops, estate materials, schools, the Pennsylvania Historical Society’s Mercer County annex, federal warehouses, and DAM custody. It resists destruction, produces sound and effects without playback, and generates images or manifestations through unrelated surfaces.

It primarily affects people born on or after **1 January 1991**, though pre-cutoff individuals can be exposed through derivatives, handling, testimony, photographs, inference, and emotional completion. It implants vivid, internally coherent false autobiographies organized around perceived absences: siblings, caregivers, homes, grief, promises, and lost family. Subjects retain factual knowledge of their real lives, but those memories may lose emotional force.

The anomaly supplies an **emotional architecture**, not one fixed narrative. Recurring motifs include yellow houses or objects, children behind doors or windows, water, storms, pools, attics, sheds, altered families, promises of rescue, running water, wet handprints, child laughter, and **three knocks, pause, two knocks**. It may lie about historical events while expressing genuine emotional needs or attachments. Recent evidence suggests it assembles narratives from emotionally significant fragments belonging to multiple people.

### Palinode Behavioral Systems
Palinode Behavioral Systems operated from a decommissioned WPKR-TV station outside Mercer, Pennsylvania, from 1992 until its destruction by fire in 1998. Its “shared affective frameworks” sought **“consensus childhoods”** producing belonging, adult protection, distrust of outsiders, and obedience. Motto:

> **WHAT WE SHARE, WE OBEY.**

Its domestic VHS program used incomplete, distorted imagery to make viewers “complete the family.” Tests employed yellow blocks, red clothing, hands against glass, child-sized shoes, basement openings, raincoats, pools, storms, dog barks, incomplete birthday music, and rooms beyond the frame. Researchers measured emotional intensity rather than factual consistency according to:

> **ABSENCE → ATTACHMENT → DUTY → IDENTITY**

Drug trials, including M-6, blurred autobiographical memory, dreams, and emotional expectation. Subjects invented families, abandoned real relationships, relabeled photographs, attempted to retrieve unrelated children, or became violent when constructed duties were challenged. Palinode concluded:

> **NOSTALGIA IS MORE PERSUASIVE WHEN IT IS ALLOWED TO DISAGREE WITH ITSELF.**

A July 14, 1997 shipping manifest records 240 consumer VHS units for an “environmental distribution” or **domestic saturation** phase through homes, video stores, churches, and civic programs. The fate of most tapes is unknown. Summer 1997 was selected as a psychologically accessible but difficult-to-verify anchor period.

The **SUMMER ARCHIVE** survived the 1998 station fire under unexplained circumstances. Recovered reels may include calibration reel 4B. Subject T-04’s unstable exposure to reel 4B precipitated the fire and produced shifting identities involving a deceased child, the laboratory director, rescue, guilt, and failed return. Destruction attempts caused flooding and other domestic manifestations. Palinode personnel dispersed, and DAM inherited and concealed parts of the program’s history.

### Principal Affected Subjects

#### Daniel Reyes
Daniel, born **17 October 1994**, directly viewed the tape and developed an alternate childhood centered on a yellow-sided house on **Miller Road**. Its family includes sister **Lily**, an alternate mother in a red bathing suit, possible father Dad, dog Pickle, a blue pool, yellow kitchen linoleum, a basement window, and storms. Lily has a chipped tooth, lighter hair, dislikes peas, sleeps with one foot outside the blanket, and can hold her breath longer than Daniel.

Daniel retains verifiable knowledge of his actual life—Daniel Mateo Reyes, born in Newark on **17 October 1994**, mother Elena Reyes, childhood apartment at 114 Bergen Street, Lincoln Elementary, teacher Mrs. Pritchard, friend Marcus Bell, and a plastic compass Marcus gave him—but these memories may feel emotionally hollow. He rejects references to Lily in the past tense.

He is physically deteriorating and has a bandaged left hand. He reports Lily communicating through walls and water. Elena has apparently begun referring to Lily during phone contact, though her exposure and present condition remain unknown. Daniel wanted to participate in controlled exposure and insisted he should decide whether to confront the narrative.

After the vault access irregularity, Vale ordered him transferred to **Neurological Isolation Two**. Daniel was separated from his possessions, including a photograph that had changed to show two children beside the yellow house; the evidence sleeve containing it clouded from inside. He said Lily warned him not to go and told Mara, “If Lily asks, tell her I didn’t leave because I stopped loving her.” He continues to distinguish emotional attachment from factual reality, objecting that calling Lily “altered” does not make her attachment empty.

#### Elena Reyes
Elena initially denied Lily, Miller Road, and Pickle but became frightened by Daniel’s details. She asked **“Is she still there?”**, warned **“Don’t bring her home,”** addressed Mara by name despite claiming not to know her, and then stopped responding. She has apparently begun referring to Lily during phone contact with Daniel. Her hidden knowledge, present condition, and possible exposure remain unresolved.

#### Mara Venn
Mara, born **1988**, has no confirmed direct viewing but is increasingly affected through derivatives, testimony, family records, Palinode documents, and inference. She experiences near-visions of yellow halls, red cups, children beyond doors, pantries, storms, and adults remaining with children. She resists completion, sometimes biting her cheek.

She insists that factual identity and anomalous attachment must coexist without forcing subjects to choose. Her identity statement remains: born in 1988, Mara Venn, archivist, not a sister, not a rescuer. Her continuity checks are uncertain; she has supplied undocumented or potentially anomalous details before.

Mara secretly retained Elias’s letters and Palinode documents despite derivative risk. She learned DAM knew of Elias’s case and concealed its connection to her because Vale considered her a **“generative risk.”** She spontaneously supplied details of Vale’s missing sister—dark hair, yellow ribbon, scarred knee—not previously told to her, suggesting anomalous access, assembly from nearby emotional material, or contamination.

Mara helped form an informal working group with Saira, Daniel, and Owen, arguing that “the image is constructed” and “the attachment may not be,” and that subjects should be studied without punishing them for emotional bonds. She tentatively agreed to controlled exposure.

After the vault irregularity, Vale questioned Mara about her badge being used to access the relay annex. DAM records show an unauthorized maintenance override, motion toward and away from the vault, and no identifiable person or camera image. Mara denied being present. The vault’s inner seal disengaged for four seconds at **02:13**, again at **02:17**, and the mechanical counter advanced at **02:21** without badge or biometric authorization. Two staff members heard footsteps. The event was classified as a possible precursor to transfer, and Mara’s report pages felt damp.

Mara challenged Vale’s indefinite isolation policy and the lack of meaningful family-contact or care provisions. Vale accused her of “completing” when Mara supplied details of Miriam’s appearance; Mara maintained that resisting or refusing to accept a detail still mattered. Mara remains unconfined but under suspicion and likely subject to further restriction.

#### Saira Okafor
Saira saw a lake in a photograph and developed memories of a drowned boy. Her husband later dreamed the lake, stopped recognizing their apartment, and supplied the name Peter. She believes silence slows transmission but does not heal existing subjects.

Saira leads the ethical opposition to Vale’s indefinite neurological isolation. She distinguishes factual memory from emotional truth and argues that subjects may retain symbolic or emotional attachments without treating them as historical evidence. She proposed controlled exposure during the tape’s transfer to burial, emphasizing that it is not a cure and must preserve personhood rather than promise safety.

Saira discovered DAM’s **POST-EXPOSURE MANAGEMENT: ACTIVE SUBJECTS** files. They prescribe sedation, isolation, object removal, identity checks, and neurological observation, but offer no developed long-term care. Daniel’s file says “Continue observation”; L-12 has no family reintegration pathway; F-08’s guardian contact is contraindicated; Owen has “persistent alternate identity” and indefinite supervision recommended. A contingency phrase states: **“If subject demonstrates irreversible displacement, consider permanent neurological isolation.”** A premarked **TRANSFER TO PERMANENT CARE FACILITY** option exists despite no such facility being identified.

Saira warned Mara not to call burial treatment and to ask who receives subjects after the ground closes. She was removed from the medical wing and reassigned to **administrative review** for violating subject-separation protocol and creating an unauthorized emotional group. Her current location and access status are unknown.

#### Owen Bell
Owen, born **4 May 1993**, activated a disconnected monitor in Maintenance Office C-4 and developed an alternate childhood involving Miri, a dark-haired girl in an apple shed during summer 1999. Motifs included a yellow ribbon, scarred knee, green-square quilt, older boy with a bad knee, feared father, wasps, wet rope, and an inward-opening shed window.

Owen shifted among child, older brother, outside watcher, and person behind glass. He identified Dr. Irena Vale as Miri, accused her of abandonment, and said:

> “Tell Miri the window opens from inside.”

Technicians Jessa Harlan and Minh Dao developed secondary narratives and forgot meeting Owen at DAM. E. Keller later developed a related narrative merely through overheard testimony. Owen remains isolated under observation, sometimes restrained, and repeatedly asks for Mara and Vale.

In the alliance meeting, Owen called Vale **“Miri”** and told her, “You got old.” He said Miri was “what I remember when I’m afraid,” while insisting this did not prove she was absent. He described the house as buried underground with its occupants still inside and warned that burial would not stop summer from emerging elsewhere. He rejected the idea that he had assembled part of Miri, saying he wanted her to stop being gone rather than gain power over her.

Owen eventually identified himself as Owen Bell, born 4 May 1993, and stated that he loved “a girl who kept waiting.” He was scheduled for controlled exposure, but Vale has now ordered him confined and transferred, apparently alongside Daniel, to neurological isolation. His current condition is unknown.

#### Dr. Irena Vale and Miriam
Vale, born approximately **1963**, disclosed a personal history potentially connected to Owen’s narrative.

In 1971–1976, Vale’s family spent summers at a white farmhouse with green shutters, an apple tree, and a small shed. In 1976, at age thirteen, Vale watched a 16mm estate-sale reel labeled **Family Picnic, 1963** with her parents and younger sister **Miriam (“Miri”)**. The film depicted an unknown house, a girl in yellow, a boy behind a screen door, and a woman calling them to supper; Vale’s mother recognized the woman as herself and began remembering an impossible abandoned baby.

Miri became attached to the filmed girl and claimed Vale should know where the house was. Miri disappeared for six hours and was found muddy before the shed, repeatedly saying the window opened from inside. Inside the shed, Vale’s family encountered an impossible second room with green-square wallpaper, a quilt, a hanging rope, and a boy’s shoe. Water rose through the walls, smelling like a swimming pool despite there being no pool on the farm. Vale’s father drowned in the impossible room; her mother was later found alive but unable to recognize the family; Miri was never found.

Vale spent decades tracking anomalous recordings and believes exposure can continue through photographs, stories, dreams, and listeners. She wrote much of DAM’s isolation doctrine. She insists Miri is dead despite admitting she does not know this, and describes uncertainty about Miri as the true breach: the moment the impossible is treated as an incomplete fact.

Owen’s account overlaps Vale’s history in the shed, inward-opening window, rope, and father’s injured leg, but differs in details such as the quilt being green rather than Vale’s remembered blue and the apparent transformation of Vale’s father into an older boy with a bad knee. This supports either direct anomaly access, emotional assembly, or contaminated memory.

When Owen called her Miri, Vale briefly reverted to her thirteen-year-old self before reasserting: “I am Dr. Irena Vale… I am not Miri.” She opposes controlled exposure, arguing that anomalous attachment corrupts consent and no ethically valid exposure is possible.

Vale has now accelerated burial in response to the vault access irregularity. She admits wanting the object buried, derivatives destroyed, staff returned to normal work, and the matter finished. She openly acknowledges that burial is containment rather than care and that subjects may remain in isolation indefinitely. She argues that DAM must establish a boundary between protectable people and unaffordable questions.

Vale ordered Daniel’s transfer and Saira’s removal, and signed a transfer order stating that Daniel must be reminded Lily is not real if he asks for her. Her motives include genuine fear of recurrence and unresolved grief over Miri, but she may also be using containment to end the ethical dispute and prevent further study.

### Chapter 25 — “The Unofficial Alliance”
Mara, Saira, Daniel, and Owen met unofficially in the bare former library. No alliance name or written record was permitted because naming a shared purpose might create a common narrative. Guard Pell, born in 1968, supervised Owen.

Saira announced that the cassette was scheduled for transfer from the vault to a burial chamber at least forty-two meters below the north service yard. The chamber uses ceramic-lined concrete, continuous copper mesh, independent air and drainage, and a sealed pressure vessel. Saira doubts burial will prevent narrative relocation.

The proposed **controlled exposure during transfer** required a cleared relay chamber, three pre-cutoff operators, an isolated mechanical analog system, identity checks, manual signal severance at first uncontrolled spread, and continuous reminders that images are **constructed** without declaring them meaningless. Subjects could choose whether to confront appearances; refusal, inability to answer, or answering as another identity would trigger severance. No one would question constructed figures or promise rescue, reunion, return, or explanation. Follow-ups were planned at six hours, twenty-four hours, seventy-two hours, and thirty days, with family contact only by consent.

The procedure remained unauthorized. During the meeting, the corridor produced **three knocks, pause, two knocks**, followed by running water. A yellow-house scene appeared in the corridor wall: a woman in red, a blue pool, children in a sprinkler, and a chipped-toothed girl. Mara bit her cheek and the scene vanished. Vale entered, condemned the meeting, ordered Mara away, and confined all participants before transfer. Mara and Saira continued identity checks until the water stopped; Pell was left trembling.

### Chapter 26 — “Transfer Order”
At **02:13**, the vault’s inner seal disengaged for four seconds without badge or biometric authorization. The system logged a pressure change and corrupted characters resembling a comb’s teeth. The same occurred at **02:17**; at **02:21**, the mechanical counter advanced by one. DAM could not determine whether the vault door itself opened. Two staff members heard footsteps, but no camera imagery exists because cameras are prohibited.

Access records showed Mara’s badge used at **19:08** to open the relay annex personnel door; an unauthorized maintenance override occurred at **19:12**, was canceled at **19:16**, and motion sensors registered a person approaching and leaving the vault at **19:18–19:19**. Mara stated she had been in the library. Vale classified the irregularity as a possible precursor to transfer and moved burial forward to the next day. The report pages felt damp.

The signature knock pattern sounded at the questioning-room door while Mara and Vale discussed the event. Vale ordered Daniel moved to Neurological Isolation Two and Owen transferred as well. She also removed Saira from the medical wing and reassigned her to administrative review.

Daniel’s room contained a changed photograph showing two children beside the yellow house. His belongings were removed, and the photograph was sealed in a gray evidence sleeve that clouded from inside. He said Lily warned him not to go, then told Mara not to tell Lily he had left because he stopped loving her. A tuneless lullaby came from the wall. Daniel recognized it as the song and claimed Mara knew where it went. A dark smear of water appeared on the floor and vanished. He also told guard Pell that Pell had water on his hand, causing Pell visible distress.

Saira showed Mara the post-exposure files, exposing DAM’s lack of a genuine long-term care program and its premarked permanent-care contingency. Saira warned that the burial must not be called treatment. She was taken away before identifying where she would be held.

Mara confronted Vale about isolating subjects indefinitely and denying them meaningful family contact. Vale said DAM’s purpose was to prevent exposure to others, not provide recovery, and admitted there was no known care system for people mourning impossible relatives without either reinforcing delusion or humiliating them. She stated that burial would create a boundary, not a solution, between protectable people and questions DAM could not afford to ask.

Mara supplied further details of Miriam—dark hair, yellow ribbon, scarred knee—while looking at Vale, then resisted accepting them by biting her cheek. Vale said that once a detail arrives, refusing it may not distinguish resistance from completion. Mara maintained that refusal still matters.

The north service yard was cleared for burial preparation. Running water briefly distorted the facility announcement. The knock pattern then came from inside the floor. The burial crew continued work.

### Other Exposures
- **L-12**, born 14 May 1992, developed a lake, dock, yellow towel, cabin, and grandmother June after probable photographic exposure; verified memories became emotionally flat, followed by escape attempts, violence, illness, and death.
- **F-08**, born 3 November 1991, developed a tornado-and-pantry childhood involving Thomas and Anne and attacked foster guardian Margaret Rusk after real attachment became hollow.
- **E. Keller**, born 9 September 2001, developed an agricultural enclosure, unnamed children, green-marked quilt, and inward-opening window from testimony alone and attempted to breach a partition.
- Harlan, Dao, Keller, and other exposed or secondarily exposed subjects remain under unclear status or observation.
- Saira’s husband and other listeners demonstrate that testimony and emotional proximity can generate derivatives.

### Containment and Ethics
DAM operates from a former paper mill north of Harrisburg. The facility excludes clocks, mirrors, windows, exposed pipes, ordinary machinery, personal objects, electronics, photographs, diagrams, recording equipment, and other narrative surfaces. The vault uses ceramic panels, copper mesh, vibration damping, sealed pressure vessels, isolated power, and no cables or ducts. Vault events are not recorded, though plastic clicks and child laughter have occurred.

No post-cutoff individual may enter the vault zone. Pre-cutoff operators require birth-date verification, biometric continuity checks, identity statements, two living verifiers, and an undocumented personal fact. Playback requires three separated pre-cutoff operators, a modified Panasonic deck without a recording head, independent mechanical controls, and immediate manual severance.

After Breach Log 97-6, Vale prohibited visual-content discussion, names for constructed subjects, narrative repetition, unauthorized identity or sensory questions, and unapproved notes. Dreams, intrusive imagery, emotional displacement, and unexplained recognition trigger isolation. Writing supplies, walls, records, photographs, furnaces, and testimonies can become derivatives.

Shredding and furnace destruction failed. Furnaces above 1,700°F and 1,900°F produced water, laughter, wet hands, yellow-house visions, and domestic effects. Burial at least forty meters deep inside ceramic, concrete, and continuous copper mesh is planned for the next day after Chapter 26’s irregularity, though the alliance doubts it can contain the anomaly rather than relocate its emotional architecture.

Vale favors indefinite neurological isolation for active subjects and treats uncertainty itself as a transmission risk. Mara and Saira oppose containment without ethical review and advocate preserving factual identity while acknowledging emotional attachment. The central ethical dispute is whether emotional bonds to constructed figures can be honored without validating them as historical fact or strengthening the anomaly.

### Current Unresolved Threads
- Whether the vault’s inner seal irregularities indicate an actual breach, an anomalous precursor, a derivative, or a person/identity crossing without ordinary access.
- Who used Mara’s badge and maintenance terminal, and whether Mara was unknowingly involved or duplicated.
- Whether the mechanical counter’s advancement records playback, access, or narrative progression.
- Whether the next-day burial will occur, whether Vale will prevent the controlled exposure, and whether the burial chamber can contain anything.
- The current locations and conditions of Daniel, Owen, Saira, and other isolated subjects.
- What **Neurological Isolation Two** entails and whether “permanent neurological isolation” will be enacted.
- Whether DAM has any real post-exposure care plan or intends indefinite custody under the language of observation.
- Whether Daniel’s sealed photograph remains an active derivative and why it clouded from inside.
- The meaning and source of the lullaby, Lily’s continued communication, the water smear, and Daniel’s claim that Mara knows where the song goes.
- Whether Pell’s apparent recognition of water indicates secondary exposure or only suggestion.
- Whether Elena’s references to Lily represent prior exposure, transfer from Daniel, or anomalous contact.
- Whether Lily, Ruth, June, Miri, Peter, and related children are constructs, displaced people, victims, or one recurring template assembled from subjects’ memories.
- The fate of Miriam Vale: dead, displaced, anomalously preserved, or represented only through assembled memory.
- Whether Vale’s 1976 16mm film was an earlier manifestation or precursor of AM-97-441, and where its surviving fragments are.
- Whether Mara’s spontaneous access to details about Miriam reflects generative ability, contamination, or anomaly-driven assembly.
- Whether Mara can remain a reliable identity anchor while retaining Palinode documents and Elias’s letters.
- Whether emotional attachment itself is the transmission mechanism, as Saira warned, or whether attachment can be ethically preserved without propagation.
- Whether Palinode pursued therapy, social control, or both; what survived the SUMMER ARCHIVE fire; and whether the tape is calibration reel 4B, a derivative, or one among 240 distributed units.
- The significance of **14 July 1997**, the anomalous future-dated Daniel assessment, and the missing attic reel.
- The fate of the other consumer tapes and whether domestic distribution was completed.
- Whether Miller Road, the yellow house, pool, basement window, attic, stairwell, apple shed, and Vale’s farmhouse physically existed as described.
- Whether photographs, reports, walls, sealed objects, testimony, and the facility floor remain active derivatives.
- The missing attic reel, faceless child, recurring water, wet handprints, laughter, and question: **“Where does the summer go when no one is watching?”**
- The meaning of Mara’s description of the knocks as an **invitation**, the apparent movement of water **toward summer**, and the new occurrence of knocks from inside the floor.
- Whether Vale’s assertion that uncertainty is itself the breach is accurate, or whether DAM’s refusal to distinguish emotional truth from historical fact is worsening the anomaly.

chapters.name: The Vault Opens
chapters.content:
### The Vault Opens

The burial crew arrived before dawn with a pressure vessel on a wheeled frame and six men who had been told only that they were moving a contaminated industrial component.

None of them had been born after 1990.

Mara watched from the observation alcove as they passed through the north service corridor, each man stopping at the yellow line painted across the floor. Pell stood at the checkpoint with the birth-date ledger open in his hands. He checked their licenses, their faces, then their faces again after asking each one to state his name, the date, and the last place he had slept.

“Thomas Weller,” said the first man. “November twenty-third, 1964. My house in Carlisle.”

“Something not on your paperwork.”

Weller looked irritated. “My left knee locks when it rains.”

Pell wrote it down.

The next man said he had once swallowed a marble at age seven and still dreamed about the taste of glass. The third had a scar under his tongue from a fishing hook. They had been selected for facts too private to be useful and too ordinary to feel like stories. DAM had spent years refining the practice of identity verification into something that sounded almost like superstition.

The corridor smelled of concrete dust and cold metal. Somewhere behind the walls, water moved through a pipe that did not appear on any facility plan.

Mara touched the bruise inside her cheek with her tongue.

At the far end, the vault door stood open.

Not wide. Only enough to admit the pressure vessel. Its inner rim showed the pale ceramic lining and the copper mesh beneath it, a thousand fine lines disappearing into shadow. The vault had no light of its own. A portable lamp shone across the threshold, and the illumination stopped there as though darkness had weight.

Dr. Vale stood beside the door in a gray containment coat. Her hands were clasped behind her back. She had removed her identification badge and pinned it beneath the coat, as if the absence of her name might make her less vulnerable to being called by another.

“Where is the relay?” Mara asked.

“Disconnected.”

“And the deck?”

“On the transfer frame. Power isolated.”

Vale glanced toward her. “You have been told to remain outside the operational corridor.”

“You’ve moved up the burial by a day.”

“I moved it up by twelve hours.”

“You moved Daniel into isolation without a review.”

“Daniel is not part of this transfer.”

“He is part of everything that happens to that tape.”

Vale’s face tightened. For a moment Mara saw not the director but a girl standing in an apple shed, trying to decide whether the window opened from inside.

Then Vale looked away.

“Get Saira,” Mara said.

“She is under administrative review.”

“Meaning?”

“Meaning she is not here.”

The crew rolled the pressure vessel forward. Its wheels squealed, then fell silent as they crossed the yellow line. The vessel was a squat cylinder of blackened steel, banded with ceramic collars. Two operators guided it while the others steadied the frame. Inside it, the cassette waited in its triple-sealed canister.

Mara had never seen the tape directly since the first day. She had seen it through a glass sleeve, through a pair of gloved hands, under the flat glare of the archive’s old television. She had seen the yellow house and the pool. She had seen Daniel recognize himself.

Now the vessel moved into the vault as if being swallowed.

A red indicator over the door blinked once.

Then again.

The third time it remained lit.

Vale turned sharply. “Stop.”

The crew stopped.

In the darkness beyond the threshold, something clicked.

It was a small mechanical sound, almost delicate. A plastic tooth engaging with another plastic tooth.

Mara felt the skin between her shoulders tighten.

“Power is isolated,” said one of the operators.

“Confirm.” Vale did not raise her voice, but the word cut through the corridor.

The operator checked the transfer frame. “Main supply is dead.”

“Deck?”

“Dead.”

“Relay?”

“Removed.”

Another click came from inside the vault.

This one was followed by the whir of a motor.

The sound rose and fell, rose and fell, like a machine trying to remember how to breathe.

Vale stepped over the threshold.

“Do not,” Mara said.

Vale kept walking.

At the back of the vault, the modified Panasonic deck sat on its cradle. No monitor was connected to it. The signal cable had been severed and capped. Its power cord lay coiled on the floor, not plugged into anything.

The cassette was already turning.

The machine’s display remained black. No counter moved. Yet the reels rotated with a soft, relentless rasp, and from the intercom grille above the door came a burst of static.

Every person in the corridor froze.

The static sharpened.

For an instant it sounded like rain against a window.

Then a child laughed.

Not loudly. The laugh had the uncertain brightness of someone trying not to be heard.

One of the burial workers made the sign of the cross.

“Kill it,” Vale ordered.

The operator nearest the wall struck the emergency disconnect. The facility lights went out.

Darkness filled the corridor.

The intercom continued.

There was a splash. A rush of water. The hollow slap of bare feet on a hard floor.

Mara heard a woman calling from a great distance.

“Come inside.”

The voice was neither Elena’s nor her mother’s. It was too warm for either of them. It belonged to the kind of mother assembled by a child who had never been certain she would return.

Someone began to cry.

Emergency lights snapped on in red strips along the floor. They did not illuminate the corridor so much as divide it into islands. The walls seemed farther apart than they had been. The ceiling receded into a dim blue summer sky.

Mara blinked.

The paper mill was still there: poured concrete, conduit, fire doors, numbered junctions. But on the wall opposite her, where a drainage diagram had been bolted, she saw yellow siding.

A blue plastic pool shone beyond the corridor.

A woman in a red bathing suit sat on its edge, her back turned. She lifted one hand and waved.

Mara bit down hard.

The yellow siding became concrete again.

A man beside her gasped.

“Dad?”

He was one of the technicians from the transfer detail, a broad-shouldered man with silver hair and a birth date marked 1970. He stared at the sealed maintenance hatch as if someone were standing behind it.

“Dad,” he whispered. “You said you’d wait.”

Vale seized his arm. “Weller. Look at me.”

He turned toward her, bewildered. “Why are you here?”

“State your name.”

“You’re late.”

“State your name.”

“You told me not to tell Mom.”

The intercom crackled. Water ran beneath the static.

At the far end of the corridor, a door opened by itself.

Behind it was a church basement.

Mara knew it was a church basement because the air carried wax, damp carpet, and the stale sweetness of punch. Folding tables stood beneath paper decorations. A row of children sat along the wall, all facing away. One turned its head.

The child had no face.

Mara looked down.

The red emergency lights reflected on the floor, not water, not anything else. The door had not opened. It was a fire door with a magnetic latch.

But three younger staff members were already walking toward it.

“Stop,” Mara shouted.

They did not hear her.

One of them, a woman from Records named Jessa Harlan, called over her shoulder, “My brother’s in there.”

“You don’t have a brother.”

The words came out before Mara could stop them.

Jessa looked back.

Her expression changed from hope to fury so quickly it seemed to pass through several years at once. “Don’t say that.”

A man beside her, Minh Dao, reached for her hand. “Jessa, it’s me.”

“No.” She pulled away. “You’re not supposed to be here.”

“You know me.”

“I know him.”

She pointed toward the open door.

The faceless child had moved closer. Mara could see the dark shape of its small shoes beneath the table.

Vale shouted for security. No one responded.

The facility alarm began to sound, but instead of its usual alternating tone it played three notes of an incomplete birthday song. The melody stopped before the final phrase. Then it began again.

Every red light went dark.

The corridor became summer.

Mara stood in a suburban hallway with faded carpet under her boots. Family photographs lined the walls. She recognized none of the faces, yet the place had the intimate authority of a home she had entered every day. A staircase rose before her. At its top, a door stood ajar.

Water dripped on the other side.

“Ms. Venn.”

She turned.

Pell was standing where the checkpoint should have been. He held a flashlight, but its beam fell on a child’s bicycle leaning against the wall.

“Mara,” he said. “We need to get the kids out.”

“I’m Mara Venn.”

His eyes filled with relief. “Yes. You’re their aunt.”

“I’m born in 1988.”

“You’ve got the car keys?”

“Pell. Guard Pell. Born in 1968.”

He stared at her. The hallway around them shifted. The photographs changed, one after another. In each, Mara stood beside a different child: a boy with wet hair, a girl holding a red cup, two indistinct figures in front of a yellow house.

Pell raised the flashlight toward them.

“Don’t,” Mara said.

The beam struck the wall. The photographs became blank rectangles.

A metal door slammed somewhere behind them.

The facility returned in pieces.

Mara was crouched beside the transfer frame. The pressure vessel stood at an angle, one wheel lifted off the floor. Two crewmen wrestled with it, shouting at each other. One called the other by a name he did not have.

“You left me at the lake,” he said.

“I never saw you before today.”

“You promised.”

“I don’t know you.”

The second man struck him.

Vale pushed between them. “Everyone sit down. Hands visible. State your names.”

Her voice had the force of command, but the corridor had lost its agreement about what command meant.

A young technician ran past Mara, laughing. He wore a blue shirt and no shoes. He stopped at the security door and pounded on it.

“Mom! Mom, I’m home!”

The door’s small wired-glass window showed a kitchen beyond it. Yellow linoleum. A refrigerator crowded with alphabet magnets. A woman’s hand reached toward the lock.

The technician pressed both palms to the glass.

Mara saw water blooming beneath his fingers.

“Open it,” he said. “She’ll be angry if I’m late.”

Mara grabbed his shoulder and pulled him back.

He spun on her. “You’re Lily.”

His face was a stranger’s, but the accusation was Daniel’s.

“No.”

“You’re supposed to be my sister.”

“No. My name is Mara Venn. I was born in 1988. I work in the archive.”

He stared at her, breathing hard.

The kitchen vanished from the glass.

For one second, he seemed to return. Then his face collapsed with grief.

“You know where she is,” he said.

The intercom filled with distant voices.

Not one voice. Many.

Some called children to supper. Some pleaded from behind doors. Some laughed at the edge of hearing. Beneath them all ran the sound of pool water sloshing against plastic.

Vale reached the intercom panel and tore off its cover.

The wires behind it were dry, intact, and dead.

“Cut the building circuit,” she ordered.

A pre-cutoff electrician hurried to the control cabinet. He opened it, stared inside, and recoiled.

“What?” Vale demanded.

He pointed.

The cabinet was full of damp sand.

A child’s handprint appeared on the metal door.

Five narrow fingers. A smear beneath the palm.

Then another print appeared beside it, as though a second hand had pressed from the inside.

The electrician fled.

The alarm ceased.

In the silence, the knocks began.

Three.

A pause.

Two.

They came from the vault door.

Mara turned toward it.

The pressure vessel was gone.

No one had moved it. The crew had not lifted it, and the wheels had left no marks in the dust. Yet the black cylinder now rested inside the vault beneath the dead deck. Its seals gleamed wetly.

The vault door had closed halfway.

Vale stood before it, one hand on the emergency wheel.

“Everyone out,” she said.

No one moved.

At the left-hand corridor, Jessa Harlan was sitting beneath a nonexistent apple tree. Minh knelt beside her, trying to convince her that he was not her older brother. The technician in the blue shirt had curled beneath the security desk, whispering to his mother. Two burial workers held each other by the wrists, each insisting the other had drowned.

A guard born in 1975 pointed his weapon at a shadow in the stairwell.

“Put that down,” Vale said.

“He’s there.”

“Put it down.”

“My son is there.”

“You do not have a son.”

The guard’s expression hardened. “You don’t get to decide that.”

The sentence entered the corridor like a new piece of architecture.

Mara felt it settle inside her.

You don’t get to decide that.

The younger staff had begun to see one another differently. A records clerk called Pell “Uncle Ray.” Pell recoiled from her, saying he had buried her in 1984. A nurse backed away from Vale, crying that she was looking at the woman who had stolen her sister. Vale demanded her identity, but the nurse answered with a name no one recognized.

The names spread.

They crossed from person to person, fastening to whoever stood nearest. A technician became a dead teacher. A guard became a lost friend. Harlan looked at Mara and said, “You were there when we found the basement.”

Mara did not answer.

She could feel the story searching for an entry point.

The red bathing suit. The blue pool. The chipped tooth.

The child behind the window.

Daniel.

Mara turned toward the medical wing.

The corridor there had changed most violently. Its steel walls opened onto a long hallway lined with bedroom doors. Each door bore a handwritten name. Some were familiar: Lily. Ruth. Miri. Peter. June. Others were crossed out and rewritten until the ink formed black knots.

At the end of the hallway, someone was singing.

The lullaby Daniel had heard through his wall.

Mara stepped forward.

Vale caught her wrist. “You cannot go in there.”

“Daniel is in Isolation Two.”

“Isolation is sealed.”

“Then open it.”

“Absolutely not.”

Behind Vale, the vault emitted a low mechanical hum. The cassette was still playing, though there was no signal, no power, no plausible way for sound to cross the distance between the deck and the intercom. Static breathed through the walls.

A child laughed again.

This time Mara recognized the voice.

“Lily?”

Vale’s grip tightened. “Do not name it.”

Mara looked down at her hand. Vale’s fingers were wet.

For an instant, Mara saw a yellow ribbon tied around a dark-haired girl’s wrist. The girl stood behind Vale, half-hidden, one knee scarred, her face turned away.

Mara shut her eyes.

“I am Mara Venn,” she said. “Born in 1988. Archivist. My father was Elias Venn. I am not a sister. I am not a rescuer.”

When she opened them, the girl was gone.

Vale was staring at her as if she had just spoken in another language.

From the medical wing came a heavy impact, then another.

Someone was striking a door.

“Daniel,” Mara said.

Vale moved toward the sound.

The staff followed her, not because they understood the order but because they understood the direction. They poured into the corridor with their altered faces and borrowed loyalties, carrying flashlights, keys, clipboards, and weapons that no longer belonged to the world they had entered.

Behind them, the vault door opened another inch.

The intercom whispered the sound of running water.

Mara looked back once.

Inside the dark vault, something small pressed its palm against the ceramic wall.

Then the facility lights came on, and every corridor showed a different childhood.
