### Lily’s Name

Daniel woke with the taste of pennies in his mouth.

For several seconds he did not know where he was. The ceiling was white ceramic, divided by narrow seams. No pipes showed. No light fixture had a shape he could later remember. The room had been designed to offer nothing that might become a doorway, a window, or a face.

A yellow towel lay folded on the chair.

He stared at it until it became a strip of kitchen linoleum, then a summer dress, then the corner of a blanket tucked beneath a child’s chin.

“Don’t,” he said.

The towel remained a towel.

Mara sat beside the bed with her back against the wall. She had not slept. Her hair was pinned with a pencil, and her hands were gray with graphite though she had not been writing. She held the pencil like a tool for keeping a door shut.

“Water?” she asked.

He looked at the empty plastic cup on the table.

“No.”

“You’ve been asleep six hours.”

“I wasn’t asleep.”

“Then you were unconscious.”

He turned toward her. “That’s not better.”

“No.”

The honesty of it made him smile, but the smile vanished. Somewhere beneath the floor, the knocking continued. Three times, a pause, then two. Sometimes it sounded like knuckles. Sometimes like a child tapping the side of a pool.

“Did you answer?” he asked.

“No.”

“Did anyone?”

“Not that I know of.”

He flexed his bandaged left hand. Pain moved beneath the gauze, clean and local. He was grateful for it. Pain belonged to the body that had sustained it. It did not require a house, a mother, a summer, or a sister.

“Tell me something true,” he said.

Mara looked at him. “About you?”

“About me.”

“You’re Daniel Mateo Reyes. Born October seventeenth, nineteen ninety-four. You grew up at 114 Bergen Street in Newark. Your mother’s name is Elena Reyes.”

He waited.

“You attended Lincoln Elementary. Mrs. Pritchard taught you in fourth grade. You hated the cafeteria’s baked ziti. You broke your right wrist falling off a bike at thirteen.”

“Lily was there.”

Mara did not ask who Lily was.

“She wasn’t,” he said. “I know. I’m not asking you to say she was.”

“She wasn’t at the hospital.”

“No. She was in the waiting room.”

“There was a waiting room,” Mara said carefully. “The other part is not verified.”

Daniel nodded. That was the narrow path: names, dates, addresses, places that had remained places. He could walk it, but it was not a home.

“What else?” he asked.

“Your mother took you to the hospital. She cried because she thought she had let you ride too far from home. The vending machine stole your quarters.”

“Those are mine.”

“Yes.”

“Lily sitting beside me and calling the vending machine a criminal—that’s hers.”

Mara leaned forward. “What does that mean?”

“It means she was the person I needed there.”

“You never told me you felt alone.”

“I didn’t tell myself.”

It was easier to speak in the facility. Everywhere else, loneliness had been a private failure, something he should have outgrown. His mother had worked double shifts at the laundry on Springfield Avenue. She came home smelling of bleach and hot metal, carried groceries in one arm, and helped him with homework while standing up. When he was twelve, she slept through his birthday because she had worked until three in the morning.

He had never called that abandonment. He had called it proof that he was ungrateful.

The Elena in the yellow-house memories had time. She had laughed beside the blue pool, watched both children run through the sprinkler, and called them in before the storm. The real Elena had done what she could with the hours left over from surviving.

“I was embarrassed,” Daniel said.

“About what?”

“Needing her. Wanting her to sit with me. Wanting someone to ask how school was and wait for the answer.” He looked toward the blank wall. “If she asked, I said fine. If she offered to help, I said I had it. Then I went to my room and pretended I’d chosen to be alone.”

“Lily didn’t do that.”

“Because she was made from the part of me that didn’t know how.”

The sentence sounded too neat, but the feeling beneath it was not. He remembered being fourteen in the Bergen Street apartment, rain ticking against the air conditioner. He had wanted to tell his mother he was afraid he would become nobody. Instead he put on headphones without music and stared at the ceiling until she went to bed.

Lily had been there.

Not literally. Never literally.

She had been the imagined person on the other side of the room who would have understood without requiring him to confess.

Mara said, “Is she a symbol?”

He disliked the word. It put her in a case with a label beneath it.

“She’s not just a symbol.”

“What is she, then?”

Daniel thought of Lily as she had first appeared on the tape: smaller than him, one shoe untied, running through wet grass. He had recognized her before he knew her name. The recognition had been the force of a door opening inward.

“She’s my sister.”

Mara’s expression tightened.

“Not in the way you mean,” he said. “Not someone born to Elena. Not someone I can find in a record or a photograph that stays the same when I leave the room. But that’s what she became to me.”

“Why keep calling her that?”

“Because that’s what she is.”

“To you.”

“Yes.”

Mara’s fingers closed around the pencil. “If we record that as an identity claim, people may hear it as confirmation.”

“Then record it correctly.”

“How?”

“Say Lily didn’t exist as a historical person. Say I know that. Then say I love her anyway.”

Mara looked at him for a long time.

“Love is not evidence,” she said.

“I didn’t say it was.”

“People hear everything as evidence when they want to.”

“Then don’t make me choose between evidence and love.”

The room seemed to contract around them. Its walls had been made to prevent stories from gaining purchase, but stories required very little: a cup, a towel, a name, someone willing to listen.

“That’s what it feels like,” Daniel said. “Every time you ask whether she’s real, you’re asking whether I’m safe. If I say no, you look relieved. If I say I miss her, you look afraid.”

“I am afraid.”

“I know.”

“If I tell you that you can love someone who never existed, I might be helping the anomaly.”

“If you tell me I can’t, you’re helping it too.”

“How?”

“Because then it defines the choice. It says I have to give her up to prove I belong here. Lily or my mother. The yellow house or Newark. Memory or fact.” He sat up slowly. The room remained a room. “It wants one of them dead.”

Mara’s breathing changed.

“The thing that wants me to believe,” he said. “That’s different from Lily.”

“Are you sure?”

“No.”

The answer seemed to matter more than certainty.

He remembered the controlled projection: the Newark apartment becoming the yellow kitchen, the worn armchair becoming a blue pool. Lily standing beside the table, her hand extended. The invitation had not merely been to follow her. It had been to stop struggling. In the house, his mother would have had time. His childhood would have a shape. His loneliness would become proof that another child had shared it.

He had wanted to go.

He still wanted to go.

“I don’t believe she’s real,” he said. “But I don’t want that to mean I stop loving her.”

Mara nodded once, as if accepting a statement in a language she had not known she spoke.

Daniel lay back. “My mother’s face is getting harder to hold.”

“I know.”

“I can remember facts about her. The mole near her left eyebrow. Her keys in the lock. The sound of her shoes in the hallway. But sometimes I see her and feel nothing.” He covered his eyes with his good hand. “Then I see Lily and feel everything. That isn’t fair.”

“No.”

“I don’t want to punish Elena for being tired.”

“You aren’t choosing this.”

“It feels like choosing.”

Mara reached toward him, stopped, and rested her hand on the blanket near his wrist.

“My father had a daughter named Ruth,” she said.

Daniel lowered his hand.

“Not really,” Mara continued. “Eventually he knew she wasn’t real. But he remembered being her father. Taking care of her. Being the person he might have been if he’d been sober, attentive, and less afraid. The tape gave him a childhood in which he protected children, then gave him a daughter to mourn.”

“Did he love her?”

“I think he loved what she allowed him to see.”

“That’s not the same thing?”

“I used to think so.”

“And now?”

Mara’s eyes shone. “Now I think the difference matters, but it doesn’t cancel the feeling.”

Daniel considered this. “Did you call her Ruth?”

“Yes.”

“Do you still?”

“Sometimes.”

“Does that mean you believe she existed?”

“No.”

“Then why keep the name?”

“Refusing to say it didn’t make the wanting disappear.”

Three knocks sounded through the wall.

Daniel held his breath.

Pause.

Two knocks.

Neither moved.

The pattern had become familiar enough to feel intimate. That was the danger. A repeated sound began to resemble a promise.

“Lily used to knock like that,” he said.

“On what?”

“The basement window. When she was locked out.”

“Who locked her out?”

“I don’t know.” He listened to the silence. “Maybe me.”

The answer seemed to come from deeper than the yellow house. He saw himself at eight, twelve, fourteen, each version standing before a closed door. Sometimes Lily was on the other side. Sometimes he was. Sometimes there was no one, only the rule that somebody had to wait.

“Maybe she was the part of me I kept outside,” he said.

Mara did not write it down.

“Good,” he said. “Don’t.”

“I’m listening.”

The knocking did not come again.

Daniel thought of the actual apartment: the radiator clanging in winter, the narrow hallway where his mother hung laundry because the basement machines were always broken, the cracked photograph of himself at six beside Elena in a coat too large for her. He had hated the picture because he believed it proved he was a burden.

Now he could see it without the yellow house covering it.

His mother was not smiling, but one hand rested on his shoulder.

He remembered the pressure.

He remembered pretending not to lean into her.

“I want to call her,” he said.

Mara’s face became guarded. “We don’t know if she’s safe to contact.”

“She’s my mother.”

“We don’t know what the exposure has done to her.”

“She asked me if Lily was still there.”

“I know.”

“She knows something.”

“Or the anomaly used something she said.”

“If I tell her Lily isn’t real, she’ll think I’m rejecting her.”

“Maybe she’ll understand.”

“Maybe she’ll think I’m sick.”

“You’ve been injured by this,” Mara said. “You didn’t cause it.”

“I know what you meant.”

“No. You know what I intended. That isn’t the same.”

The distinction was so careful it nearly broke him.

“I want to tell her about Lily,” he said. “Not because I think Lily lived in that house. Because she’s part of what happened to me.”

“That may expose her further.”

“Then help me say it without making it a fact.”

Mara said nothing.

“Tell her I remember having a sister. Tell her I know I didn’t. Tell her I’m sorry I was lonely when she was doing everything she could. Tell her I love the sister I remember, and I love my mother who was there.”

His voice shook on the last sentence.

The room offered no comfort. No pool water, no lullaby, no red bathing suit moving through sunlight. Only ceramic walls, the bandage, and Mara’s hand resting on the blanket.

He had spent weeks trying to determine which childhood belonged to him. The question had made him feel as if he stood before two locked doors, required to choose one and burn the other. But the apartment had not vanished because the yellow house existed in his mind. Elena had not become less tired because another version of her laughed beside a pool. His loneliness was not fraudulent because Lily had been invented to answer it.

The childhood he wanted was not the childhood he lived.

Both facts could hurt.

Mara said, “What will you call her?”

Daniel looked at the closed door.

“Lily.”

“Not your sister?”

“She is my sister.”

Mara waited.

“She’s the sister I remember,” he said. “That’s different from saying she was there.”

“And if someone asks whether you believe in her?”

“I’ll say no.”

“And if they ask whether you love her?”

He thought of the yellow house, the wet grass, the chipped tooth, the hand held out to him. He thought of Elena asleep at the kitchen table with one shoe still on. He thought of himself at fourteen, wearing silent headphones, waiting for someone to notice.

“Yes,” he said. “I’ll say yes.”

Mara nodded.

For the first time since waking, Daniel felt the room tilt—not toward the house, but away from it. The yellow towel remained folded on the chair. His mother’s name remained Elena Reyes. Lily remained where she had always been: not behind a door, not beneath the floor, not in a photograph, but in the shape of the life he had needed and had not known how to ask for.

He closed his eyes.

“Stay,” he said.

“I’m here.”

“Not Lily.”

“I know.”

“Not my mother.”

“I know.”

“Just stay as yourself.”

Mara’s hand tightened slightly on the blanket.

“I’ll try,” she said.

It was not a promise the house could keep for them. It was smaller than a promise, and therefore safer.

Daniel breathed in. The air smelled faintly of wet wool and rain, but beneath it—beneath the facility, the lake, the basement, the impossible summer—he found the remembered scent of bleach and hot metal.

His mother coming home.

He held it carefully.

Then he held Lily too.

## AM-97-441 — Updated Story-So-Far Summary

### Anomaly and Provenance

AM-97-441 is a dusty VHS labeled **HOME MOVIE—SUMMER ’97** (inventory **M-97-4B**) with contradictory provenance involving the Voss house, Miller Road, churches, thrift shops, schools, the Mercer County historical annex, federal warehouses, Palinode Behavioral Systems, and DAM custody. It resists destruction and can produce sound, imagery, and narrative effects without power or playback. Manifestations propagate through walls, floors, photographs, testimony, dreams, screens, sealed objects, smells, writing, and other narrative surfaces.

It primarily affects people born on or after **1 January 1991**, though pre-cutoff individuals can be contaminated through derivatives, testimony, inference, emotional proximity, and affected subjects. It implants vivid, internally coherent false autobiographies without necessarily erasing factual memories; factual memories may remain accessible but emotionally hollow. Narratives center on absences and duties—siblings, children, caregivers, homes, grief, promises, and failed rescues—rather than one fixed history.

The anomaly assembles emotionally significant fragments from multiple subjects and sources. Historical claims may be false while emotional attachments remain genuine. Recurring motifs include yellow houses or objects, red clothing, blue pools, storms, basements and attics, sheds, children behind glass or doors, wet handprints, running water, child laughter, incomplete birthday music, and **three knocks, pause, two knocks**. Many narratives contain someone waiting in an impossible place, making departure feel like betrayal.

### Palinode Behavioral Systems and Calibration Reel 4-B

Palinode operated from a decommissioned WPKR-TV station outside Mercer, Pennsylvania, from 1992 until its destruction by fire in 1998. Its “shared affective frameworks” sought **“consensus childhoods”** that produced belonging, obedience, adult protection, and distrust of outsiders. Motto: **WHAT WE SHARE, WE OBEY.**

Domestic VHS experiments used incomplete motifs—yellow blocks, red clothing, hands against glass, children’s shoes, pools, rain, storms, sheds, basements, dog barks, and unfinished songs—to make viewers generate missing family relations:

> **ABSENCE → ATTACHMENT → DUTY → IDENTITY**

Drug trials including M-6 blurred memory, dream, and emotional expectation. Subjects invented relatives, relabeled photographs, abandoned real relationships, attempted to retrieve unrelated children, or became violent when constructed duties were challenged. Palinode concluded:

> **NOSTALGIA IS MORE PERSUASIVE WHEN IT IS ALLOWED TO DISAGREE WITH ITSELF.**

A 14 July 1997 manifest records 240 consumer units intended for “environmental distribution” through homes, video stores, churches, and civic programs. Most remain unaccounted for. The SUMMER ARCHIVE survived the 1998 fire; recovered material may include calibration reel 4B. Subject T-04’s exposure to reel 4B precipitated the fire and involved shifting identities, a dead child, rescue, guilt, and failed return.

Calibration reel 4-B, dated **08/19/97**, presents Palinode researchers explaining that incomplete emotional architecture makes viewers generate missing relations, while contradictions increase perceived accuracy. Palinode sought political “consensus childhoods,” but subjects instead formed private, mutable families. The researchers concluded that the anomaly establishes **“appetite,”** not obedience: an urge to retrieve or preserve what is missing. They warned that restoring, copying, or comparing reels could produce confidence and doctrine. The reel ends by asking what the viewer has been made willing to surrender.

It shows an attic containing tapes labeled by seasons and years, including **SUMMER ’97** and **NO ONE WATCHING**, plus a wet-footed child beneath the attic window. Its status as authentic Palinode footage, anomalous reconstruction, or lure remains unknown.

### Principal Subjects

#### Daniel Reyes

Daniel, born **17 October 1994**, directly viewed the tape and developed an alternate childhood at a yellow-sided house on Miller Road. Its family included sister **Lily**, an alternate mother in a red bathing suit, a possible father, dog Pickle, a blue pool, yellow kitchen linoleum, a basement window, and storms. He retains factual identity—Daniel Mateo Reyes, Newark-born, mother Elena Reyes, 114 Bergen Street, Lincoln Elementary, Mrs. Pritchard, friend Marcus Bell, and Marcus’s plastic compass—but real memories can feel emotionally hollow.

Elena initially denied Lily but later asked **“Is she still there?”**, warned **“Don’t bring her home,”** addressed Mara by name, and stopped responding. She may now refer to Lily during calls with Daniel, suggesting either contamination or anomalous use of genuine family material.

During the vault crisis, Mara extracted Daniel from an impossible kitchen behind a purple-crayon door labeled DANIEL without entering. Lily later manifested as an older adolescent in a wet yellow shirt, combining Daniel’s narrative with genuine facts about his loneliness, Newark life, Marcus, and Elena. She called herself **“the part of you that kept waiting”** and urged Daniel to enter the yellow house. He grounded himself by separating verifiable fact, belief, and emotion. He acknowledged loving Lily because she was there and waited, while admitting he could not verify the house, Pickle, red bathing suit, or Lily’s factual existence. He called her **“the sister I remember.”** The house collapsed after he refused to enter; Lily knocked **three, pause, two**.

Daniel later recognized a projected Ruth/Lily/Miri composite as something **“wearing her,”** not Lily: **“the part that wants me to believe.”** He remains physically present with Mara and Saira, exhausted and bandaged on the left hand. He still believes Lily may be behind Isolation Two, but whether this distinction is stabilization or another implanted role remains unknown.

In controlled observations, a projection shifted from Daniel’s Newark apartment into the yellow-house kitchen and produced Lily. Daniel distinguished factual identity from emotional truth: Lily represents the person who would have understood his loneliness, and he wanted a sister. He refused Lily’s hand and refused to enter. Afterward he accused DAM of forcing him to choose and prove he deserved the real world, finally stating:

> **“My mother’s name is Elena Reyes.”**  
> **“The truth is that I miss the person I never had.”**

#### Chapter 36 — Lily’s Name

Daniel woke in a ceramic containment room with the taste of pennies in his mouth. A yellow towel briefly appeared to him as linoleum, a dress, and a blanket before stabilizing as a towel. The physical pain in his bandaged hand helped him distinguish bodily fact from narrative intrusion. The facility still smelled faintly of wet wool and rain, and the knocking continued beneath or beyond the floor.

Mara grounded him with verified facts: his name, birth date, Newark address, Elena’s identity, school, Mrs. Pritchard, and the broken wrist. Daniel recalled Lily beside him during the real hospital visit but accepted that the waiting-room Lily was not historically verified. He identified Lily as the imagined or anomalously generated person who answered his unacknowledged loneliness and need for someone to notice, understand, and stay. He rejected the term “mere symbol,” insisting that she is his sister in an emotional and identity sense, not a documented biological person.

Daniel described Elena’s real exhaustion and his shame at needing her. The yellow-house Elena possessed time and attentiveness that the real Elena, working double shifts, often could not provide. Daniel recognized that Lily represented the part of him that did not know how to ask for care. He does not want Lily’s unreality to erase his love for her, nor does he want DAM to make him choose between Lily and Elena, alternate memory and fact, or attachment and safety.

Mara disclosed that her father had a daughter named Ruth who was not historically real but whom he remembered loving and protecting. She still sometimes uses Ruth’s name without believing Ruth existed. Mara now acknowledges that the distinction between historical existence and emotional attachment matters but does not cancel the feeling.

Daniel stated that the anomaly’s coercive demand is not simply “believe Lily” but “surrender one attachment to prove loyalty to another.” He believes the anomaly wants either Lily or his mother to be treated as dead. He also suggested Lily may be **“the part of me I kept outside,”** linking her waiting to his own repeated experience of standing before closed doors.

Daniel wants to contact Elena and explain, without asserting a false history, that he remembers having a sister, knows she was not historically present, and loves both the sister he remembers and the mother who was actually there. Mara warned that contact could expose Elena further or be interpreted as confirmation. Daniel asked her to help him communicate the distinction.

He asked Mara to stay “as yourself,” not as Lily or his mother. She agreed only to try, avoiding an absolute promise. The chapter ends with Daniel holding both the remembered scent of Elena—bleach and hot metal—and his attachment to Lily without treating either as proof of the other. His current formulation is:

> Lily did not exist as a historical person; Daniel knows this.  
> Lily remains his sister and an emotionally real part of his life.  
> Love is not evidence, but its lack of evidentiary status does not make it unreal as an experience.

His attachment remains intact; he is more capable of distinguishing fact from emotional truth but increasingly grieves the life he did not have. Contact with Elena and the status of her references to Lily remain unresolved.

#### Mara Venn

Mara, born **1988**, has no confirmed direct viewing but is increasingly affected through testimony, Palinode records, Elias’s letters, family documents, and inference. She experiences near-visions of yellow halls, red cups, children behind doors, pantries, storms, and adults remaining with children. She maintains:

> **Mara Venn, born 1988, archivist, not a sister, not a rescuer.**

DAM knew of Elias’s case and concealed its connection to her, labeling her a **“generative risk.”** Mara has spontaneously supplied details of Vale’s missing sister Miriam and may possess generative ability, anomalous access, emotional assembly, or contamination. Her badge was used to access the relay annex before the vault incident, though she denied being present.

A manifestation of Ruth, accompanied by an apparent Elias, assembled details from Daniel’s Lily narrative, Owen/Miri, Vale, Palinode motifs, and Mara’s longing. Mara rejected the historical claim while stating:

> **“I remember wanting you.”**

She affirmed that she was born in 1988, her mother was Celia, Elias was ill and drank, and she had been an only child. The house collapsed. Elias said, **“Tell her I tried,”** and a damp letter contained:

> **I know she was not real.**

Mara later destabilized the composite by identifying borrowed details and asking, **“Who are you when no one is remembering you?”** She remains affected but has strengthened the distinction between longing, attachment, and historical fact.

During Chapter 36, Mara recorded or verbally supported Daniel’s distinction between Lily as an emotional identity and Lily as a historical person. She admitted that preserving Ruth’s name does not mean believing Ruth existed. Her role is shifting from fact-verifier toward witness to emotionally owned meanings, though she fears that acknowledging such meanings may help the anomaly propagate.

#### Saira Okafor

Saira saw a lake in a photograph and developed memories of a drowned boy. Her husband later dreamed the lake, stopped recognizing their apartment, and supplied the name Peter. She believes silence slows transmission but cannot heal existing subjects.

Saira opposes Vale’s indefinite neurological isolation and distinguishes factual memory from emotional truth. Her controlled-exposure protocol requires consent, pre-cutoff operators, mechanical equipment, identity checks, immediate severance at uncontrolled spread, and follow-up care. DAM’s older files prescribe sedation, isolation, identity checks, object removal, and observation but no reintegration or long-term care.

She uses grounding statements based on legal names, birth dates, current locations, and verifiable present facts, without describing or denying visions. She established a mechanically limited playback channel during the vault crisis: one source, one wall surface, no speakers or intercom. Her observations of Leah, Thomas, and Daniel produced useful distinctions but also acute grief, rage, and accusations that DAM was stealing or invalidating subjects’ only meaningful childhoods.

Saira supports continued care while refusing to treat emotional attachment as historical evidence. She records subjects’ self-defined meanings as declarations rather than symptoms or proof. Her position is that people need shared facts to live together but are not required to surrender every impossible thing they love. DAM must contain coercive and violent effects without requiring subjects to surrender impossible attachments.

#### Leah Mercer

Leah, born **14 May 1992**, appeared in the manifested waiting room, initially identified herself as “June,” and partially stabilized under Saira’s protocol. During observation she viewed a dock, water, a yellow towel, and a woman’s voice calling **“June”** and her nickname **“Lee-Lee.”** Leah identified June as her grandmother despite records indicating June died in 1987, before Leah’s birth. The image represented being noticed if she failed to return and having someone choose her.

Leah later acknowledged that June never lived, never met her, and never held her hand, while insisting June remained her grandmother and the attachment belonged to her. She wants continued controlled exposure because **“the dock is hers now,”** though renewed drowning attempts remain a risk. Her declaration records that June and the dock were not historical, but the need to be noticed, not hurried, and permitted to return is her own emotional truth.

#### Thomas Rusk / F-08

F-08, born **3 November 1991**, was previously known only by designation; his name was restored as **Thomas Rusk** during a lucid interval. He developed a tornado-and-pantry childhood involving Anne and a boy he alternately identified as his brother or himself. He attacked foster guardian Margaret Rusk after real attachment became hollow.

Controlled observation established his legal identity, Trenton birthplace, foster placement at age four, and Margaret’s role as foster guardian. The projection showed Anne protecting a boy in a pantry during a tornado. Thomas described its meaning as being chosen, kept safe, and not temporary. He acknowledged Margaret’s genuine care but accused DAM of stealing the only childhood that felt complete.

He later stated that the pantry and Anne were not historical and that Margaret did not steal him, while retaining the emotional truth of being protected:

> **“I believe I was supposed to be protected.”**

Thomas wants further exposure stopped and objects to calling the memory merely false or clinical.

#### Owen Bell

Owen, born **4 May 1993**, activated a disconnected monitor and developed an alternate childhood involving **Miri**, a dark-haired girl in an apple shed during summer 1999. Motifs include a yellow ribbon, scarred knee, green-square quilt, wet rope, wasps, a feared father, an inward-opening shed window, and an older boy with a bad knee.

He shifted among child, brother, watcher, and person behind glass. He identified Vale as Miri, told her **“You got old”** and **“Tell Miri the window opens from inside,”** and said Miri was “what I remember when I’m afraid.” He wanted her to stop being gone rather than control or replace her. He warned that the house was buried underground with its occupants inside and that burial would not stop summer emerging elsewhere.

Owen is confined in **Supervision Three**, a cornerless ceramic-lined room with no reflective surfaces, loose objects, labels, ordinary narrative materials, or ordinary plumbing. He wakes frequently and addresses an unseen Miri. His hair was cut after he wound it around his fingers and called the strands “wet rope.”

His narrative connected to Dr. Irena Vale’s childhood trauma. He identified Vale as Miri and repeated the shed instruction. Vale briefly saw a shifting girl behind the observation pane—Miriam, then a composite of affected children—before the image vanished. Owen was sedated after pounding the wall in the **three-knocks, pause, two-knocks** pattern.

Under Saira’s grounding questions, Owen identified himself, his birth date, Supervision Three, the disconnected monitor, the hand he saw, and his desire to return to where he was safe. He eventually rejected direct identity between Vale and Miri:

> **“Miri isn’t you.”**

He explained that Miri was who he became when someone stayed: a protective identity or emotional role formed in the shed narrative. Vale had been standing where Miri should be, so he called her by that name. Owen cannot determine whether Miri or the shed was real but retains the emotional truth of having felt safe and protected. He still wants to enter the shed because:

> **“Because no one leaves if they’re still waiting.”**

His physical security, location before Supervision Three, and possible role as a source or displaced narrative remain unclear.

#### Dr. Irena Vale and Miriam

Vale, born approximately **1963**, spent summers at a farmhouse with younger sister **Miriam (“Miri”)**. In 1976, at thirteen, she watched an estate-sale 16mm reel labeled **Family Picnic, 1963**, showing an impossible house, a girl in yellow, a boy behind a screen door, and a woman calling them to supper. Miri became attached to the filmed girl, disappeared for six hours, and was found near a shed containing an impossible second room with green-square wallpaper, a quilt, hanging rope, a boy’s shoe, and rising water smelling of a pool. Vale’s father drowned there; her mother survived but no longer recognized the family; Miri vanished.

Vale believes uncertainty is the breach: the moment the impossible is treated as an incomplete fact. She insists Miri is dead despite admitting she cannot know this. She authored much of DAM’s isolation doctrine, opposes controlled exposure, and accepts indefinite isolation without care as possible containment.

During the vault event she briefly regressed toward her thirteen-year-old identity when called Miri. She attempted to ignite the emergency furnace, arguing that blind destruction was preferable to continued exposure, but stopped when Saira’s mechanical shutter closed the projection channel.

Chapter 35 forced Vale to confront the possibility that her trauma and guilt had been incorporated into Owen’s Miri narrative. She saw a composite girl rather than a verifiable Miriam and acknowledged that the anomaly may have used all of them. She admitted that DAM’s removal of names, family references, and emotional attachments reduced subjects to hazards and treated grief as evidence of spread. She now recognizes that a locked door can become another invitation, though her doctrine has not formally changed.

Vale retains genuine guilt associated with being thirteen when Miriam disappeared, independent of whether the shed, film, or related history was real. She did not enter Supervision Three or answer Owen’s knocks. Her continuing role in the pressure-vessel burn remains unresolved.

### Other Exposures

- **L-12**, born 14 May 1992, developed a lake, dock, yellow towel, cabin, and grandmother June after probable photographic exposure; factual memories became emotionally flat, followed by escape attempts, violence, illness, and death.
- **E. Keller**, born 9 September 2001, developed an agricultural enclosure, unnamed children, green-marked quilt, and inward-opening window through testimony alone and attempted to breach a partition.
- Technicians **Jessa Harlan** and **Minh Dao** developed secondary narratives after Owen’s exposure and forgot meeting him. E. Keller later developed a related narrative through overheard testimony.
- Saira’s husband and other listeners demonstrate derivative spread through testimony and emotional proximity.
- Pre-cutoff personnel are no longer reliably protected. Jonah Price, born 12 June 1989, and others experienced familial insertions. Pell was called “Uncle Ray”; Thomas Weller insisted his son was in a basement; a guard claimed his father was in a manifested hospital room.
- Minh Dao, born 1990, was found beside the laundry elevator, sobbing and insisting he had been in Jonah’s third-grade class. Jonah grounded him by repeating Minh’s legal identity and birth year. His final condition is unresolved.
- At least two additional exposed technicians remain in the west corridor. Leah previously experienced a medical-wing crisis in which a linen cart became a bathtub or drowning site.

### Documentation and Emotional Ownership

After controlled observations, the observation room developed a persistent domestic odor resembling wet wool, lake mud, and a basement after rain. The room remained physically unchanged. Repeated knocking continued from beneath or beyond the facility.

Saira and Mara established a policy of recording subjects’ emotional meanings and ownership claims without certifying corresponding people, places, or events as factual. Leah accepted June’s factual impossibility while retaining June as her grandmother and the dock as emotionally hers. Thomas accepted that Anne and the pantry were not historical while retaining the meaning of being protected.

Jessa Harlan insisted she had been in Owen’s class, though records contradicted this. She accepted that Owen was not her classmate, the apple shed was not part of her childhood, and the girl and setting lacked historical verification. She nevertheless claimed the fear, waiting, and girl as emotionally hers. She demanded that the record state that she did not meet Owen before the monitor, the shed was not in her childhood, and the associated girl, fear, and waiting belonged to her emotionally. She called Owen **“waiting”** when the knocking sounded and insisted he was beneath the floor; no one investigated or answered.

The archive category remains unresolved between *patient declarations*, *emotional truths*, *retained meanings*, and *adopted memories*. Chapter 36 reinforces a crucial distinction: preserving an emotionally real attachment or name does not require treating it as historical evidence. However, documentation, naming, and even careful witnessing may themselves become derivative narrative surfaces.

### Containment Doctrine and Breach History

DAM operates from a former paper mill north of Harrisburg. The facility excludes clocks, mirrors, windows, exposed pipes, ordinary machinery, personal objects, electronics, photographs, diagrams, recording equipment, and other narrative surfaces. The vault uses ceramic panels, copper mesh, vibration damping, sealed pressure vessels, isolated power, and no cables or ducts. Vault events are not recorded.

No post-cutoff person may enter the vault zone. Pre-cutoff operators require birth-date verification, biometric continuity checks, identity statements, two living verifiers, and an undocumented personal fact. Playback traditionally requires three separated pre-cutoff operators, a modified Panasonic deck without a recording head, independent mechanical controls, and immediate manual severance.

After Breach Log 97-6, DAM prohibited discussion of visual content, naming constructed subjects, repeating narratives, asking unauthorized identity or sensory questions, and making unapproved notes. Dreams, intrusive imagery, emotional displacement, unexplained recognition, and domestic sensory effects trigger isolation. Writing materials, walls, reports, photographs, furnaces, smells, and testimony may become derivatives.

Destruction attempts through shredding and furnaces at 1,700°F and 1,900°F produced water, laughter, wet hands, yellow-house visions, and domestic effects. Burial was planned at least forty-two meters below the north service yard in a ceramic-lined concrete chamber with continuous copper mesh, independent air and drainage, and a sealed pressure vessel. Birth-date protection is demonstrably insufficient.

In Chapter 32, Vale attempted to place the wet pressure vessel in DAM’s emergency furnace for a sealed burn without playback or observation. Mara and Saira argued that prior destruction attempts may have distributed or amplified effects. Saira reported that the medical wing had become a lakeside cabin and Leah was attempting to drown herself in a bathtub that was actually a linen cart.

Saira, with pre-cutoff operators Jonah Price and Tamsin Rourke, established a mechanical relay using identity cards, separated operators, copper shutters, and a controlled wall surface. The modified Panasonic deck operated without visible tape, power, or signal cable, producing water, a dog bark, child laughter, rain, a lullaby, and a narrow yellow-and-red projection. The channel was reduced without speakers or intercom; a copper shutter now limits the source to a thin wall aperture.

The projected child’s hand prompted Vale’s recognition of Miri. The emergency furnace was not ignited. The pressure vessel and relay produced repeated knocking from the vault corridor, then farther away and beneath the floor. No one answered.

Chapter 33’s voluntary observations caused no physical breach but produced acute grief, anger, and perceived dispossession. The method showed that factual history can be distinguished from emotional truth, but may intensify subjects’ sense that DAM is forcing them to choose between reality and attachment.

Chapter 35 confirmed that containment rooms and observation barriers may themselves become narrative surfaces. Supervision Three produced an apparent observation-pane manifestation and allowed Owen’s Miri narrative to merge with Vale’s unresolved history. The shutter and sedation ended the immediate event, but the facility continued to produce unexplained water movement and knocking.

Chapter 36 indicates that even a yellow towel can become a shifting narrative trigger, while bodily pain and verified identity statements remain useful grounding tools. Daniel and Mara did not answer the recurring knocking. Their careful use of Lily’s and Ruth’s names suggests that emotional acknowledgment without factual confirmation may be a possible stabilization strategy, though its safety is unproven.

### Current Unresolved Threads

- Whether the vault event was a physical breach, anomalous transfer, narrative relocation, or movement of identities without bodies.
- How the pressure vessel entered the vault and whether the cassette remains physically present.
- Whether the deck is playing reel 4B, whether the projection comes from the cassette or another source, and what the absent signal or counter represents.
- Whether calibration reel 4-B is authentic, reconstructed, or a lure.
- Whether the anomaly has escaped into the facility, staff, burial workers, or every available narrative surface.
- Whether the pressure vessel can be destroyed, whether furnace heat would distribute its effects, and whether Vale will activate the burn.
- Whether controlled observation stabilizes subjects, merely gives them a more painful vocabulary for divided memory, or creates another breach.
- Whether Owen is physically secure in Supervision Three, displaced, trapped, or functioning as narrative material; whether he can leave the facility or the shed narrative.
- Whether Miri is a construct, Miriam’s displaced identity, Owen’s protective self-state, a composite, or a recurring fragment assembled from multiple memories.
- Whether Vale’s guilt is an independent genuine trauma, anomalously induced, or being used as a bridge into Owen’s narrative.
- Whether Lily remains confined to Isolation Two, Daniel’s attachment, the facility, or a wider narrative field.
- Whether Daniel’s recognition of the composite as “the part that wants me to believe” is genuine stabilization or a new implanted interpretation.
- Whether Daniel’s planned contact with Elena is safe, and whether Elena’s references to Lily indicate contamination, genuine recognition, or anomalous manipulation.
- Whether acknowledging Lily as Daniel’s emotionally real sister without treating her as historical evidence reduces coercion or provides the anomaly a subtler channel.
- Whether Mara’s Ruth analogy and rejection of the composite interrupted propagation or only changed its form.
- Whether Saira’s and Mara’s grounding methods stabilize subjects without reinforcing the anomaly.
- Whether Vale’s denial-and-separation doctrine is protective or intensifies attachment and identity collapse.
- Whether identity exchanges among pre-cutoff staff are temporary contamination, permanent displacement, or evidence that birth-date protection has failed.
- Whether the yellow house, church basement, farmhouse, hospital waiting room, camp, bedroom hall, paper mill, shed, and furnace chamber are separate narratives or one assembled environment.
- The meaning of the faceless child, child handprints, wet seals, damp sand, lullaby, pool sounds, voices calling Mara Lily or Ruth, and attic label **NO ONE WATCHING**.
- Whether Lily, Ruth, June, Peter, and Miri are constructs, displaced individuals, victims, or recurring fragments assembled from multiple memories.
- The fate of Miriam and the 1976 16mm film; whether it was a precursor to AM-97-441.
- The missing attic reel, recurring water, wet handprints, and question: **“Where does the summer go when no one is watching?”**
- Whether burial can still occur and whether it would contain the cassette, relocate its emotional architecture, or bury affected people and derivatives with it.
- The fate of other consumer tapes and whether Palinode’s domestic-saturation program remains active outside DAM.
- Whether Leah’s June narrative, Thomas’s Anne narrative, Daniel’s Lily narrative, and Jessa’s or Owen’s Miri narrative will persist, cross-contaminate one another, or alter the controlled relay.
- Whether documenting emotional truths creates a new derivative surface or a safer alternative to narrative denial.
- Whether the archive category—especially **retained meanings** or **adopted memories**—will stabilize subjects, confer anomalous legitimacy, or provide the anomaly with a formal channel.
- What caused the domestic smell, water beading on Thomas’s cup, impossible water movement, and persistent knocking beneath the floor, and whether these indicate a new physical or narrative breach.

chapters.name: A New Containment
chapters.content:
The first decision was not to destroy the tape.

The second was not to release it.

They made both decisions in the room where the paper mill’s original owners had once weighed pulp, beneath dead pipes and a ceiling too low for comfort. The walls were ceramic-lined. The drain had been welded shut. Even so, the room smelled of wet wool, lake mud, and a basement after rain.

Mara stood at one end of the steel table. Saira Okafor held a folder containing no photographs, descriptions, or accounts of the vault crisis—only names, dates, positions, and legal findings.

Dr. Vale sat between them in a gray burn suit, its collar open. Ash marked the skin beneath her left eye.

“Say it plainly,” Vale said.

Saira closed the folder. “The cassette remains in Department custody. It will not be transferred to any outside agency, contractor, researcher, or court.”

“Indefinitely?”

“Until safe disposition can be demonstrated.”

Vale’s expression hardened. “There is no safe disposition.”

“We know destruction attempts produce derivatives. We know burial has not occurred. We do not know whether the pressure vessel contains the original object, a substitute, or an empty container carrying a persistent effect.”

“And you intend to keep it.”

“We intend to contain it.”

“That is a distinction for lawyers.”

“It is a distinction for the people still alive.”

Mara looked at the folder. “What does public release mean?”

Vale turned toward her. “Litigation. Journalists. Committees. Private laboratories. Copies made by people who believe copies are safer than originals. Someone born in 2004 watching a degraded file on a phone and remembering a family that never existed.”

“No one is proposing public release,” Mara said.

“Not today.”

Saira placed a sheet of paper on the table. “The immediate order is drafted. No disclosure outside DAM and designated medical authorities. No transfer without joint authorization. No person born after the cutoff enters the vault zone. Affected subjects remain under protective custody until individual assessments establish that they can consent to their care.”

Vale gave a short, humorless laugh. “Protective custody.”

“You called it neurological isolation.”

“I called it what it is.”

“You proposed sealed rooms, no unapproved language, no family contact, and no names in the records.”

“To prevent spread.”

“To prevent people from speaking about themselves.”

Vale’s fingers tightened against the table. “If Daniel says Lily is real, someone may believe him.”

“If we tell Daniel he cannot say Lily’s name, he may believe we are erasing her.”

“She is not real.”

“Neither was the house,” Mara said. “The grief was.”

The room seemed to contract around the sentence.

Vale looked at her with something like pity. “You think meaning is harmless.”

“No. I think pretending it doesn’t exist is dangerous.”

“The anomaly survives in meaning.”

“It survives in coercion,” Saira said. “It makes people choose: believe this person or betray that one, accept the house or abandon the child inside it. If we demand that every subject surrender the attachment, we reproduce the same demand.”

Vale stood. “And if you let them keep it?”

“Then we teach them to distinguish it.”

“Distinguish what?”

“Fact from attachment. History from emotional truth. A person they can verify from a person they carry.”

“Consent requires a stable self.”

Saira’s voice softened. “Then we help them build one.”

For a moment, Mara thought Vale would leave. Instead, she sat again and pressed both hands flat on the table.

“Indefinite isolation is the only policy that has not failed.”

“Your policy has not been tested against care,” Mara said.

She thought of Daniel holding a yellow towel until it stopped becoming linoleum, dress, and blanket. Leah asking to keep the dock. Thomas saying he believed he was supposed to be protected. Owen calling Miri a name that had become both shelter and wound.

“Isolation has not cured anyone,” Mara said. “It has made the department the largest and most frightening object in their world.”

Saira slid the directive toward them. “The revised protocol needs signatures.”

Vale did not touch it.

“What happens to testimony?” Mara asked.

“No copies,” Saira said. “No transcripts containing imagery, sensory detail, invented names, or narrative sequence. No audio, video, or sketches.”

“Then what survives?”

“Non-descriptive records.”

“That sounds like a way of saying nothing.”

“It is a way of saying only what we can safely say.”

She pointed to a paragraph.

“Subject Daniel Reyes, born 17 October 1994, retains factual identity and autobiographical information alongside unverified autobiographical attachments. He requests that one attachment be recognized as emotionally significant without being certified as historical.”

Mara read the next line. “Subject’s declaration is preserved as a statement of ownership, not evidence.”

“Ownership?”

“His meaning belongs to him,” Saira said. “The department does not call it proof. It also does not call it nothing.”

Three dull impacts sounded beneath the floor.

Pause.

Two more.

No one moved.

Mara felt the rhythm in her teeth. She imagined a child beneath the drain, waiting for an adult to answer. She kept her eyes on the welded steel and repeated silently:

*Mara Venn. Born 1988. Archivist. This is the paper mill. The floor is concrete.*

The knocking stopped.

Vale opened her eyes. “You will regret this.”

“Probably,” Mara said.

The next morning, they moved the cassette.

It was not dramatic. No alarms sounded. The object traveled inside a pressure vessel nested within a second vessel, suspended in a padded frame. Two pre-cutoff operators pushed the cart along a ceramic track while three separate systems verified their birth dates and identities.

Mara watched from behind the inner threshold.

The vault had been altered after the crisis. Copper mesh no longer connected to the facility. Cable channels were filled with ceramic dust and resin. No duct, drain, or conduit passed directly into occupied space. The door had become two doors separated by an empty vestibule.

“Source-isolation rule,” Saira said beside her. “Nothing enters or leaves with the source unless decontaminated and examined by pre-cutoff personnel. No personal names in the vault. No unsupervised pause.”

“What counts as a pause?”

“More than five seconds without a grounding statement.”

“Because silence is dangerous?”

“Because silence gives the subject room to supply material.”

The operators positioned the pressure vessel inside the suspension locker. They did not say the cassette’s name or describe its label.

“Object present,” said the first.

“Container intact,” said the second.

“Personnel identity continuous,” said the third.

The locker closed. A ceramic plate descended over the seam. Copper shutters moved into place. The final sound was a small, decisive click.

The vessel was gone from the room.

The room did not feel empty. It felt as if something had been asked to wait.

In the medical wing, the new policy began with the subjects.

Daniel sat at a bolted table, his left hand bandaged, his right around a paper cup. Moisture had appeared beneath the cup that morning, forming a dark ring like a shoreline.

A pre-cutoff nurse read the opening statement.

“You are Daniel Mateo Reyes. You were born 17 October 1994. You are in the medical wing of the Department of Anomalous Media. You have been exposed to a cognitohazardous recording. You have the right to receive information about your condition, refuse nonessential procedures, request a support person, and define your emotional experience, provided immediate safety concerns are addressed.”

Daniel looked at Mara. “That’s new.”

“Yes,” Saira said.

“Am I allowed to say her name?”

Saira did not ask which name. “You may say the names of people you remember. We will record them without treating them as historical verification.”

Daniel’s shoulders lowered.

“I want Lily in the record,” he said.

“She will be,” Mara replied.

“As my sister.”

Mara felt pressure gather behind her eyes, the beginning of a yellow hallway. She held her voice steady. “As the person you identify as your sister, and as someone whose historical existence has not been verified.”

“That sounds like quotation marks.”

“It keeps the record from claiming what we can’t prove.”

“And if I don’t want her protected by your wording?”

“Then we record your objection too.”

He stared at the cup. “I hate that you’re making me choose the right sentence.”

“We’re trying not to make you choose between people,” Saira said.

“Feels like the same thing.”

“You’re allowed to say so.”

Daniel leaned back. “I know Lily wasn’t in the apartment. I know my mother raised me alone. I know where I went to school. I know Marcus stole my compass and gave it back with the needle stuck.”

He looked toward the blank ceramic wall.

“But when I remember Lily’s hand on my shoulder during the storm, I still feel her there.”

Saira nodded. “That feeling is yours.”

Daniel’s eyes filled. “Is that supposed to help?”

“No. It is supposed to be accurate.”

They offered him long-term care: a physician, a therapist trained in divided memory, regular contact with Elena if both consented, supervised visits with Mara, and the right to revise his declaration. No one promised erasure. No one promised that distinguishing Lily from history would make the grief smaller.

Daniel signed with his right hand. The signature wandered, then steadied.

In the adjoining wing, Leah agreed to treatment but refused the phrase “false grandmother.” Thomas requested that the pantry account be labeled neither delusion nor recovered memory. Jessa Harlan demanded a statement that she had never been Owen Bell’s classmate, though she still felt the shape of his absence beside her.

The department created a category for such statements.

Not *evidence*.

Not *symptom*.

Not *contamination narrative*.

**Retained meaning.**

Vale called it a breach surface. Others argued that official recognition might lend authority to the anomaly. Saira answered that erasing a declaration did not make it disappear; it only left the person alone with it.

Mara drafted the archive language:

*The subject reports an attachment to an unverified person, place, or event. The subject distinguishes the attachment from documented history. The attachment is emotionally significant to the subject. No factual conclusion is drawn. The subject retains rights to care, privacy, bodily safety, communication, and revision of this statement.*

Saira read it once.

“Remove ‘reported.’”

Mara did.

“Better,” Saira said. “Less clinical.”

The archive was stripped of photographs, diagrams, tape boxes, and descriptions of houses, weather, voices, songs, and impossible rooms. Names and dates could remain. Emotional claims could remain. Details that gathered into doors could not.

Mara disliked the omissions. They felt like amputations.

But when she imagined writing Lily’s chipped tooth, the yellow linoleum, the red bathing suit, she saw the details assembling themselves.

So she left them unwritten.

At the end of the week, Saira convened the remaining staff. They met in a gray conference room with no one sitting near the door. Vale had been removed from operational authority pending review.

Saira placed the revised protocol on the table.

“Containment remains our primary duty. The source is sealed. No copies, images, recordings, sketches, or descriptive reproductions will be retained. The birth-date cutoff is an access control, not a guarantee of immunity. Anyone experiencing recognition, domestic sensory displacement, familial insertion, intrusive childhood material, or patterned knocking must report it without penalty.”

A guard raised his hand. “Without penalty?”

“For reporting,” Saira said.

“What if someone exposes themselves trying to help?”

“Then we treat the exposure and address the violation afterward.”

Another guard asked, “Are we allowed to tell subjects their memories are false?”

“You may state what is documented. You may say when a person, place, or event cannot be verified. You may not use uncertainty to demand surrender of emotional experience.”

“And if that experience causes harm?”

“Intervene to prevent harm, using the least coercion necessary.”

A sound came beneath the floor.

Three knocks.

Pause.

Two.

A guard stood so quickly that his chair struck the wall.

Saira raised one hand. “No one answers.”

Mara placed both feet on the floor.

“Mara Venn,” she said.

One by one, the others followed with names, birth dates, current locations, and verifiable facts. No one described what they heard.

The knocking stopped.

That night, Mara visited Daniel before leaving. He sat on the edge of his bed. The room smelled faintly of bleach and hot metal.

“Did you sign the care agreement?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“You can change it.”

“I know.”

“Are you going to keep Ruth in your records?” he asked.

“Not as a historical person.”

“That wasn’t what I asked.”

Mara sat beside the door. “I’ll keep the fact that I remember wanting her. I’ll keep that she mattered to my father, though she wasn’t real. And I’ll keep that he hurt people while believing in her.”

Daniel considered this.

“Lily mattered to me before I knew she wasn’t real,” he said.

“I know.”

“She still matters.”

“I know.”

He nodded, testing the room. Nothing changed. The walls stayed ceramic. The bed stayed a bed.

“Will they bury it?” he asked.

“Not yet.”

“Good.”

“Why?”

“If it’s underground, I’ll still know where it is.”

Mara thought of the pressure vessel in its sealed locker, the vault behind two doors, the copper shutters waiting in their tracks.

“That’s not why it hasn’t been buried,” she said.

“I know.” He gave her a faint smile. “You’re getting better at not lying.”

“I’m trying.”

“Stay as yourself.”

The request was smaller than a promise and harder to honor.

Mara remained until he slept. In the corridor, the lights hummed. Somewhere deep in the facility, water moved through a pipe removed years ago.

She did not investigate.

In the records room, she placed Daniel’s signed declaration in its envelope and wrote the authorized heading:

**SUBJECT RETAINS MEANING WITHOUT FACTUAL CERTIFICATION.**

Beneath it, she added his name.

Daniel Mateo Reyes.

The letters looked ordinary.

That was the point.

No copy of the tape existed. No image had been preserved. No account described the yellow house, the shed, the lake, or the child beneath the floor. Yet the names of the living remained, along with their rights, attachments, refusals, and uncertainty.

In the dark beyond the walls, something knocked once.

Mara held her pen above the paper.

Then she set it down and began the next record.
